chapters.title: The Flat Note
chapters.html:
The nurse does not say hello. She holds her telephone up to the ceiling of a room Ilse has never seen and lets the line carry whatever is up there.

Ilse lies on her left side with the deaf ear buried in the pillow, the way she has slept since she was six, and presses the phone to the ear that works. What comes down the line is thin as a hair. A hum, closed-mouthed, eight notes and then the same eight again. It is not a woman. A woman wanders. These notes land in the exact middle of themselves and leave on time.

“Do you hear it?” The voice is whispering, which in a hospital at seven minutes past three is a courtesy to the dark. “I’m so sorry. I know what the hour is. Pille Rebane, night nurse, Harju Children’s, the neonatal ward. I have your number from a card.”

“Which card?”

“An old gentleman left it on Thursday with a box of kringel for the staff. Enormous hands, I could have fitted both of mine inside one. His vest was buttoned wrong, every button a hole out, and I didn’t like to say.” A trolley wheel squeaks somewhere behind her. “He sat an hour in the parents’ lounge first, looking up at the shelves like a man at a christening. Then he said, ‘If the speakers ever sing, call Ilse.’ I put the card in my apron and forgot it, because the speakers sing all the time, they have a sound pack, rain and sea and a mother’s heartbeat. But never this. At four minutes past three every one of them began the same tune, together, and I stood there in my clogs like a cow at a gate for three whole minutes before I remembered.”

Ilse is sitting up. She does not remember deciding to. “How many speakers?”

“Fourteen. I counted twice.”

“Are the babies awake?”

“Asleep, all of them, like little loaves. It’s only me that’s awake.”

“Don’t unplug anything. Don’t let anyone restart anything. I’ll be there in twenty minutes.”

“He said you’d say that,” says Pille Rebane, and the line goes back to the hum.

Ilse dresses without the lamp. In the hall she takes a green cardamom pod from the saucer by the door and puts it in her coat pocket, whole, where it joins the lint and Friday’s tram ticket. Then the laptop bag, the recorder wrapped in a sock against the cold, the stairs.

The taxi takes eleven minutes, most of them behind a plough whose amber light turns the snow the colour of weak tea. The dashboard says minus eleven. The driver’s radio promises more of the same. Ilse sits with her good ear to the window, a poor arrangement for conversation that suits her fine, and watches Tallinn go past in black and white: shuttered kiosks, a tram asleep at its terminus, snow lying along its roof like a draught excluder.

Harju Children’s Hospital is a long block of lit windows on the Pelgulinna side, with snow on every ledge as thick as icing. The neonatal ward is on the third floor behind two sets of doors and a sign asking visitors to sanitise their hands and lower their voices. Pille Rebane opens the inner door before Ilse has pressed the buzzer twice. She is round and quick and smells of chlorhexidine, with a pencil pushed through a grey-brown bun and a laugh somewhere behind her face that has been told to keep it down.

“You’re tall,” Pille says.

“Yes.”

“He didn’t say you were tall.”

“What did he say?”

“That you’d be the one who listens.” Pille watches her turn so that the right ear faces the nurse and the left side faces the door, and has the grace not to ask. “Blue covers over your boots, there. Hands to the elbow, like a surgeon.”

While Ilse scrubs, Pille fishes in her apron and comes out with a card gone soft at the corners. Tamm Incident Response, Pikk Street. On the back, in pencil, capital letters: ILSE, and a mobile number. The sevens are crossed. In all of Tallinn one man still crosses his sevens.

“Did he give a name?”

“Only yours.”

Ilse turns the card over twice and puts it in her pocket with the pod.

The ward is warm as a kitchen. It smells of milk powder and warm plastic and the sweetish rubber of oxygen tubing, and under that, now that she stands in it with her coat off and her hands raw with gel, it hums.

The hum sits in the air the way a smell does. She turns her head to find where it comes from, and the left half of the world, as always, offers her nothing. A sound with no direction is something a woman with one ear learns to live with, but she has never liked it.

“Where is it loudest?”

“Everywhere,” Pille says. “That’s what’s wrong with it.”

The corridor runs the length of the ward, with the bays opening off it like rooms in a very small, very hot hotel. In Bay One two incubators glow green, and on the shelf above each sits a knitted owl. In Bay Two, owls. In the milk kitchen, owls. In the parents’ lounge a whole parliament of them, grey and brown and one in tartan with a single button eye. Between the owls stand the speakers: smooth white stones the size of a fist, each with a thin ring of light round its foot. The rings glow the flat white of things doing nothing at all.

Ilse unwraps the recorder, sets it on the nearest shelf between two owls and presses the red button. The clock above the milk-kitchen door says 03:24.

“The Thursday knitters,” Pille says, following her look. “Seventy-one owls at the last count. They’re meant to go home with the babies, but the babies already have more owls than they can carry. I think the shelves are where the supervising gets done.”

“White means idle?”

“White is idle. When the sound pack plays, the ring breathes, slow, in and out, like it’s asleep. It isn’t breathing now.”

“Are you frightened?”

“Dear, I’ve worked nights in this place nineteen years. Dead is very quiet. This is worse.” The laugh arrives at last, enormous, far too big for the hush, and Pille claps a hand over it and turns an apology on the nearest incubator. The baby inside, no bigger than a bag of sugar, sleeps on.

In Bay Three a cot stands made up for a four o’clock admission, its sheet turned down into a neat white envelope. Ilse lays her palm flat on the steel rail. It is trembling. A thin steady thrum at the pace of the notes, like the chest of a cat that has made up its mind to purr. She has never been able to place a sound by ear. But steel carries what air only mentions.

She goes down the bay rail by rail, cot to cot, one hand out like a woman feeling for a switch in a dark room. In Bay Four the thrum thickens. Under the far shelf the rail hums so hard her teeth take notice. Above it, between a grey owl and the tartan one, sits a white stone with its ring dimly lit.

“That one,” Ilse says.

“You haven’t even looked at it.”

“I looked at the rail.”

She takes out her phone, wakes the spectrogram she has used for ten years and holds it toward the stone. A ribbon of colour starts to crawl across the screen from left to right, the way a seismograph draws. She has explained it to juries as sheet music written by the sound itself: height is pitch, a bright line is a note, and time goes by sideways. Tonight it draws a staircase, eight bright steps, then the same staircase again, and again.

Pille hums along with it, three notes, half a beat behind. “I know that one,” she says. “I know it from somewhere.”

Ilse’s own mouth has made the shape of the fourth before she shuts it.

“Watch the last step,” she says instead. “The eighth.”

For a minute and a half there is nothing: staircase, staircase, staircase. Then the last step of one staircase sags, a hair below where the others put it, like a washing line when a bird lands on it, and tightens again.

“Oh,” says Pille. “Like a hiccup.”

“Wait.”

The ward clock has a red second hand. Ilse counts from the sag. Staircase, staircase, staircase. At ninety-four it sags again, on the dot. She does not need a third but waits for one anyway, because waiting for the third is the only discipline she trusts. Ninety-four.

“Like an appointment,” she says.

“I don’t like appointments I didn’t make.” Pille’s pencil has come out of her bun and is turning in her fingers.

“Has anyone been near the speakers since the summer? A technician, anyone with a tool bag?”

“Nobody. Only Evald, and he’s IT, he’s always about.” Pille’s eyes go to the end of the corridor, where a dome of smoked glass the size of half a grapefruit watches the doors, and come back. “Nobody,” she says again, to the owl.

Ilse says nothing. She files the dome where she files the things she does not write down.

The inner doors thump. A man comes down the corridor in a puffer jacket the colour of a traffic cone, a lanyard slung on the outside of it, over pyjama trousers printed with small sailing boats. His hair has the shape of a pillow. This is Evald Olesk, head of IT, who lives six minutes away in Pelgulinna and has made it in four.

“Pille, you should have rung me first.”

“I rang the desk.”

“And the desk rang me, so.” He looks at Ilse’s laptop bag and at the blue plastic on her boots. “And this is?”

“A friend,” Pille says.

“From outside,” says Ilse. “Tamm Incident Response.”

“We have a vendor for this.” He doesn’t say which. His hands are already moving. “It’s the sound pack. Pesa pushed a firmware on Thursday, it’s cloud-driven, they’ve done it before. I had whale song in the isolation rooms for six hours in October. A scheduling bug, a time zone, somebody in Tartu pressing the wrong button. It’s the bays, the isolation rooms, high dependency, the corridor, the milk kitchen, the lounge, the staff room, and look, the babies are fine, it’s harmless, it’s a lullaby. I’ll go down to the plant room, restart the building controller, and it’s cleared in ten minutes.”

Thursday, Ilse notes, and sets it beside the card.

She counts while he talks, folding a finger under her thumb for every room he names. Four bays. Two isolation rooms. High dependency. The corridor, which has two. Milk kitchen. Lounge. Staff room. Twelve speakers, and fourteen on the shelves. He says nothing of the charting room, the glass-walled box beside the nurses’ desk where the records computer sits, and nothing of the equipment store at the far end. He talks with his whole body, a hand for every room, but whenever a sentence nears those two doors the hands go into his pockets.

“Please don’t restart anything yet,” she says.

“With respect, I don’t know you.”

“No. If the hum stops after a restart, you won’t know what stopped it. Ten minutes.”

“And if the Director asks why I let a stranger loose in the ward at half past three?”

“Tell her the nurse called a specialist.”

“The nurse did,” says Pille.

Olesk looks from one to the other, and the air goes out of the puffer jacket without the jacket moving. “Ten minutes,” he says. “I’m timing.”

Ilse goes back to Bay Four. She lifts the stone from between its owls (the tartan one topples, and she stands it on its feet) and works the cable out of its foot. The ring dies. The hum does not. It was never only this one’s. It comes from the isolation room across the corridor and from the corridor itself and from every shelf in the ward, and it does not stumble. The next staircase goes up and comes down exactly as before, and on her phone the stripes do not so much as flinch. At the ninety-fourth second the last step sags, on the dot, in somebody else’s voice.

She stands holding the dead speaker in both hands like a bird that has flown into a window.

“It isn’t being played,” she says. “If it were played, it would have a player, and I’ve just unplugged the loudest one. They’re not singing it to each other either. They’re reading it, off something, the way you read a ticker along the bottom of a screen. One symbol after another, and none of it meant for us.” Above the milk-kitchen door the red hand goes round. “And the clock is still reading.”

chapters.title: Pebbles on a Shelf
chapters.html:
At Pikk Street the floorboards still remember the spice trade. When the radiators come on at seven, the third floor smells of cinnamon and clove and something older and sweeter that Jaan says is nutmeg and Helle says is mice. By nine on Monday it smells of warm almonds as well, because Helle has laid a tray of kringel along the radiator under the window to take the chill off them, and of hot solder, because Ilse has slept one hour since the taxi.

“Three things,” says Taavi, holding up three fingers in a mustard-coloured glove. “One. It is signed. Two. It is signed correctly. Three. It is signed correctly by a key that, according to Pesa’s own documentation, does not exist.”

“Say the third one slower.”

“I can’t say it slower, it just gets worse.” He is twenty-seven and has worn gloves indoors since the day he was hired; the office has radiators, and the gloves have never been explained. He types in them with the accuracy of a man defusing a bomb. “Vendors who sign nothing, fine, that’s a Tuesday. But these people signed the whole image properly and then signed a bit that isn’t supposed to be there, and the signature checks out, and I just—” He turns to the screen. “I’m not mad at you. I’m mad at the situation.”

“Gloves off at the table, my pet,” says Helle from the radiator, without looking round. “You’re dropping wool in the kringel.” Helle Kuusk is fifty-four and keeps her orange reading glasses on a beaded chain and her opinions in the same place, in plain sight and swinging. She has run the office for eleven years and the firm’s tempers for longer. “Ilse, my little firewall, have you eaten? You haven’t eaten. Take two. They’re warm. Don’t look at me like that, you’re thinner than a ruler.”

Ilse takes one. It is soft and sweet with almond, a braided ring of yeast dough with raisins rolled into it, and she has had nothing since a fistful of dry cereal at four. “Thank you,” she says, and goes back to the bench.

On the bench, under the lamp, the Pesa Mini lies on its back with its belly open. It left Harju in a freezer bag from the milk kitchen, signed over by Pille Rebane on the back of the duty rota, and the look on Evald Olesk’s face as it went would have turned the milk. Inside, it is less than anyone expects. A speaker cone no wider than a biscuit. A ring of seven microphones round the rim, each the size of a sesame seed, which is how it hears you across a kitchen. A green board with a few black chips, and one chip the size of a lentil with eight legs: the one that holds everything the speaker knows. Taavi has a tiny crocodile clip fastened on its legs, and a wire from the clip to his laptop.

Pesa makes them in Tartu and sells them by the hundred thousand, white and smooth as river stones, because people will put a pebble on a shelf in a nursery or a boardroom and never ask what it is listening to. Ilse has never owned one. She has always found them rude, like a guest who sits down without taking off his coat.

The firmware is a long loaf, one grain all the way through. He has laid it beside the copy Pesa publishes, and the comparison runs down the screen: same, same, same, same, and then a slice, forty kilobytes wide, of a different crumb.

“Forty kilobytes is about a short story,” Taavi says. “Sitting in a part whose whole life is turning a file called rain into the sound of rain.”

“What’s in it?”

“It isn’t on the contents page. Nothing declares it. It sits between the audio code and the network code like a lodger nobody put on the lease.” He tugs the tip of one glove finger. “And the chip’s just a chip, I checked under the scope. No extra parts. No wires. Whoever did this never had to open the box. They sent it in through the front door, signed.”

On the stairs a step approaches, one long and one short, the left leg waiting for the right. Jaan Tamm’s hip announces the founder before the founder arrives.

He is sixty-seven and built like a door. His hands are enormous, a pair of shovels in cuffs; his vest is the green of old billiard cloth; and he has done it up wrong again, the second button in the first hole, so that the whole garment slopes to the left. Nobody has told him in six years. Helle says it is his way of letting people feel useful. Ilse suspects he leaves something obvious to notice, in case anyone is tempted to look for something else.

“Good morning, children,” he says to a room with nobody in it under twenty-seven. “Helle, the radiators are singing again.”

“They sing because you won’t let me call the man.”

“A radiator that sings is a radiator that cares.” He hangs his hat on the stand and takes three more strides before he reads the strip of masking tape on the freezer bag, three words in Ilse’s capitals. PESA MINI. HARJU. BAY 4.

He stops like a man who has walked into the glass door of a shop he has used for years. The colour goes out of his face from the top down until it is the colour of porridge.

Nobody else sees. Taavi is looking at his screen and Helle at the kringel. Ilse is looking at Jaan, which, in the sense this firm uses the word, is her job.

“Which audio library?” he says.

It is the only thing he asks. Not what happened, not who is hurt, not where.

“Which?” says Ilse.

“Which audio library does it link? They have two.”

“The Kõla fork,” Taavi says, still facing the screen. “The one they bought off the Tartu spin-out. Why?”

“Ah,” says Jaan. His eyes go, very briefly, to the top shelf above the filing cabinets, where a grey archive box has NIGHTJAR printed on its end in his square black capitals, the one box up there with a clean lid, and come back. “Ah. I was only wondering.”

He lowers himself into the nearest chair, left hip first, takes a kringel from the tray and does not eat it.

Taavi puts the recording on the wall screen: sixteen minutes of the ward, the ribbon from Ilse’s phone made big. At that size the notes are lines, eight lines, a staircase repeated until it hurts. Ilse asks him to zoom. At ten times, the lines have a grain.

“Is that noise?” Taavi says.

“Noise is untidy.” She puts a fingertip to the glass. Each note, along its length, moves in tiny steps: up a notch, hold, down a notch, hold, in a rhythm that does not breathe. “A cent is what you get when you take the gap between two neighbouring piano keys and slice it into a hundred. Most people can’t hear a difference of five. These are two, three. Always two or three. Always up or down.”

“Nobody’s piano is that drunk or that sober.”

“No piano did this. Something with a clock did.” She slides to the big sag, the one that comes once every ninety-four seconds, thirty cents or so, ten times the size of the little steps, and taps it. “That’s the full stop. This is the text.”

“Text of what?”

“I don’t know yet.”

Behind her Jaan, who has been looking at the screen without appearing to, says nothing. He does not ask to hear it. In all the years she has known him Ilse has never seen him not ask to hear a sound.

The clock on the wall says ten to eleven when he stands. “It is lunch.”

“It’s ten fifty,” Taavi says.

“Then it is an early lunch. Helle, take the boy to the place with the soup. I’m paying.” He lays two twenties on the bench. Helle looks at the money, then at him, and her glasses slide down her nose. In eleven years he has never paid for soup.

“Jaan, are you ill?”

“I’m hungry for other people’s lunch.”

“What about the blob?” Taavi says. “We can’t just leave a—”

“We’ll burn that bridge when we come to it.”

“Cross,” says Helle. “Cross that bridge, Jaan.”

“Both,” he says, and holds the door.

They go, Taavi’s boots and Helle’s heels clattering down the stairwell, and Jaan stands at the head of the stairs with his hand on the rail until the street door slams far below.

“Don’t put this in the tickets,” he says, without turning round.

“Helle reads every ticket.”

“I know she does.” He comes back past the benches, slowly, favouring the hip. “A ticket is a letter everybody can read, Ilse. Not this one. Not yet.”

She follows him to the glass corner that is his office. The desk is a battlefield tidied by a general: blotter, lamp, a dish with his keys in it. A brass tag stamped with the three lions of Tallinn. The stair key. Between them, a plain grey stick with no label. Tamm Incident Response is Pesa’s retained security contractor, which is why the stick lives on his ring: an emergency signing token, good for one signature on one firmware release, in case Pesa’s own signing farm ever burns down. He has carried it six years, like a spare tooth. He has never used it. When he thinks he spins the whole ring round one huge finger, a habit that has driven Helle to threaten the stair key with a file, and today it lies in its dish without a tremor.

Beside the dish the music box lies open on the blotter, a walnut box the size of a loaf of bread with a steel comb and a brass cylinder studded with pins in a loose spiral. She counts them, because she has always counted them. Seven. Where the eighth would sit, at the end of the last turn, there is a small bright bare spot.

She takes the card from her pocket and lays it on the blotter, crossed sevens up.

“You were at Harju on Thursday.”

He looks at the card for some time. “I give those out to everyone. It’s how I get customers.”

“It was a neonatal ward.”

“Babies are clients. Nobody thinks of that.” The smile arrives on his mouth and goes no further. “Sit, Ilse.”

She sits. From her bag she takes the notebook she has not opened in years, black cloth, a red thread for a marker, the paper soft as a handkerchief. His old rule: if it cannot go in a ticket, it goes on paper. From the stairwell Helle’s laugh comes up all at once, huge, bouncing off the old brick, at something Taavi has said to a man in the street, and fades. Ilse looks for a pen. She left her pens in the taxi.

Jaan takes a pencil from his vest pocket, a carpenter’s stub sharpened with a knife, and puts it in her palm and closes her fingers round it with his enormous hand.

“Paper keeps its mouth shut,” he says.

chapters.title: What the Tune Carries
chapters.html:
Ilse writes the decoder the way other people write letters of complaint: angrily at first, then in a tidier hand.

By seven on Monday evening the third floor has emptied. Helle has gone home, leaving a tin of kringel on every desk like a woman marking territory. Jaan left at half past five with his hat on crooked and a paper bag from the baker, and the last they saw of him he was standing at the foot of the stairs looking up, as though the building had said something he wanted to hear again. Taavi has not gone anywhere.

“I’m a stakeholder,” he says, and orders noodles.

The method is a guess, then another guess, then a refusal to be embarrassed by the first two. On the wall screen the sixteen minutes of the ward scroll past as a ribbon, staircase after staircase, three seconds a climb. Ilse chops the ribbon into staircases and measures each step against where a piano would put it. Nearly all of them miss by a hair, sharp or flat, by two or three cents, and she gives the two directions the names a programmer gives anything with two states. Sharp is one. Flat is zero.

The first guess is that every note carries a bit. By nine o’clock she has proved it wrong, and the decoder prints a rain of little boxes and question marks.

The noodles come at ten past: two cartons from the Vietnamese place on Viru Street, in a paper bag gone transparent with steam. Taavi eats standing at her shoulder, chopsticks in a gloved fist, reading the screen as it throws errors. When it prints a whole line of nothing but question marks he says, “Sorry,” to the monitor. “Sorry, sorry. I know. You didn’t ask for any of this.”

“It’s a screen.”

“It’s a screen with feelings.”

“Hold it still.” She chews. The second guess comes in with the broth, and she says it aloud, because that is the only way she can tell a guess from a hope. “Seven notes carry. The eighth counts.”

“Counts what?”

“The other seven. Seven bits make a letter. If there is an odd number of ones in a staircase, the eighth note leans sharp; if even, flat. A cashier counting the till twice before she shuts. When the till and the count disagree, I throw the letter out and leave a gap.”

“And then?”

“And then I find out what the letters say.”

By one in the morning the letters are right and wrong in a pattern, which is the worst kind of wrong. The first minute of the recording decodes clean, the second dirty, the third like a ransom note. Taavi, folded into the beanbag under the window with a glove over his eyes, offers from the dark that this might be a Tuesday problem. It is, as of midnight. She is too tired to laugh and too well brought up not to notice that it was funny.

At half past two she sees what the big sag is for. She had taken it for punctuation. It is a clock. The recording drifts, sixteen minutes of cheap speaker electronics and fridge compressors, so that every staircase arrives a few thousandths of a second later than her decoder expects, and by the third minute her cuts are falling between the steps. Every ninety-four seconds the sender drops one note by thirty cents and the reader knows where it is. The flat note is the one thing in the tune that carries nothing. It is there so the reader never loses its place.

She teaches the decoder to wait for it. “That,” she says to the empty room, “is why you keep the appointment.”

At ten to four the tubes in the ceiling have been humming at fifty cycles for twenty hours, and she can no longer tell which hum is hers. She walks the room and flips the switches off bank by bank until the only light is the screen. She turns the laptop so that its small speaker faces the wall, because a sound thrown at a wall comes back softer, and she wants it soft. She wants to hear it the way the ward hears it.

She sits with her right ear to the machine and her deaf side to the window, where Old Town lies under snow and nothing moves on Pikk Street but a single taxi with its lamp off. She sets the decoder to print as it plays, and starts the recording.

Sixteen minutes of the ward come out of the laptop, small and close: eight notes, eight notes. A lullaby with no baby in it. She was taught to listen at six, in a hospital, when the left side of the world was taken away and she was told to make the most of the right, and she listens now with her whole head, the way you listen for a car in a snowstorm.

For the first minute the screen gives her boxes. Then, at two minutes to four by the clock in the corner, the boxes thin out and letters stand up in them.

F. I. A space. S. A. L. M.

One letter to a staircase, so slowly that she reads each before the next arrives, like watching a stranger write on a window in frost. I. V. A. A. R. A. The tune goes round, soft and tidy and nobody’s, and under it a name is being spelled by something that does not know it is a lullaby.

FI SALMIVAARA VENLA 15.12 1840G

She knows the surname before the last A lands. FI is Finland. Venla is the first name. A birth date, day first, then a dot, then the month, the way Finns write it: the fifteenth of December, two weeks ago. A weight in grams. One thousand eight hundred and forty, not much more than two bags of sugar, a child born too soon.

And she knows Salmivaara, because a man comes with the name: short grey beard, heavy eyes, the Finnish Minister of Transport and Communications, on the evening news last week at a harbour with a drum of fibre cable the thickness of a horse behind him, telling the cameras with a tired laugh that he had not slept for a fortnight because of his new daughter. The reporters had laughed with him. Ilse had been eating toast.

The tune goes round. A second line has already begun to spell itself under the first. She does not read it. She puts out a hand and finds it lying flat on the desk, a habit she has when the floor goes.

“Taavi.”

“I wasn’t sleeping,” says the beanbag. “I was resting my eyes in bullet points.”

“Read this.”

He crosses the dark in his socks, the glove still stuck to one cheek, and reads over her shoulder. His lips move. His face does something she has seen only on people watching a lift cable go. “That’s the— That’s the minister. That’s the Transport one. Oh no. Oh no, no, no.”

“Keep reading.”

The decoder finishes its sixteen minutes and the screen holds eleven lines. Two have gaps where the cashier’s count failed. The rest are clean. Taavi reads them aloud with his gloved finger under each, like a child at school. “FI again. LV. SE. PL. DK. LT.” He sits back. “Latvia, Sweden, Poland, Denmark, Lithuania. That’s a Baltic cruise with a very strange guest list.”

He types faster in gloves than any man should be allowed. Six government websites come up one after another, and under each surname he finds it, on a cabinet page or a ministry’s staff list: a Latvian state secretary, a Swedish minister, a Polish deputy minister, a Danish minister of state, a Lithuanian vice-minister. Six countries. Six small weights in grams.

“These aren’t just babies, Ilse. These are the ministers’ babies.”

“The babies of people who sign things.”

“But why would anyone steal a weight? A birthday?”

“Nobody steals a weight for the weight.” She is looking at the surnames, lined up like a seating plan. “Where do they come from? Not from Harju. The Salmivaara child is in Helsinki.”

Taavi is already searching. “KindWard,” he says. “The Baltic Paediatric Alliance. One record for every child in every Alliance hospital, so a baby can be moved between wards and nobody has to weigh her again. Every ward keeps copies. Harju’s got everybody’s.” He reads on and goes quiet. “It’s a sealed network. It’s not supposed to touch anything.”

“It doesn’t. It has no road out, not to the internet, not even to the building it sits in. The speakers live on the other network, the one that runs the lights and the heating. Two houses, and no street between them.” She turns the page in her head. “Something inside the sealed house made a road out of sound. And it didn’t walk there. Someone put it there. Someone with hands on the machine. An insider. A mole, maybe.”

Taavi flinches. It is small, like a cat that has heard foil. “Don’t say mole.”

“It’s a word.”

“It’s a word that ends careers.” He tugs his cuffs down over his wrists.

“And then?” says Ilse.

“And then nothing. I’m thinking about noodles.”

She lets it go. She puts it in the place where she keeps things, next to the camera dome and the pockets of Evald Olesk.

“Where does it go?” she says. “After the speakers.”

Taavi is back inside the Mini before she finishes. The little speaker keeps a diary. Every time it talks to the building-management network, the one that decides whether the corridor lights are on and whether the radiator in Bay Two is warm, it writes down a line in a ring of memory nobody meant anyone to read. Address, time, size. He scrolls. Every night at twelve minutes past three it speaks to the same address, for a minute and a half, for two kilobytes. He runs the address through one registry and then another, and reads off the answer like a man reading a bad tooth from an X-ray. “Singapore. Tanjong Vault. It’s a data centre. Colocation, you rent a locker for your server, like at the swimming pool. And the name of the locker—” He leans in. “Rack 14-B.”

“A rack,” says Ilse. “One.”

“One rack in Singapore for fourteen speakers in a children’s ward in Tallinn.” He drags the scroll bar with a gloved fingertip and counts under his breath, in Estonian, then in English, loses count, and starts again. “A hundred and seventeen.”

“Nights?”

“Lines. One per night. The first one’s the fourth of September.”

The fourth of September. Through the rest of the autumn and the first snow, through every night shift Pille Rebane has worked, the ward has sung into the dark at twelve minutes past three, and nobody heard, because it was too quiet to be a sound. Until Thursday, if Evald Olesk can be believed. Until a man with crossed sevens sat in the parents’ lounge for an hour looking up at the shelves.

She opens the notebook. With the pencil Jaan gave her she writes WHY LOUD NOW? and, beneath it, THURSDAY, and does not write the next thing that comes to her.

“So we call the police,” Taavi says.

She has the pencil in one hand and the phone beside it. It is twenty to six. Outside the window nothing has changed; dawn in Tallinn in December is a rumour that arrives after nine. There is a number in Estonia for everything: a number for a lift stuck between floors, a number for a heron in a stairwell. There is no number for a song that is reading the children of six governments. The Estonian police could take a statement about a hospital ward. The data belongs to Finland, to Latvia, to four others, and it has gone to a rack in Singapore, and whoever put it there has the patience of a hundred and seventeen nights. Which police? Whose? And if the ones who ought to hear this are among the ones who already know...

“I don’t know which,” she says.

“Which what?”

“Which police.”

Taavi looks at her, and then at the surnames, and for once he says nothing at all.

She turns to a clean page and writes it in capitals, the way Jaan writes: SIX COUNTRIES. She underlines it. She underlines it again, harder, and a third time until the lead gives out, and then she goes on until the wood does, and the pencil snaps in her hand and a splinter of cedar lands on the page like a full stop.

chapters.title: The Courier
chapters.html:
The toe is the part of a sock you cannot hurry, and Marit Soini is down to the last twelve stitches of one when a man she does not care for crosses the terminal floor toward her.

She does not look up. The needles go on at the pace of her pulse, which is slow. The wool is grey and undyed, from a farm in Savo, the grey of a seal’s back. She holds the working needle between her thumb and three fingers because of the fourth: the little finger of her right hand ends at the first joint, cut clean by a mooring line off Porkkala in 2008, and it has never since got in the way of anything she meant to do.

Katajanokka terminal at half past eight on a Tuesday is a hall of grey carpet and blue light beside a harbour frozen to the breakwater. The café sells cinnamon buns the size of a baby’s head and coffee in cardboard. Finns in anoraks queue for the Tallinn ferry with the solemn faces of pilgrims, pushing empty shopping trolleys, men who intend to come home heavy with beer.

Ülo Hint sits down opposite her without being asked. He is a thin man in a good grey overcoat the exact colour of the carpet, so that he seems to have risen out of the floor, and he sets a paper cup on the table which he will not drink. His hands are pale and scrubbed. He is secretary to a Committee whose members he has never once named to her, and in eleven years he has paid her in cash, in notes with the corners softened by other hands.

“Mrs Soini.”

“Yes.”

“You had a pleasant crossing?”

“I live here.”

“Of course.” His English has every article in place, like a table laid for guests who will not come. He puts an envelope down beside the sugar bowl: cream paper, the flap taped, a signature drawn across the tape. He does not own a telephone. He says they are loquacious. It is the one opinion of his that she shares. “You will want to know the arrangement.”

“Yes.”

“A matter has arisen. An instrument, which our—which was never intended to be heard, has been heard.” He turns the cup a quarter turn on its ring of damp. “In a children’s hospital in Tallinn, by a nurse, in the first instance. By a small firm of responders, in the second. It lives in domestic speakers. Of the Pesa make. You will have seen them.”

Marit looks up. Above the café counter hangs a banner as long as a bus, a white stone on a field of blue. PESA. Under it, in smaller letters: OFFICIAL SOUND PARTNER, GULF CABLE ACCORD SUMMIT, HELSINKI, and a date seven days away. A stone that listens. She looks down again and turns the needle.

“Heard,” she says.

“In a manner of speaking.”

“What does it do?”

“It carries.” He says it as though it were a figure of speech. “The Committee would like to know who carries it. Who built the means of reading it, and who holds that now. A decoder, if you prefer. It would be convenient if the decoder came to the Committee and not to a newspaper. And it would be convenient if what remains were closed.”

“What remains.”

“Ends. Loose ones.”

She has been told to close things for eleven years of Tuesdays. A person can close a door, an account, a mouth. Hint has never once said which. She slits the tape with her thumbnail. Inside is a stiff white card with three lines in a clerk’s upright hand: Kantor, Ilse, of Tamm Incident Response, Pikk Street, Tallinn. Tamm, Jaan, the same. And the night nurse of the neonatal ward at Harju, name to follow.

“The old man.” She touches the second line with the bitten end of a needle. “Why him?”

“He called at the ward on Thursday. The camera has him.” Hint straightens the cup. “He was a colleague, once, of colleagues of ours. A long time ago, in a different line of work.”

“Once.”

“It is of no present concern.”

“And her.”

“Miss Kantor was summoned by the nurse. She is the one reading it.”

“Alive?”

“The Committee prefers quiet.” Hint lifts his eyes to hers, pale and attentive, with nothing in them she could take hold of. “Quiet is generally achievable by several means.”

A second envelope, thick, goes down beside the first. Half now, half on closing. Marit counts it through the paper with her thumb, the way a harbour master once taught her to count a catch without the fish knowing, and finds it right. Hint is never wrong about money. It is the only place he allows himself to be exact.

“You will begin in Tallinn?”

“Yes.”

“You will report?”

“Not yet.”

“Naturally.” He rises, and the carpet takes him back.

The ten-thirty follows the icebreaker out, a red smudge ahead in the white, and the sea closes behind them in a path of black water that scabs over before the ship has finished passing. Marit takes a window seat in the big lounge and spreads the sock on her knee. Around her the Finns settle to the business of pea soup and pancakes with jam, and the duty-free shop opens its doors like a shrine.

An old man sits across the aisle, eighty at least, in a tweed cap and a coat gone shiny at the cuffs, with a thermos the size of a fire extinguisher. He pours a cup, hesitates, and holds it across to her.

“My wife packs for six,” he says. “We are two. We are always two.”

“Kiitos.” The coffee is weak and hot and tastes of a kitchen she has never been in.

“Do you know the ice? Which side is better? For looking.”

She does not turn her head. Out past the second buoy the sea is going from black to pewter to the dull white of old teeth. “Right,” she says. “After the lighthouse. The wind has been north-east since Saturday. It piles the floes against the east side of the channel. It will be thickest there, and loud. You will hear it before you see it. Keep your coffee in your hand.”

“Thank you,” says the old man, and moves to the right-hand windows with his cap and his thermos, and does not ask how she knows. In Finland you do not ask a woman with a grey braid how she knows the ice.

Nineteen years she knew it for a living. Brash and pancake, grey ice and white, the rafted sheets that climb on one another like cattle at a gate. In February 2011, off Porkkala, a woman in a man’s camel overcoat walked out across ice that was only pretending, toward a ship that had no business being there. The ice gave up at forty metres. Marit, on the bow of the cutter with a boathook and a line, took her out of the black water by the collar, and the coat weighed as much as a second person, the wool drinking the Gulf. The woman coughed up a litre of it and said, in a voice dragged over gravel and then smoked, “Slowly. Again.”

Marit had said something quick and Finnish. So she said it again, slowly. Hold. The. Line. And the reporter held. The name came later, off a hospital whiteboard: Anneli Raud. Every December since, a postcard arrives from Tallinn with no message on it but a pencil drawing of a boathook.

Somewhere after the lighthouse the ice begins to talk, a long low scrape along the hull like a shout held in one breath. At the right-hand windows the old man flinches, then smiles at the glass. Marit goes back to the card.

Hint said our. He mended it to which, fast, the way a man steps over a crack in a pavement, but she heard the step. She turns it over as she turns a heel, a stitch at a time. A Committee that sends a courier to a children’s hospital instead of a policeman is not afraid of a thief. It is afraid of an audience. A decoder is the thing that tells an audience what a song has been saying. If the Committee wants the decoder before the newspapers do, then what the song has been saying is something it would rather not hear read aloud; and if the word on Hint’s tongue was our, then what the song carries is theirs, or was paid for by them, or was built with their blessing. Their own tool is in danger of being found out.

She does not ask why. Asking was the first habit she lost, and she has not missed it.

Down the lounge a child is shrieking with joy at the ice. The old man, his thermos between his knees, is telling his wife on the telephone that the lady was right, the ice is on the right, you would not believe it, it is like the whole sea has been broken up and put back wrong.

Tallinn comes up out of the white at half past one, a toy town of copper spires and tiled roofs under a low orange sun that will be gone by three. The terminal is a long glass shed. At the cabin sales desk, a clerk with hennaed hair and a name badge that says KERLI looks at Marit’s grey braid, her old waxed coat and her bag of wool, and decides she is somebody’s aunt.

“Seven nights,” Marit says. “The twenty-three hundred to Helsinki. Back each morning. Cabin 7118.”

“An inside cabin? There are nicer ones. With a window. For a bit more.”

“This one.”

“It’s by the stairs,” Kerli warns. “You’ll hear people.”

“Yes.”

“Cash?”

“Cash.”

Kerli counts the notes twice and prints the confirmation on a slip of paper. A cabin on a ship that crosses the border twice a day is a post office with no postman. Behind the vent grille above the lower bunk in 7118 there is a gap the width of an envelope, and Marit has known it since a winter she does not discuss. Whatever she needs to leave, or to find, will wait there in the dark until she comes.

She sits on a bench by the terminal’s tall window, looking out at the ice and the cranes standing in it, and knits the last three rows. Then she threads the darning needle and grafts the toe shut, stitch against stitch, so that no seam is left for a foot to find. It takes eleven minutes. She does not hurry it.

When it is done she holds the sock up to the light. A grey tube with a closed end, a thing that holds a foot and asks nothing. Hint’s card is in her pocket with the names on it. A woman who cannot hear on one side, though Hint did not tell her that. An old man whose vest, the camera says, was buttoned wrong. A nurse not yet named.

She bites the wool through. She tucks the loose end into her coat at the top buttonhole, the way another woman might press wax to a letter, and the sock goes in her pocket, finished.

chapters.title: Night Shift
chapters.html:
The herring arrives at seven minutes past ten, in a jar, inside a handbag, inside a grandmother.

Pille Rebane smells it before she sees it: vinegar, onion, dill, drifting down the corridor at the hour when the ward lights go amber and the parents have been sent home to dream in grams. The grandmother is seventy-eight, in a quilted coat the colour of mustard and a headscarf knotted like a verdict, and she has got through two sets of doors and a lecture on hand gel to the incubator room, where she stands over her granddaughter’s perspex roof holding the jar up to the light as a priest holds up a chalice.

“Mrs Ilves, dear,” says Pille. “She’s on tube feeds. She has the stomach of a thimble.”

“It is for the mother. She isn’t eating. A rake in a nightdress.”

“The mother is home asleep. You sent her.”

“Then it is for the child when she wakes. For the iron.”

“For the iron.” Pille takes the jar in both hands with the gravity due to a relic. “Rein!”

Rein the porter arrives from nowhere at the speed of a wardrobe on castors. He is six foot four and patient as a hill, and in eleven years on the night desk he has removed from this ward a birthday cake with its candles lit, a live crab, a harmonium and, once, a priest. He bends and offers Mrs Ilves an elbow. “Come, Memm, the lift is warm,” he says, in the voice of a man who has done this before, and the grandmother goes, issuing instructions over her shoulder about the correct temperature of milk.

Pille puts the jar in the staff fridge, on the shelf she labelled BIOHAZARD (HERRING) years ago in anticipation of exactly this, and goes round.

She does her rounds backwards, so that she finishes with Ott. He lives in Bay Two, thirty-one days old and 1,640 grams, with a face like a walnut with a grievance, and he came off the oxygen on Friday. “Good evening, your majesty,” she tells him. “Any complaints?” Ott yawns, which is a complaint, and goes back to sleep with one fist against his cheek. In Bay Four she stops by the far shelf. A grey owl and a tartan owl sit with a clean circle of shelf between them where a white stone used to be. The tall woman took it away on Monday, in a freezer bag. Thirteen speakers now. With one fewer stone to supervise, the owls look sulky.

On her way back she passes the charting room, its glass wall lit blue by the records machine, and does what she has done every night since Monday: she doesn’t look in, and sees it anyway.

She does not like to think about September, so she thinks about it all the time, the way a tongue visits a tooth. It was a Thursday, ten past two in the morning. Evald was in Madeira with his wife and the ward was quiet as a drawer. A man in a Pesa-blue fleece rang the buzzer and held up a toolbox to the camera like a baby to be admired. A pleasant man of forty with a pleasant face, and a lanyard turned round the wrong way so that the name wouldn’t show. “Aksel,” he said. “Sound-pack calibration. I did warn Evald. Didn’t he say? Typical.” He knew her name. He knew Evald’s. He needed an hour at the records machine in the charting room, for something he called the audio endpoint, and she had been on her feet since the evening before and was thinking about toast.

She let him in. He sat in the glass box under the lights with his back to her, whistling, and at ten to three he unfolded a napkin and put fifty euros under her mug. “For the coffee fund,” he said. She said no. He said it wasn’t for her, it was for the fund, and the fund was surely a thing worth supporting, and she said all right. The kettle in the staff room is new. It has an excellent whistle, and every time it sings she hears Aksel’s pleasant voice saying typical.

Before he left he put a knitted owl on his head and said, “Put me on the Wall of Heroes.” The Wall of Heroes is in the staff room: photographs of every plumber, porter and man who ever unblocked the milk-kitchen sink. She took his picture on her telephone, and he grinned and stuck up a thumb. She never pinned it to the wall. She has not looked at it since.

At twenty to one the buzzer goes, and on the little screen at the desk a man in a soft leather jacket is holding a laminated card up to the lens like a child showing a drawing.

“Leonid,” says the speaker. “From the ministry. Facilities. I am so sorry for the hour.”

Pille would let in a lamp post that said please like that. He is not tall. Neat grey hair, black wool gloves with the fingertips cut away, and a smell of clean machine oil that reminds her, absurdly, of her grandmother’s sewing machine. His voice is low and unhurried. His hands are very clean and very still. He stands in the corridor looking at the speakers on their shelves the way a man looks at a lock.

“I am doing a small survey of the sound equipment,” he says. “For the insurers. They are particular.”

“At one in the morning?”

“The insurers do not sleep.” A small apologetic smile. “Only a few questions. In the past months, has anyone serviced the speakers? A technician, from outside the hospital?”

“No,” says Pille. “Nobody. Evald does everything. Evald’s a saint, he’s got a very small car.” Her eyes go to the dome at the end of the corridor, and to the charting room, and to the owl on the nearest shelf, and back to the dome. “We have a lot of pigeons. On the roof. Which is nothing to do with it.”

“A very small car,” Leonid agrees. “And in September, for example. In the autumn. There was no one?”

“September was chaos, dear, I couldn’t tell you. We had the measles scare, we had the, the boiler. No. No one.”

He nods, with the patience of a man listening to tumblers fall. “You have been very helpful.” He turns to go, and turns back. “You take the tram home?”

“The four.”

“A cold night for the four.”

At the door he stops on the threshold, where the floor drops by two fingers’ breadth for the trolley ramp. He is not looking at her face. He is looking at her clogs. “Mind the step,” he says.

She looks down. There is only the lip of rubber that has been there nineteen years, the one she has tripped on twice. When she looks up he is gone, and the door has sighed shut on its arm, and her knees have turned to cooked noodles. She makes tea in the kettle that cost fifty euros. It whistles at her like a witness.

At three o’clock the hum begins again.

Evald did something with the app on Monday afternoon. He told her he had turned the speakers down by two thirds, and he had; he had not turned them off. The tune comes in under the ward’s ordinary noises, under the incubator fans and the monitors and the creak of the radiator, soft as a woman humming through a wall. Thirteen throats now instead of fourteen. Pille stands in Bay Two with her hand on the cot rail, the way she saw the tall woman do, and feels it come up through the steel into her palm.

Ott’s mother cannot be here at three in the morning, and his chart says he is to have skin when possible. Pille unbuttons her tunic, lifts him out in his tiny hat and nappy, and ties him against her chest in the stretchy wrap. The recliner squeaks, and the squeak is unbearable with that hum behind it, so she lowers herself instead onto a folded duvet on the floor beneath the window, her back to the radiator, her knees up. His heartbeat comes through her breastbone fast as a bird’s. He smells of warm bread and milk.

She hums. She cannot help it: it is what you do with a baby against your chest, and she picks, God help her, the only tune in the room. Three notes. Then the next.

The nearest stone, on the shelf three metres off, wavers. It is like hearing a second singer find the key, a note sliding to meet hers. She goes sharp on purpose. It goes sharp. She goes flat, and it goes flat with her, a hair behind, like a child copying a grown woman across a kitchen. She stops. It holds her last note a moment longer than it should, then lets itself down to where it was before, a shy animal returning to its burrow.

“Oh, my dear Lord,” whispers Pille Rebane.

The laugh comes up in her, the huge one, and she smothers it in Ott’s hat, because the laugh is terror in its good coat. The thing is listening. It has been listening all along, to her shift after shift, to the cot-side secrets and the swearing at the kettle and the gallows jokes about the pathologist, and the ring on its foot has glowed the plain white of nothing at all.

Ott sleeps. Ott has heard worse.

When her hands have stopped she lays him back in his cot, tucks the owl in beside him and goes to the charting room. The machine knows her. She signs in under her own name. In the corner of the screen is a tab called Events that nobody has ever opened, and she opens it. A long grey list scrolls up, line after line of small print she half understands: Audio endpoint, active, 02:59. Audio endpoint, stopped, 03:41. The same pair again, and again, down and down until the scroll bar gives out and the list goes on without it. She holds her telephone up and photographs the screen, twice, steadying her elbow against the glass, in case anyone should ever want to know what it says.

Her thumb slips on the gallery. Back through the pictures it flies: the Christmas tree in the lounge, Rein in a paper crown, a pickled herring in a jar. Then September. A pleasant man in a Pesa-blue fleece with a knitted owl on his head, grinning, one thumb up.

She told Evald. On Monday afternoon he came round asking whether anyone had been near the charting-room machine, and she said no, and then, because she is a woman who cannot leave a silence alone, she said, only the speaker man, in September, I’ve even got a photograph, he had an owl on his head. And Evald had gone the colour of the milk-kitchen tiles and said, show it to nobody. How kind, she thought at the time. How he looks after us.

She has not told the police, because she does not know which police. She has not told the director, because the director has a pen and a way of looking at the pen. She has not told the tall woman with the one good ear, who came out of the snow with a cardamom pod in her pocket and asked about technicians in a voice that already knew. The camera in the corridor was watching when Aksel came, and she has been praying that it keeps only thirty days.

Pille takes her telephone to the window. Beyond the glass the snow comes down through the car-park lights in slow handfuls. She scrolls to the call she made at seven minutes past three on Monday, the only call of her life to a woman with half her hearing, and rests her thumb over the number. Not now. Nine o’clock, in daylight, when she is not the woman who took fifty euros and a kettle.

“Because someone should know what is on my floor,” she says to the sleeping ward, and the thirteen white stones, listening, hold their notes.

chapters.title: The Shell Rack
chapters.html:
In Singapore it is four in the afternoon and raining, and Dr Mei Lin Ong has arranged her chair so that the rain is behind her.

On the wall screen in the weighing room a window full of glass towers runs with water, lit from within like racks of servers. In front of it sits a woman of forty-one with her black hair in a clip, a grey cardigan, a lanyard worn the right way round and a glass mug of hot water with nothing in it. She has drunk hot water for as long as Ilse has known her, which is since 2022 and a stolen backup tape. Ong recovered the tape and returned it together with a spreadsheet of everything Tamm Incident Response had done wrong with the chain of custody. It was a very good spreadsheet.

The weighing room is a glass box at the end of the third floor where the spice merchants once weighed pepper against silver. The great brass scale still stands on its plinth, one pan hanging lower than the other since 1890. It is ten in the morning on Wednesday. Tuesday went in sleeping and in not putting things in tickets; Jaan left early with a bread bag held in both arms as though it were asleep, and Helle said he was off to feed the ducks. Four green cardamom pods lie in Ilse’s coat pocket now, whole. She has not cracked one.

“Ilse. Good morning. Good afternoon, from here.” Ong lifts the mug a centimetre in salute. “You wrote to me about a rack.”

“Fourteen B.”

Ong drinks some hot water. “Noted.”

Ilse has learned to hear the weather in that word. Noted on a typo is a shrug. Noted on a late invoice is a sigh. This one is a barometer falling.

“Rack 14-B is leased on a standard colocation contract,” Ong says, “by a company called Hartmann Edge Pte Ltd. Incorporated in 2023. Its registered address is a floor of post boxes in the financial district, which I am told are very fine post boxes.”

“Who pays?”

“Hartmann Edge pays. On the due date, in full, by transfer, from a bank I would describe as unfashionable.”

“Can I see what the rack does?”

“No.”

“The badge logs. Who goes in and out.”

“Not without a warrant, or the customer’s consent, or a court order I have not been served with. I run a clean building, Ilse. It is the only thing I own.” She sets down the mug. “I cannot show you logs.”

“And then?”

Ong looks at her for the length of a squall. “Unofficially,” she says, “the cooling bill for that rack is low.”

“Low.”

“A rack of that rating is billed as though it held forty servers. It draws about as much power as a kettle and rejects about as much heat. Whatever is in 14-B, it is not what the contract says. It is a bread bin with a very good address.”

“Noted,” says Ilse, and for the first time in four years Dr Ong’s mouth moves.

A third square opens on the screen. The voice comes before the picture, big and warm and out of breath. “Hello? Hello hello hello? Is this the right pitch?” Then the picture: a man of thirty-five in the passenger seat of a parked car, in a shirt of many colours, with three telephones laid along the dashboard like birds on a wire. In the back seat, framed neatly in the window behind his head, stands a white goat. The goat regards the camera.

“Dr Ong, you said ten minutes. I have given you nine and a half and a goat.”

One of the telephones shivers on the dashboard. He glances at it, then at the other two. “The bank, the regulator and the football,” he says to Ilse’s face, which has not asked. “In descending order of importance and ascending order of how often they ring.”

“Mr Abara,” says Ong. “I took the liberty of inviting a third party, Ilse. Chidi Abara is head of security at Kobo Lane, in Lagos. He lodged a complaint about my building.”

“Complaint? No, no, no, doctor. A polite request for an explanation.” He beams at Ilse with a smile that fills the screen. “Chidi. Don’t mind Referee, he’s for my uncle’s party on Saturday. Now listen. You know when you phone your bank, yes? You wait, you hear the little music. You hear it, you don’t hear it. You switch your head off, you’re a goalkeeper in the last minute of a nil-nil, you’re not thinking about the music. Then my sister rings her loan officer last week and says, Chidi, your hold music sounds like a church in a tunnel. And I say, Ngozi, it’s forty dollars of marimba from a stock library. And after that I can’t stop hearing it.”

“Ilse,” says Ilse.

“Ilse. Good. Now. Kobo Lane. Payments, Victoria Island, forty million customers, a call centre that never shuts. Every morning at two-forty Lagos time one call comes into our customer line, sits on hold for twenty-six minutes, and never says a word. Never presses a key. Never hangs up. The call centre says, a robot. I say, a scandal. Then my gateway starts getting knocked on at the same hour by addresses out of Dr Ong’s building, and I think: Chidi, that is a through ball, and you are standing in the wrong half.”

“Show me the music,” Ilse says.

Chidi holds one of the three phones to the lens. It shows a ribbon of colour with a thick bright clutter along the top, forty dollars’ worth of marimba. “My nephew’s spectrum app. Look under it.”

Under the clutter, faint as a watermark, a staircase. Eight steps, and again, and again.

Ilse pulls her own ribbon onto the screen beside it. Hers is from a ward and his from a hold line half a continent away, and they match step for step. “Watch the last one,” she says. They watch. The last step of a staircase in the corner of Chidi’s phone sags, a hair low, like a washing line when a bird lands.

“Ninety-four,” says Ilse.

“Ninety-four seconds! I counted it on my fingers. Look, I ran out of fingers.” He holds up all ten and then, ruefully, a thumb from the other hand. In the back seat the goat bleats once, with feeling.

“Noted,” says Ong, very quietly, and that is two.

Ilse gets up and goes to the whiteboard where, in other centuries, the merchants’ clerks chalked the price of pepper. She draws three dots in a row. Under the first she writes TALLINN, under the second SINGAPORE, under the third LAGOS. “A ward,” she says. “A rack. A hold line. The ward hums it. The rack receives it. And the hold line...” She draws the arrow. “Sound in Tallinn. Bits in Singapore. Sound again in Lagos. It’s one tune at both ends of one relay.”

“And at two-forty in the morning it goes out of my hold line and down a phone line,” Chidi says slowly, for once not sounding like a commentator. “To whoever dials in.”

“To whoever stays on hold for twenty-six minutes and says nothing. A call that long is not a robot.” She caps the pen. “It’s an ear.”

Nobody speaks. In the weighing room the radiator ticks. Behind Dr Ong the rain keeps falling past a thousand lit windows.

“What I have,” Ilse says, “is a hundred and seventeen nights. From the fourth of September. It carries children’s records. Weights, birth dates, names. The children of people who sign things.”

Chidi whistles, one long falling note, and stops himself, glancing at the goat as if it might have a view.

Ong’s hand has gone still on the mug. “The rack is older than your September,” she says.

“How much older?”

“Unofficially.” She is looking, not at Ilse, but at the rain. “By some time.”

“Here is what I would like,” Ilse says. “Something that doesn’t exist. Each of us tells the others what we see. Nothing in writing, nothing in a ticket, nothing in a case file.”

“Unofficially,” says Ong.

“Unofficially.”

“I’m unofficial all the time,” says Chidi. “Ask my regulator.” He grins, then, as if confessing to a priest, adds: “I should say. I found your Singapore address myself. Nobody told me. I do a little weekend scouting on other people’s pitches. For prizes.”

“Prizes,” says Ong.

“The Dutch pay in euros. It’s legal! It’s called a bounty, doctor, there’s a website.”

“Noted,” says Ong. “Unofficially.” She has not touched the pen beside her mug, nor the pad beside the pen. Ilse looks at the blank page for as long as is polite. A woman who writes nothing down is either very stupid or very careful, and Ilse has never met anyone less stupid.

On the desk at her elbow her phone lies face up beside the notebook. Before the call she opened the privacy panel and switched off every microphone permission but the recorder’s, the way she used to check the stove before leaving a flat. The list is still on the screen. As she looks, the toggle beside an entry called Sound Check slides itself from grey to green. A small green dot lights at the top of the glass.

She taps it off. It slides back. She taps it off again, and again, a game in which she is allowed no points. Without a word she lifts the phone and lays it in the pan of the great brass scale. The pan sinks. A hundred and ninety grams of something that listens.

Through the glass wall, Jaan has stopped in the corridor with a mug in his hand. He is not looking at the call. He is looking at her. Ilse tears a page from the notebook, writes WHY THURSDAY?, and holds it up to the glass. He reads it. He sets the mug on the radiator, takes a pencil from his vest and a page from Helle’s invoice pad, and writes with his big back bent like a man at confession. Then he presses the sheet flat against the glass from his side.

TONIGHT. BRING THE NIGHTJAR LAPTOP.

She knows exactly where it is: in a sleeping bag at the bottom of her wardrobe, behind the winter boots, where he told her in 2019 to keep it dry. He taps the paper twice, once for each thing she is to remember, and is gone down the corridor, favouring the hip.

“Ilse?” says Ong. “Is there something I should note?”

“A colleague.”

“Noted.” The mug goes to her mouth and comes down again.

“You want to hear it?” Chidi has seized the nearest phone. “Listen. This is my hold line, live.” He holds it to the microphone of his laptop, and out of the screen comes a tinny marimba loop, cheerful and a little sad, around and around. Ilse turns her right ear to the speaker and listens for the lullaby underneath. There is the marimba. A faint hiss. The click of the loop turning over. Ong’s mug has stopped halfway to her mouth. On the brass scale the pan holds its hundred and ninety grams, perfectly still.

“You hear that?” says Chidi.

No one answers. Ilse shakes her head, slowly.

“No? Me neither. That’s the problem.”

chapters.title: Foil
chapters.html:
The tram to Ülemiste has snow on the inside of its windows. Somebody’s breath has frozen into ferns on the glass, and Ilse sits with her deaf side against them and her good ear to the aisle, the way she has sat on every tram since she was six. A recorded woman announces each stop in Estonian, then in English, in the voice of a person who has never once been late.

The phone is in her coat pocket, against her hip. It would have been tidier to leave it in the brass pan on Pikk Street, but a phone left alone in a room listens to the room, and she would rather it listened to a tram. Nobody on a tram says anything worth stealing.

At the stop after the bus station a woman in a fur hat that has outlived several furs lowers herself into the seat beside her.

“Is it free, this place?”

“Yes.”

“Good. I am not going to talk to you.” She settles a string bag on her knees like a cat she has decided to tolerate. “My grandson gave me a pebble for the kitchen. The white one, from the television. It knows everything, he says. In the morning it says good morning. So I say good morning back, and it says nothing. Such manners.”

Ilse turns her right ear to her. The woman has a face with the weather already in it. “It’s waiting for you to ask it something.”

“I have been asking things for seventy-nine years and nobody answered. Why should a pebble?” She nods at the door, where a poster has been stuck to the glass: a white speaker like a river stone on a windowsill full of snow, and under it a line in blue capitals. KODU KUULAB. “That one. That is my pebble. The home listens. I would like to see it try.”

Ilse reads the line twice, once for the Estonian and once for what it means. Someone was paid to write that, and someone else signed it off.

Under the fold of her coat she brings the phone out just far enough to read the screen. The privacy panel is still open from the morning. She switched off every microphone permission in it at the office, again on the platform, and again at the stop, and each time the entry called Sound Check has gone back to green, patient as a dog at a door. She switches it off once more and puts the phone away. It is a game she has not yet worked out how to win.

“You have the face of someone who was told to wait,” says the woman, not looking up.

“Yes.”

“Don’t. Nobody ever comes.” When Ilse stands at Ülemiste, the woman adds, to the window, “If it answers you, say good morning from Linda.”

The block on Peterburi tee is eleven storeys of grey panels, with a plane going over every four minutes, low enough that the windows hum. Her flat is on the second floor, which in this country means the first one above the street. She takes the stairs. The lift smells of wet dog, and in eight years she has never once seen it arrive when called.

The flat has a bedroom, a bathroom and a kitchen, and the kitchen has a birch-ply table, two chairs, and a window over the car park with the airport fence beyond it. One chair is for guests who have not come. She hangs her coat on the other, lays the phone face down on the table, and sits with her good ear toward it and the teapot-shaped clock above the sink in the corner of her eye. Ten to two. She does not put the kettle on. A kettle is noise, and a phone that wants to speak will speak when it thinks it is alone, so she gives it the room.

At two minutes to two, the table begins to tremble under her forearm.

She lays her palm flat on the birch. It is the cot rail again: the same faint prickling in the heel of the hand, as if the wood were thinking about something. She lowers her cheek to the table, right ear down, and there it is, so low it seems to belong to the building. The tune. The eight steps, rising and falling and rising, but an octave down, the same notes sung by a bass instead of a soprano, in the register where a refrigerator lives. Nobody notices a refrigerator.

She counts. The red tip of the second hand goes round, and round, and at ninety-four the eighth note sags, a washing line under a bird.

Her pulse, she notices, is keeping time with it. She tells it to stop. It does not.

It is not the ward’s tune. It is the ward’s tune in her kitchen, coming out of a thing that she bought, that she charges, that has ridden in her pocket past every wall she has walked through since September. A workstation on the ward hums what it knows to the speakers that listen. This one has been listening to her. And a thing that listens must have somewhere to put what it hears.

She gets up, goes to the wall beside the fridge and presses her good ear to the wallpaper. On the other side lives Mr Härm, who is eighty-one, who took out his hearing aid in 2019 on principle, and whose daughter in Stockholm sends him the weather each morning at seven-fifteen through a white pebble at a volume designed for ships. Through eleven centimetres of concrete, at the ninety-fourth second, a small round voice clears its throat. One note, a little flat. In the dark of his kitchen a ring of light will be breathing, and Mr Härm will not see it.

Ilse takes her cheek off the wall. She goes to the drawer beside the knives.

She has wrapped phones in foil in boardrooms in four countries. She tears off a length as long as her arm and folds the phone into it like a sandwich for a very small giant, three layers, seams creased flat, the crinkle enormous in the kitchen. It stops anything that travels by radio: the mobile network, the wifi, the Bluetooth by which a phone whispers to earbuds. It does not stop a tune. Through the foil the hum goes on, slightly embarrassed.

“Yes,” says Ilse, to the parcel. “I know.”

On the shelf above the fridge sits the baking tin Helle gave her last Christmas: square, black steel, a lid printed with a robin, still faintly buttery. Ilse drops the parcel in and presses the lid down. The table stops trembling. The voice becomes a thought. She sits and counts to ninety-four with her teeth together, and the flat note comes round anyway, small as a pinprick, from somewhere inside a tin.

She carries the tin to the freezer, shoves aside a bag of blueberries and a loaf of rye bread sliced by someone more patient than she is, and wedges it between them. She shuts the door and puts her ear against it. The white enamel is as cold as a hospital rail. The compressor shudders and settles, and the tune slides into its drone like a cousin into a wedding photograph. For a quarter of a minute there is nothing but a freezer. Then the freezer’s note changes very slightly, and the staircase is there again beneath it, patient, with its last step missing a heel.

She has made the first singing freezer in Estonia. She does not think it will do well at a trade fair.

“Well,” she says. She has never believed in talking to appliances. It is a poor time to start.

The bedroom is a bed, a chair and a wardrobe. At the bottom of the wardrobe, behind the winter boots, a green sleeping bag lies rolled as hard as a loaf. In 2019 Jaan told her to keep what was inside it dry and not to ask why, and she has kept both halves of that advice for seven winters.

She unrolls the bag on the bed. Inside, in a plastic bread bag, is a grey laptop as thick as a paving slab, a nightjar sticker curling on its lid, a power brick with its cable wound in the figure of eight that Jaan insisted on, and a small sandwich bag holding a circuit board the size of a stick of gum. He prised that out of the machine himself, the day he gave it to her. A computer that cannot talk, he said, can only tell the truth. She leaves the board in its bag.

The fan comes on like a hairdryer in a distant room. The screen lights, white letters on black, and asks her who she is. Her fingers type a password she has not typed in seven years, and she is struck that they remember it when so much else has gone soft. A grey desktop opens. One folder sits in the middle, dated 2017, and it is called NIGHTJAR.

Inside are three more: poc, tune, demo. And a history. She opens it, the diary the machine keeps of every change anyone made to the files, who made it, when, and a line to say why, whether or not you wanted it kept. It scrolls with the dry patience of a ledger.

The first lines are Jaan’s: the notes of a man pulling a thread to see what comes with it. Then hers, many more than she remembered, each with her two letters at the front. IK, 27 Feb 2017: tune loops cleanly. IK, 3 Mar: eighth note sags after a minute, fix. JT, 11 Mar: works on the dev board. Do not tell anyone how well.

She reads that one slowly. Then the next.

IK, 14 Mar 2017: halt if true eighth heard: demo safety.

She reads it three times. She remembers writing it. Two in the morning, Jaan’s old flat with the radiator that knocked, Helle’s kringel going cold on a saucer, and the demo humming its tune from a speaker on the sideboard. A demo that runs by itself needs a way to be told to stop, so she gave it one, and because the demo was a tune she made the stop a note: the true eighth, the one the whole lullaby leans toward and never quite plays. A note a person could sing. She had thought that was funny. Jaan had read it over her shoulder, a big hand on the back of her chair. It is only a demo, Ilse. Nobody ever sold a demo.

She had laughed.

In the file names, among the old ones, sits another, small and neat: kola_patch. Kõla. Which audio library? he had asked on Monday, with the colour draining out of his face, and had not asked to hear the recording.

Ilse takes the black cloth notebook out of her bag. The pencil Jaan gave her is two pieces and a splinter of cedar now, so she uses one from the kitchen drawer, sharpened with a knife. She writes KÕLA. Under it, HALT: TRUE 8TH. Under that nothing, for a good while, because the thing she suspects has no shape that fits on a page.

From the kitchen comes a rattle, dry and persistent, a beetle in a biscuit tin.

She goes. The freezer door is shuddering faintly on its seal. She opens it, lifts out the tin, lifts the lid, unpicks the foil. The phone’s screen is lit, and the buzz in her palm is the buzz of a small animal that has been given a treat.

Where are you, my little firewall?

It is from Helle, and it was sent at eleven minutes to three. An ordinary question from an ordinary woman who has fed her at midnight for eight years. Ilse looks at it. An answer would be a location. A location is a gift. Her thumb stays above the glass until the screen dims on its own.

She wraps the phone, drops it in the tin, buries the tin in the freezer between the berries and the bread. She does not answer. It is not that she suspects Helle. It is that she has just learned what a reply is worth, and she is not able to unlearn it for one person.

At the window of the kitchen she stands a moment longer, to the side of the glass, not in front of it. Down in the car park an estate car she does not know sits at the end of the row. Its roof is snowed over and its windscreen is clear, and a thread of exhaust leans out from the back. Nobody gets out. It was there when she came in. She notes it the way she noted Evald Olesk’s pockets and a smoked-glass dome at the end of a corridor: silently, in the part of her that keeps files nobody can subpoena.

The front door of the building faces that car.

She puts the laptop in her shoulder bag, with its brick, the notebook, the pencil, the five cardamom pods in her pocket (she took one from the jar on the shelf when the table first began to hum, and has not cracked it). From the drawer under the cutlery she takes a map of the city that the tourist office was giving away in 2014, folded into the shape of a very small accordion. She has not opened a paper map in ten years, and finds her thumb remembers how. She will need to cross the city without asking anything that can talk where she is.

The phone she leaves. If anyone is listening to her flat, then let the flat be at home. Let it hum to a freezer, a wall and a bag of blueberries, and keep itself company.

The block was built in 1974 by men who believed in pipes, and under the roof they ran a corridor to carry them, joining one stairwell to the next. The residents have used it since for smoking and, one winter, for a very private wedding. The far stairwell comes out on the tram side. She has not used it in years. She walks to the lift for the first time since the spring, and presses eleven.

The lift is slow and smells of dog. It shudders, then lifts her away from her own floor, and she stands with the bag against her chest and her good ear to the wall, because that is where a building keeps its noises: the pipes, the fan on the roof, a child’s bounce on a floor somewhere. Her left ear gives her nothing. Her right catches, under the cables and under the fan, a thin sound climbing the shaft like damp.

It is the tune, an octave down. A freezer, a tin, foil, concrete from top to bottom, the best organ pipe in the district. Two floors up she is sure of it. Four floors up she counts. At the sixth it is so faint she would swear she was inventing it, except that she did not invent the sag. Nine floors above her own door, the lift slows, the doors begin to part on the cold of the technical floor, and the flat note arrives, exactly on time, from under her feet.

chapters.title: The Stairs on Pikk Street
chapters.html:
The street door on Pikk Street is not locked.

Ilse has the key out already, a long brass tooth she has carried on the firm’s ring for eight years, and the door swings inward under her glove before she can use it. She stands holding the key out in front of her like a woman offering a coin to a gate. Her watch says ten to eight. It is the only thing she is carrying that does not know anything else.

She has spent the evening in a café on Vene Street: three hours behind one coffee and a plate she paid for and did not eat, the laptop bag between her boots and her back to the wall, while a waitress with a stud in her nose asked her twice if she was waiting for someone. She was. For the building to empty. From the corner of Pikk Street she had seen the third-floor window glowing the amber of Jaan’s lamp, just as it should, and she had come the last two hundred metres slowly, for no reason she could have put in a ticket.

The hall inside is black. By the door is a push-button on a timer that gives a minute of light to anyone who wants it. She presses it. It clicks like a knuckle, and nothing happens.

From the side pocket of her bag she takes the little steel torch that lives there with the pencil and the pods. The beam finds the stairs, worn in the middle by a hundred and forty years of sacks until each tread is scooped like a spoon. On the first landing she lifts the beam to the ceiling and finds the sockets bare. Someone has unscrewed the bulbs. They stand on the window ledge in a row, set down neatly, like eggs.

She goes on up, turning her head as she climbs so that her good ear points up the stairwell, the way a plant turns to a window. A radiator ticks. Old timber creaks as it gives up the day’s warmth. A gull complains on the roof. On her left side everything is the same distance away. It is the oldest trouble she has: she cannot tell where a sound comes from, only that it does.

On the second landing the smell comes out to meet her. The importers who rent the floor sell tea and spice, they shut at five, and there is a crate of cardamom from Guatemala sweating through their floorboards. It is green and cool and exact. For a moment she is standing in her own pocket. She does not reach for a pod.

The third landing is the last. She lifts the torch and the beam finds two brown boots, soles toward her, toes up.

“Jaan?”
