She says it the way you say it to a man dozing in a chair.

He sits against the wall below the red fire extinguisher with his legs straight out and his hands open on his thighs, palms up, as if waiting to be handed something. The billiard-green vest is buttoned wrong: second button in the first hole. His eyes are shut. His white hair stands off his head in the beam like a dandelion that has been told to be calm. Somebody has been tidy with him.

She kneels. She pulls off her right glove with her teeth and puts two fingers under his jaw, where the big pulse lives. His skin is not yet cold. That is a thing she would rather not know.

It is a long minute. She has no watch she can read in the dark, so she does what she learned at six in a hospital bed, when a nurse put a hand on her back and said, count it: she keeps time with her own blood. Her pulse is fast. She knows its number. Ninety-four to the minute, the number of a woman who is frightened, and she lets it count. Under her fingers there is only the warmth of him. At ninety-four she takes them away.

Below his left ear is a bruise no bigger than a stamp, the colour of a plum. No blood. No cut. He might be asleep, if sleeping men were that colour.

“Jaan,” she says again, in the voice for people who cannot answer. She wants to fix his buttons. Her hand is already on the way to it. She makes it go back to her knee.

In the breast pocket of the vest is the stub of a carpenter’s pencil, whittled with a knife. She does not take it. On his belt loop a steel clip hangs open with nothing on it, and she stares at that for some seconds before she understands: his key ring is gone. The stair key, the brass tag with Tallinn’s three lions, the plain grey stick on its loop. She does not know whether he still hung the stick there. She has no way to ask him.

She stays crouched, her right ear turned to the stairwell above, and listens as hard as one ear can. The building is large and quiet and she has half of it.

The office door stands wide. The lamp on Jaan’s desk is lit, left on as for a visitor, and the room is so neat she almost laughs. Helle’s tins are in a row on the desks with their lids fitted. Taavi’s beanbag has been plumped. The chair in Jaan’s room is pushed in square to the desk, and the left-hand drawer is open a hand’s width, nothing in it disturbed that she can see.

On the blotter is a clean rectangle in two years of dust, the size of a walnut box.

She looks at it. She thinks of Tuesday, and a man going down these stairs with a paper bread bag held in both arms like something that might wake, and then the thought has no floor, and she lets it go. In front of her on the desk is a beige telephone older than Taavi.

She lifts the receiver. A dial tone, flat and clear. She dials with her glove back on.

“Emergency.”

“There is a man dead at the old spice warehouse on Pikk Street. Third floor, the landing. My name is Ilse Kantor.”

“Is he breathing?”

“No. I checked for a minute.”

“Are you in danger?”

Ilse looks at the open door, and the black beyond it. “I don’t know.”

“Stay on the line. A unit is on its way.”

“I’ll be on the landing,” Ilse says, and puts the receiver down. Then she picks it up again and wipes it with her sleeve, earpiece, handle, mouthpiece, in the long steady strokes of a woman polishing a spoon. She knows as she does it that it will be the first thing she is asked about. She does it anyway, and puts it back.

She goes out to the landing and stands with her back to the wall, so that nothing can be behind her, and sweeps the torch low across the old green lino between the stairhead and the office door.

The print is at the threshold. A boot, half melted, wet as a tongue, the tread a stack of chevrons climbing the sole, V upon V. She holds the beam low to read it. She lays her own boot beside it, not touching. Hers is a forty-one. This is longer by three sizes, a forty-four, maybe, and it is pointing at the stairs, at the way out. It is the only print on the whole floor.

Ilse looks at it for a time that she would not be able to defend.

A man who unscrews every bulb on four floors and sets them out like eggs does not forget to lock a door. A man who closes a dead man’s eyes and straightens his legs does not leave one print in the one place a torch will find it by accident. The door downstairs was left on the latch the way a door is left for a guest. Tonight, Jaan had written on the glass, and she had thought it was a thing only the two of them knew. Somebody else had known that the person coming up these stairs in the dark tonight would be her.

They come up loudly, the way people come who have nothing to hide and a great deal to carry: two constables young enough to still be embarrassed by their own radios, snow melting on their shoulders, torches in her face. “Down,” she says, “please,” and they lower them. Behind them on the stairs something heavy is breathing and not pretending otherwise. It stops at the second landing for a long moment and says a word to the smell of cardamom.

Inspector Kristjan Lepik comes onto the third landing like a wardrobe being delivered. He is the biggest tired man she has ever seen: a long loose wool coat, a cap with the ear flaps tied up on top, a face that lives somewhere between a smile and a sigh. He looks at Jaan, and for a while he does not look at anything else.

“Tamm,” he says.

“Jaan Tamm. He owns the firm. Owned.”

“Owned.” He lowers himself, with a groan, to one knee. His hand does not touch anything. “Not breathing.”

“No. I checked. For a minute.”

“A whole minute. Most people give up at ten seconds.” He gets up again, by stages. “You are the one who telephoned.”

“Ilse Kantor.”

“Kantor.” He tries it for size. “What is in the bag, Miss Kantor?”

“A laptop.”

“Why do you carry a laptop to a murder?”

“I didn’t know it was a murder.”

“No,” says Lepik, quite kindly. “Most people don’t.”

He does not ask her to move. He walks the landing instead, slowly, with his hands behind him like a man in a gallery, and the constables hover at his elbows. He bends over the vest and straightens. He looks at the gap where the bulbs are not. “Cardamom,” he says to the air.

“The importers on the floor below.”

“Of course. The importers.” He sniffs again, as if the smell might say more. “And you waited for the office to empty, you say.”

“I didn’t say. But yes.”

“You say it now. Why?”

“He asked me to come tonight.”

“Asked.” His eyes come round to her, mild and steady, like a lamp on a ship that has already seen you. “When?”

“This morning. In writing.”

“In writing.”

“On paper, held against a glass wall. Through a glass wall.”

“And the paper is where?”

“He took it.”

“Convenient,” says Lepik.

“Yes,” says Ilse. “For somebody.”

The inspector looks at her ear, the turned head, the white streak at her temple. She waits for him to ask. He does not. He looks down at the floor instead, where the beam of her torch has been pointing for a minute and a half, like a finger.

“There’s a boot print at the office door,” she says. “Wet. A forty-four, I think. Chevron tread. Going out.”

“You measure boots.”

“I measure everything.”

“Do you.” He steps over and looks. He is silent for as long as it takes a kettle to think about boiling. Then, to a constable, without raising his voice: “Photographs, please, before anyone breathes on it.” And to her, more gently, like a man putting a coat round someone: “The telephone in his office. Did you touch it?”

“I used it.”

“And then?”

“I wiped it.”

“Why?”

“I don’t know,” Ilse says, and it is the truest thing she has said all day.

“No,” he says. “Nobody ever does.” He is looking at the laptop bag, and then at her, and then at Jaan again, who goes on sitting, patient, with his hands held out. “Tell me one more thing and then I shall let you sit down. This man had a cup of tea and a lamp and an appointment. He knew you were coming?”

The building is very quiet. Somewhere under her the street door, still on the latch, has begun to knock softly in the draught.

“Yes,” says Ilse, and listens to the word go down the stairs without her.

chapters.title: The Drop Cabin
chapters.html:
Marit Soini is turning the heel of the second sock when the man comes out of the warehouse door.

She has been in the hired car since four. It sits thirty metres up Pikk Street with its nose to the kerb and its engine off for the cold, and a flask of tea between her thighs. The car smells of the last driver’s dog. Snow comes down through the lamplight one flake at a time, each taking its time, as if it were being paid by the hour. Over the afternoon she has watched the door the way she once watched a grey sea for a smaller grey thing in it: a woman in orange spectacles carrying a tin under her arm, going home at six; a thin young man in mustard gloves, walking like someone late for something he dreads; and at five past seven a man in a leather jacket with a flat canvas bag, who rang the bell, waited, and was let in.

She did not think about him. Locksmiths ring bells. The firm on the third floor has a great deal of locking to do.

Thirty-six minutes later he comes out and draws the door to behind him, and does not lock it. A locksmith who does not lock. That is the first thing. The second is the bag. It hung from his hand when he went in as a flat bag hangs. It swings now like something is in it, and he carries it a little out from his leg, the way you carry a pail that is full to the brim.

Marit has understood the weight before she understands the rest, as you read a sea from how a boat sits in it. She puts the needles down. Her hands stay where they are on the wheel. She had been told to expect a search. At the very worst she had expected paper. She had not expected thirty-six minutes, and she cannot get them back.

He walks up Pikk Street without looking round. It is the walk of a man who has never been followed, because it has never occurred to anyone to try.

She follows on foot. A woman of fifty-two in a waxed coat, with a canvas knitting bag over her arm, is the best disguise in the north. She keeps a house and a half behind him, and she does not need to see him, because the snow does the work: the print of a boot in the new fall, a stack of chevrons, V upon V, climbing the sole and pointing the way he goes, like the track of a gull. Under the Great Coastal Gate, past the fat tower, out along the dark side of the old wall, and into Kalamaja.

It is a district of wooden houses, tall and thin and painted the colours of old sweets, standing in lanes that are not wide enough for a conversation. Windows are lit. Somewhere a person is frying onions. The man walks into a lane that ends in a snowbank and a white van, tight against the bank as if tucked in, and Marit stops at the corner and becomes a woman who is looking for a dropped glove.

The van has lettering on its flank. SARAPUU & POEG, LUKSEPAD, 24 H. And a mobile number, and under it, the plate: 913 KPL.

Sarapuu and son. Locksmiths, all hours. She says the name once in her head. A son, then, somewhere. She has never in her life had cause to find that sad until this moment, with the lane quiet and the onions frying and the lamp on the corner making a small yellow room out of the snow.

The man gets into the cab and turns on the dome light. She sees him now, as well as she’ll ever see him: neat grey hair, a soft jacket, black wool gloves with the fingertips cut off. He takes a rag from the door pocket and cleans the gloves, finger by finger, as carefully as if he were polishing a pair of spectacles. Then he cleans the steering wheel. Then he lays the bag on the passenger seat, and, to her astonishment, passes the belt across it and clicks it home.

The van starts. The headlamps wake the snowbank. It goes out of the lane without hurry and turns left and is gone, and she is standing at the corner with a glove in her hand that she never dropped, and the number in her head like a pebble in a boot.

Behind her, back up the hill, a siren winds up and stops. Then another. Then a third, nearer.

Marit does not look round. She knows what they have found. The car is on Pikk Street, a hundred metres from three police cars, hired in a name that is not hers. She will fetch it tomorrow, or never.

The harbour at night is orange: sodium light on ice, on black water, on the white flank of the Nightboat, which lies at the quay with its funnel painted with a blue wave and its gangway down, taking in the first of the evening’s lorry drivers and pensioners and lovers. A tugboat sounds its horn, two notes, a fall and a rise, like an old man clearing his throat to begin a story. The cold is so clean it has an edge.

“Seven-one-one-eight,” says Kerli, behind the desk, with the sorrow of a woman for whom a cabin has gone unslept. Her hair is hennaed the colour of a fox. “Again no sailing?”

“No.”

“Seven nights paid for, two gone, and not a hair on the pillow. That is the most loved cabin in the fleet, and the mattress is beginning to feel unwanted.”

“The telephone,” Marit says. “Is it free?”

“For you, two euros a minute, and I won’t listen.” Kerli slides a grey handset across the counter, coiled cord, a laminated card taped beside it of dialling codes from before the euro. “I will, of course. It’s a quiet night.”

Marit dials a number she learned by heart because she was told never to write it down. It rings in a hall somewhere across the water. A porter answers in Finnish, and she says a name, and she waits.

“Yes,” says Ülo Hint.

“It is Soini.”

“Mrs Soini. A ship’s telephone. How enterprising of you.”

“A man is dead on Pikk Street. The older one.”

The line hums. Behind it she hears a clock, and the wood of a room with high ceilings. “I see,” says Hint.

“Not mine.”

“No. I should hope not.”

“Yours?”

“The Committee engages you for quiet, Mrs Soini. I have never in my life found a corpse quiet.” The voice is as gentle and exact as a surgeon’s. “I am sorry to hear of Mr Tamm. I am sorry, in a general way, for any man.”

“Then who?”

“That is a question for a different party.”

“There is a different party.”

“I did not say so.”

“You did,” says Marit, and waits.

Hint is quiet so long that she can hear Kerli, at the other end of the counter, turn a page. “I will tell you what I can,” he says finally. “The woman, Kantor. She lives until the decoder is in the Committee’s hand. She is to be watched, and kept, and her habits noted. If she is harmed, you will have harmed the only door that opens. And no more telephones. They are loquacious.”

The line clicks, and goes.

Marit lays the handset down on its cradle like a thing that might wake. “Four minutes,” says Kerli. “Eight euros. There is a sandwich, if you like, left from the lunch.”

“No.”

“Sad, with the herring.”

“Another time,” says Marit, and goes out on deck.

She does not know what she wants from the cold. The wind off the gulf is steady, and the ice at the edges of the basin is a grey plate that cracks and knits and cracks again. She leans on the rail, and for a minute she is on a black sea with a boat hook in her hands, listening for a voice.

At the foot of the gangway, under the lamp, a man is standing alone. She sees the hands first. The face is a hat brim and a cardigan collar above the lapels of an overcoat, and from her height and in that light it could belong to anyone. But the hands are lit like something laid on a plate. They take a mandarin from a pocket and begin to peel it, in a slow spiral that does not hurry and does not break. The thumbs know where they are going. The peel falls away from the fruit in a single orange ribbon, longer and longer, and he lets it hang, turning, in the lamplight, as if to see through it.

They are soft hands, with clean nails. Hands that would feed pigeons in a square in the morning, from a paper bag, and sign a paper in the afternoon with the same unhurried tenderness. She has not met a man like this. She has met his hands in other men, in a corridor, at the end of a table, on the wheel of a car that waited. They are never in a hurry because the hurry is done by other people.

He looks up. He sees her at the rail, forty feet above him, a woman in a waxed coat with a knitting bag, and he nods. He does not smile. He nods the way a man nods over a garden fence to somebody he has lived next to for years. Then he lays the whole peel on the bollard like a ribbon on a gift, and goes off down the quay toward a dark car whose driver has already got out to open the door.

Marit watches the peel until it lies still. Then she goes below.

Cabin 7118 is inside, on deck seven, by the stairs. It has two bunks, no window, a basin the size of a hat, and a vent grille above the lower bunk held with two screws that a ten-cent coin will turn. In the gap behind the grille sits a flat tobacco tin, and in the tin the half of Hint’s fee that she would not carry. She does not count it. She leaves it, replaces the grille, and sits on the lower bunk with her bag on her knee.

The engines wake somewhere under the deck. It is a long way away, and then it is not, a thrum in the steel that she feels in her teeth and the bones of her feet before it reaches her ears. In an hour the ship will sail without her. She will go ashore at half past ten, as she did last night, past Kerli, who will not ask.

She takes out the sock and begins to count.

She did this once on a deck. After a night’s work she would count the heads. Not the saved, the lost: the ones the sea took while her hands were full of another. You go down the list in the dark by feel, and each one has a face, and the faces do not change however many times you count.

These are not the sea’s.

A customs officer in Klaipėda, who took a farm and a signature. A bank clerk in Daugavpils, who took a ticket to Montreal and a different name. A lawyer in Gdynia, a printer’s widow in Tartu, a young man in Turku with a stammer who signed with the wrong hand. Seven more like them, with envelopes, and weather, and the station clock stopped at the same hour. In nine cases the paper was enough. In the tenth, a man in Narva took the paper and then the stairs. The eleventh she does not know. A woman in Gdańsk who never answered the door.

Eleven, she thinks. She keeps the strip with their names in the lining of this bag, in a pocket sewn for the purpose, and she has never once taken it out to read it.

The card from Hint said Kantor, Tamm, and a nurse. The word close was on the envelope, as it always is, in his pale hand. Nobody had told her to close an old man on a landing. Whoever went up those stairs tonight was working from some other list, and took no pleasure in it, and afterwards cleaned his gloves.

She sets down the needles. The cabin is cream-painted steel, and has nothing in it to look at, and the wall faces her like a patient face.

“Nine one three,” says Marit, aloud. “K P L.”

It is odd how a number sounds, said in a closed room. A thing in her head can be put away. A thing said aloud has a place in the room, and she is in the room too. She could write it on a slip, and put it behind the grille, and by morning Hint would have it, and by evening the Committee. A man who cleans his gloves would be easy for them to find.

She does not write it. She says it again, softly, once, so it will not be lonely. She has not decided what she means by that. She knows only that the plate now exists out loud, and that she has let a lane in Kalamaja keep its snowbank and its van, and that she is, for the moment, a woman who has let Sarapuu go.

Under the deck the engines settle to a long steady pulse. She looks down at the sock in her lap. Three rows under the needle a stitch has dropped and begun to run, a small ladder in the grey. She finds the crochet hook in her bag, and picks up the stitch, and takes it up row by row.

chapters.title: The Voicemail
chapters.html:
The tube light in Interview Room Three flickers at a rate Ilse’s eye cannot ignore: nine pulses in the time it takes Inspector Lepik to unwrap a mint. Under it the room goes bright, dim, bright, and everything on the table, the cardboard folder, the paper cup, her own two hands, is briefly a photograph of itself.

“Mint?”

“No.”

“Nobody takes the mint. Twenty years I have been offering.” He puts it in his cheek and settles back, and the chair says something unflattering. It is Thursday, ten past ten. She slept two hours in her coat in a cash hotel on Lai Street where the lock was a postcard, and she can feel every minute of the other twenty-two behind her eyes. “Once more, from the beginning. You went home.”

“Ten to two.”

“Ten to two. And left again at?”

“Twenty past three.”

“Twenty past three. The tram to the centre. A waitress on Vene Street says you came in at ten to five, asked for the corner, and sat there for three hours behind one coffee. Tall. White streak, here.” He touches his own temple, which is bald. “She was worried about you. She wanted to know if you were all right.”

“I wasn’t.”

“The coffee?”

“No.”

“Ah.” He turns a page. “At twenty-five to eight you paid. Pikk Street is four minutes from that café. The emergency call is logged at seven fifty-one.”

“I stopped at the corner.”

“To do what?”

“Look at his window. The lamp was lit.”

“The lamp.” Lepik rolls the mint across his teeth. “Our pathologist is a cautious woman, and she will not be pinned, but she likes the time between half past seven and a quarter to eight. So when you stood on the corner admiring that lamp, Miss Kantor, the man who lit it was most probably already sitting on his own landing.”

The tube goes dark and comes back. Ilse looks at the folder. For fourteen hours she has been very careful not to do that sum, and he has done it for her, kindly, in the voice you use to tell someone their bus has gone.

“Your telephone,” he says. “We have not got it.”

“I left it at home.”

“All afternoon, all evening. The network says it has been in your flat since two o’clock, four kilometres from Pikk Street, with a battery that scarcely falls. It hasn’t moved. It hasn’t been used. It is very well behaved.”

“Yes.”

“A woman goes to meet her employer on the night he dies, and leaves her telephone behind.”

“I put it in the freezer.”

Lepik looks at her for the length of one flicker. “The freezer.”

“With the blueberries. In a tin.”

“A tin.”

“There’s a robin on the lid.”

He writes it down. She watches the pencil. It writes robin. “Miss Kantor. People who want an alibi leave their telephones at home. People who want to be found take them. Which are you?”

“I don’t want an alibi.”

“Nobody ever does. Why the freezer?”

“It was behaving oddly.”

“Phones do. Mine has lately taken a view on my diary.” He sighs, and the chair sighs with him. “That is not an answer.”

“It’s the one I have.”

He lets it lie. Then he reaches under the table and sets the laptop on it between them, and lays two fingers on the lid as if taking its temperature. “Older than my daughter.”

“It’s from 2017.”

“Whose?”

“Mine. The firm’s. Jaan’s, in the end.”

“And he asked you to bring it.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“He didn’t say.”

“Didn’t.” The word goes round his mouth with the mint. “What is on it?”

“Nothing I have read since 2019.”

“Since.” He taps the lid. “Is it joined to anything? The internet, the firm?”

“It can’t be. He took the card out himself. It’s in a bag at my flat.”

“Can’t.” He turns the laptop on its back and copies the serial number on the underside into his notebook, one digit at a time, upside down. Then he turns it over again and slides it to her side of the table. “I have no ground for keeping it, which I regret, and no wish to, which I do not. Yet.”

He opens the folder. “Tamm Incident Response. Eleven employees at its peak, four today. It owes the tax board forty-one thousand euros and the owners of the spice warehouse seventeen, and the lease is up at the end of the month. Did you know?”

“No.”

“Mrs Kuusk keeps the books.”

“Yes.”

“She will tell me it is cash flow.” He pronounces the term as if it were a minor saint. “Everything is cash flow, until it is a funeral.”

Behind him stands a grey filing cabinet with a label on its bottom drawer in thick black marker: EVIDENCE. Lepik leans back with a groan, hooks the drawer open with one finger, and comes up with a sleeve of ginger biscuits. “These rooms run on them,” he says, and holds one out to her.

“No.”

“Nobody takes the biscuit either.”

The door opens without a knock, and Helle Kuusk comes in the way weather comes in, all at once, with a smell of butter. Orange glasses on their beaded chain, a good grey coat buttoned to the chin, a paper bag in each hand. Behind her follows a lawyer so young his suit still has the creases from its box, and behind the lawyer, in mustard gloves and with his shoulders somewhere near his ears, Taavi.

“My little firewall!”

The bags go down on the table. Ilse is embraced, the whole length of her, with the cold of the street still in the wool. “I rang and rang! They told me at a desk, a desk, as if I were a person who goes to desks! Oh, my darling, you’re thin. And Jaan. Oh, Jaan.” Her face breaks like a plate and goes on weeping, loudly and honestly, a rain that has no intention of stopping for a lawyer. The lawyer produces a handkerchief too late. Helle wipes her glasses on her own, replaces them, and says, “I have brought kringel.”

“Mrs Kuusk,” says Lepik, “this is an interview.”

“Then I shall be quiet in it.” She sits. The lawyer says his name is Saar, that he acts for the firm, and that Miss Kantor is welcome to his services if she wishes. Ilse says she will manage. “She’ll manage,” Helle tells the table. “She always does. Inspector, have a kringel.”

Lepik, helplessly, holds out the biscuits in trade. Helle takes one before anyone can intervene, and eats it.

“Too much ginger.”

“That,” says Lepik, “is from the evidence drawer.”

“Is it?” She chews. “Then it’s evidence of too much ginger.”

The lawyer closes his eyes. Ilse does not look at Helle. She is looking at Taavi, who has not sat down, and who is not watching Helle’s face. He is watching her hands. Helle’s hands, which in eight years Ilse has never seen at rest, which flutter round a kringel like a conductor’s, are lying on the table perfectly flat. Taavi watches them the way he watches a progress bar.

Ilse files it, and says nothing.

“Since I have you all,” says Lepik, mildly, “the doors. The street door on Pikk Street and the door of the office show no mark of force. No scratch, no jemmy, no drill. Whoever came in had a key, or was let in by someone who did.”

“Jaan let everybody in,” Helle says. “The postman. The girl who sells honey. He was a trusting man.”

“So I have been hearing. How many sets of keys to the premises?”

“Four. Jaan, me, Ilse, Taavi.”

“Four.” He lets that settle. “Mr Tamm’s was clipped to his belt.”

“The clip was empty,” Ilse says.

“Yes,” says Lepik softly. “I saw.” He puts out a broad palm. “Humour me.”

Helle’s comes out of her handbag first, a ring with an orange fob and seven keys, clinking. Ilse lays hers down beside it. Taavi has to pat three pockets before he finds his and sets it on the table as carefully as a thing that might go off. Three rings, a flat grey light, and a fourth that is nowhere on the table.

“Thank you,” says Lepik. “Don’t leave the city, Miss Kantor.”

“Where would I go?”

“People surprise me. It is the only pleasure in the job.”

At the foot of the stairs on Pikk Street the constable on duty lifts the tape for them like a man holding a door at a wedding. On the third landing a rectangle of blue tape has been laid on the lino where Jaan sat, as though the wall were being papered. Ilse steps over it.

The police have taken Jaan’s computer and the firm’s servers, and the office feels it, a house after a burglary has taken only the televisions. Taavi walks to his desk and sits. Helle fills the kettle in the kitchenette, because what else is there, and Ilse goes into the weighing room for the quiet, with the great brass scale and its lower pan and the whiteboard where the dots are still drawn, TALLINN, SINGAPORE, LAGOS.

On the shelf under the board sits a grey plastic loaf with a cassette window and a red light blinking: 1.

It has been blinking since yesterday afternoon, in a glass room that two policemen walked through and took for a dead appliance. It is not a computer. It is the firm’s old answering machine, on the firm’s old number, which a few clients who distrust the modern world still ring; Jaan would not let anyone throw it out. A message left on it goes nowhere but a tape. It has no ears of its own and tells nobody.

She presses play.

The tape hisses. A woman’s voice, recorded in another century, announces, “Wednesday. Sixteen. Twelve.” A click. A cough, and a long breath out through a big nose, and a chair taking weight. Then Jaan.

“Ilse. It is Jaan. I am speaking to a machine that cannot repeat what I say to anyone, which is a quality I have come to admire in my old age.” A pause; the radiator ticks behind him. “It is a little after four. If you are hearing this you have thought of the old telephone before the new one, and I was right about you, which is a comfort. Come tonight. Do not hurry. The stairs are patient.” Another pause, shorter. “And Ilse. The music box. Count the pins again.”

The tape hisses on to its end. The machine clicks, and falls silent.

She stands very still. On Monday she counted seven pins on his blotter, in a spiral, and a bare bright spot where the eighth would sit. Count the pins again. As if the number might have changed in her absence.

She goes out into the open office to tell Taavi. His chair is empty and turning slowly. She lays her hand on the seat: warm. His screen still glows, a progress bar at ninety per cent. His mustard gloves are not on the desk. His phone is, in a biscuit tin with the lid on, where it can think about its behaviour.

Helle comes in with a tray, three cups and a plate. “Where’s my pet?”

“Gone.”

“Gone where?”

“I don’t know.”

“He does that when he’s frightened.” Helle sets down the tray with great care. “He goes and eats something.” Her glasses hang on their chain and do not swing. She is looking, Ilse sees, at Taavi’s chair, and not at anything else in the room.

Ilse goes back into the weighing room and shuts the glass door. Four rings, three of them on a table that morning. The fourth is in the pocket of the man who unscrewed the bulbs. The doors showed no mark, and doors are not opened by being wished at. A key walks through them as easily as a draught. Someone with the firm’s key had stood on that landing, or had been let in by someone who had it. And one of the other three was in a young man’s pocket, and the young man has left his phone in a tin and walked out in the middle of a dead man’s voice.

She plays the message again. The first time for the words. She plays it a third time with her eyes shut, for the man: the cough, the chair, the patience, a voice with no hurry in it because the hurry was already over. The tape runs out. The machine clicks.

She presses eject and slides the cassette into the pocket of her coat, with the pods. Then she takes one of them out, a small green husk with a seam down its side, and sets it between her back teeth, and cracks it.

chapters.title: The Photograph
chapters.html:
Director Ene Vilu has uncapped the pen before Pille is through the door.

It lies on the blotter at an angle that speaks of rehearsal, beside two sheets of cream paper squared to the edge of the desk. Pille takes in the pen, the paper, the silver bob cut by someone who charges for straight lines, the rimless spectacles, and a smile that closes like a ledger. And she thinks: oh, my dear. I have been to this wedding before.

She passed Evald Olesk in the doorway just now, orange puffer rustling, hands in pockets, eyes on the top button of her coat. “Pille,” he said, to the button. “Dear.” She thought nothing of it. She thinks nothing of it now.

“Sit down, Pille. Thank you for coming in on your day off.”

“For you, Director, I’d come in on my funeral.” Pille sits. The chair is the low kind, designed so that the person in it looks up. “Is it the Christmas rota? I’ll swap if somebody else wants the twenty-fourth. Dead is very quiet, you know, on the twenty-fourth. Alive is the trouble.”

Vilu does not laugh. She turns the two sheets round with one finger. “It is a short form. A confidentiality undertaking. The ministry has asked that members of staff with a particular responsibility for the unit’s building systems should sign.”

“Building systems.” Pille reads the heading with her lips. Confidentiality Undertaking in respect of Building Systems and Associated Matters. “Associated with what, dear?”

“With the building.”

“Everything is associated with the building. I am associated with the building. I have been for nineteen years, and it has never once signed anything for me.”

“It is a standard form.”

“Which ministry?”

“The relevant ministry.”

Pille reads on. Associated Matters, it appears, means anything she has seen, heard or suspected on the premises since the first of September. She reads that line twice. September. She keeps her face where it is, which takes work, because it is a face made for saying everything at once.

“And if I don’t sign?”

“I would hate that.” Vilu takes off her glasses and rubs the bridge of her nose with one neat finger, and Pille sees she is tired too, tired to the bone, and then sees that it makes no difference. “There is still on the table, as you know, the proposal to consolidate neonatal services at the Mustamäe campus. The ministry has been generous in agreeing to shelve it. Shelves, Pille, are things that things can be taken down from.”

It’s a good line. Pille has seen worse used on better. For one second she is in the incubator room at four in the morning, and the little glass roofs are all in a row with their green lights, and every one of them has a name on a card in her handwriting.

“I’ll think,” she says. “I think very slowly. It’s the chlorhexidine.”

“Until Monday.” Vilu replaces the glasses. “There is also the photograph.”

“Which photograph, dear?”

“From September. The technician. I understand you took one. The ministry would prefer to have it than to have it loose.”

“I take a great many photographs. Mostly Ott’s toes.”

“Pille.”

“Mostly his left toe,” Pille says. “The right one’s shy.”

Vilu says nothing. She has the stillness of a woman who can wait out a lie the way a heron waits out a pond. Pille stands, folds the cream paper in thirds, puts it in her bag, and walks out of the door with her back as straight as the pencil in her bun. It is only in the corridor, beside a poster about hand gel, that she finds she can’t feel her knees.

She has told one living person that the photograph exists. One. And she knows what he was wearing when he came out of that door.

Her mother’s flat is on the ground floor of a long grey block on Kopli Street, with a view of the tram loop and a window box of plastic geraniums that she insists need no watering. Pille lets herself in with her own key and is met by a smell of cabbage soup and hairspray and the particular warm dust of an old person’s radiator. Salme Rebane is eighty-three, in a quilted dressing gown the colour of a plum, sitting under a crocheted blanket with a pencil and the crossword, and she lifts her head like a cat that has heard a tin.

“Who’s that?”

“Mum. It’s Pille.”

“Pille’s at work.” Salme examines her, narrow-eyed. “You’ve her nose. Are you Jaak’s second cousin? From Pärnu?”

“If you like.”

“I don’t like. But sit, sit, you’ll have soup.” She goes back to the crossword. “Seven across. Eight letters. A person who is always expecting the worst.”

“Mother.”

“Pessimist,” says Salme, with great satisfaction, and fills it in.

On the shelf above the radiator, among the china dogs and the doilies, stands a white pebble the size of a fist. It is the gift the hospital gave every staff family last Christmas, with a card, To thank you for your service. Its ring of light breathes slowly, white to pale and back. Salme talks to it as she would to a nephew who wasn’t bright. “Pesa, put on the radio.” A man begins to read the shipping forecast. “Not that one. The one with the songs.” Another man begins to sing. “That’s the one.”

Pille ladles herself soup because it would be rude not to. Then she puts the cream paper on the table, because she has to put it somewhere, and says, “What do you make of that?”

Salme reads, with the pencil moving along the line like a finger. At the foot of the page her lips purse. “It’s a very rude wedding invitation.”

“Is it?”

“You are invited to attend, and say nothing.” She sniffs. “I went to one like that in ‘seventy-one. The groom was a Party man. They served a ham the size of a child, and nobody said a word.” She pushes the paper back. “Don’t sign. You’ll be wanting to say something.”

“What would I want to say?”

“I don’t know, dear. You’ve that look. Like a person with a hot potato in the mouth.”

Pille laughs. She can’t help it; the laugh comes up out of her like a cork, and the old woman beams, pleased with herself, and Pille wipes her eyes with the back of her wrist. Then she takes out her phone, thumbs to the picture, and holds it out. “Mum. Do you know this man?”

On the screen, a pleasant man of about forty in a Pesa-blue fleece grins at the camera under a knitted owl, thumb up. He is a man the world has always found it easy to forgive.

Salme takes the phone in both hands and holds it a long way off. “Oh, that’s the Rebane cousin,” she says. “The one who sells cars.”

“Which Rebane?”

“The one with the teeth. He sold Jaak’s brother a car with no floor. You put your foot through and you were driving a bath.” She nods at the thumb. “You can tell he sells cars. Look at the thumb.”

“Mum, he’s a technician.”

“He sells cars, dear. You’ll never see a technician with a thumb like that.”

Pille takes the phone back and looks at the screen for some time. It is the stupidest, kindest piece of detection she has ever been offered, and it is no use at all, and it makes her want to put her head on the table. She finishes the soup instead. At the door her mother says, “Will you come again, cousin? You’re good company for an Estonian,” and Pille kisses her on the plum-coloured shoulder, and the pebble on the shelf breathes white, then pale, then white.

At the hospital at half past two she does not go up to the ward. She goes to the foot of its stairs and stands on the third-floor landing, in the corridor’s mouth, with the smoked-glass dome at the far end looking back down the length of it. Two of the day staff pass with a trolley and give her a look. She gives it back.

Pille puts her heels together, turns out her toes, lifts her arms into a round, and begins to dance.

It is not a good ballet. She is forty-four, in clogs, with a bun like a bird’s nest and nineteen years of lifting people in her back. She does a plié. She does a second, deeper, with a tremor. She extends a leg behind her in what the nurses will later describe as an arabesque and what the porter will describe as a woman trying to start a motorbike. She curtsies to the dome. “Swan Lake, dears,” she tells it gravely. “Act Two. I’m the smaller one.”

If nobody watches that camera, nothing will happen. If somebody does, he will come.

It takes three minutes and ten seconds. She is halfway through a pirouette when the stairwell door opens, and she turns on her heel and finds him at her elbow, orange, rustling, hands deep in his pockets and the collar of the jacket damp with sweat in a corridor that is nineteen degrees.

“Pille. Pille, please.”

“That was quick, Evald.”

“I was passing.”

“From where? IT is on minus one.”

“From... the Director’s.” He hears himself. His mouth tries a smile, which comes out the wrong way up. “You shouldn’t clown at the cameras, dear. They log.”

“Who logs?”

“I’m only saying.”

“Did you tell Ene about my photograph?”

“What photograph?” He says it much too fast. And then, because he is a man who has never in his life been able to hold two things at once, he says, “I have a mortgage, Pille. I’ve two girls. They asked, and they asked so politely.”

Pille looks at him. She sees the sweat, and the mortgage, and the two girls, and a man in a sailing-boat pyjama who stood in this corridor on Monday morning and told the whole ward it was a glitch. She was going to be very angry. She finds she can’t manage it; there is no room for it behind the other thing.

“I deleted it, Evald,” she says, and puts a hand on his arm, and watches the relief run all the way down him like water down a window. “Weeks ago. A mistake. It was gone before the Director ever asked.”

“Thank God,” says Evald, and means it, and goes.

The lodge by the loading bay has forty hooks on a pegboard, each with a green lanyard and a numbered card, and a ledger for the contractors on the counter beneath. A man named Tõnis, who has spent twenty years being the front of the building, eats sunflower seeds and spits the husks into a saucer. She says she wants to look at September. He says, why not, and turns the book round.

There is the Thursday. Pille runs a finger down the line of pale handwriting. Cleaners. A man to mend the lift. A woman from Pesa in the spring, in March, with a clipboard and a van. Between the first and the end of September, not one technician. She counts the hooks. All forty are full; none were taken down that week.

“He came at ten past two in the morning,” she says. “In a blue fleece, with a toolbox.”

“At ten past two in the morning the lodge is a dog, dear, and the dog’s asleep.” Tõnis spits. “Who let him in?”

“Me.”

He considers her, and the saucer, and her face. “Ah,” he says. And turns the ledger back round, gently, as if it were a patient.

At half past five she is under the shelter at the Kopli Street stop, with the four’s headlamps still a long way off through the snow and her feet beginning to go, when a tall woman steps out of the dark and stands, slightly turned, as if the street had something to say on one side.

Pille knows her at once, though she has only seen her once, at three in the morning with a cot rail under her palm. The streak of white at the left temple. A scar through the right eyebrow. A coat to the calves and a leather bag across the chest, and the head angled to put the right ear forward, the way a person tilts a cup.

“Nurse Rebane.”

“Dear God. You.” Pille moves round to the woman’s right, and stands there like a bodyguard. “I rang you. Twice. A lovely rhythm of ringing and nothing.”

“My phone’s in a freezer.”

“Of course it is. Mine’s in my bra.” She pulls a face. “How did you find me?”

“A porter the size of a wardrobe. He said you take the four, and that you’re always early.”

“Rein tells anybody anything. It’s why he’s a porter and not a spy.” The wind moves the snow along the street in long, quiet sheets. Pille looks up into the long, grave, tired face. “I had something to tell you. Wednesday morning, at nine, in daylight, I was going to ring.”

“Tell me.”

She tells her. In September, a Thursday, ten past two. A man called Aksel, a blue fleece, a lanyard turned backwards. A fifty-euro note under a mug, for the coffee fund. An hour alone with the records machine in the charting room, while she held the fort and did a drip-chart and thought about her feet.

Ilse listens. She does not interrupt. When Pille stops, she says, “And then?”

“And then I bought a kettle.”

“A kettle.”

“With the fifty. For the staff room. It screams.” Pille’s voice cracks on the word and she stops, and the corner of Ilse’s mouth does something small and unwilling. “I let him in, dear. I held the door. I even took his photograph, with an owl on his head, for the Wall of Heroes. I thought he was funny.”

“He was meant to be.”

“I know that now, do I?” Pille wipes her face with the back of her mitten. “What is it? What did he put in my machine?”

So Ilse tells her. The carrier, the hum, the flat note every ninety-four seconds. A hundred and seventeen nights since the fourth of September. And what it carries, out through the speakers on the shelves among the knitted owls, a tune with names in it: weights, birth dates, children of ministers in six countries, off Harju’s records, read out to the dark.

“Our babies,” Pille says.

“Some of them. Babies of people who sign things.”

“They’re singing my babies.” She says it quite quietly. “Every night.”

“Yes.”

“And me with the kettle.”

The four comes round the curve at the end of the street with its bell going. Neither of them moves. When it has stopped, and opened its doors, and closed them again, and ground away, Pille says, “And the old man? Your kringel man. In the vest. He sat an hour in the parents’ lounge looking at my speakers, and he gave me a card, and he said, if they ever sing. How is he?”

Ilse does not say anything for a while. She has the look of a person walking out onto ice, slowly, to the place where the weight is.

“He died last night,” she says.

Pille cries. It is one proper cry, without ornament, doubled over a little with her mitten pressed against her mouth, the way she once cried at nineteen over a boy who was not worth it and a baby who was. It lasts as long as it lasts. The tall woman stands on her right side, saying nothing, and does not pat her. Pille is grateful for it. Then she straightens up and sniffs, enormously, and pulls the pencil out of her bun, and her hair comes down on one side like a bird that has changed its mind.

“Right,” she says. “Hold out your hand.”

“What?”

“Not yours, mine. Hold the pencil.” She gives it to Ilse, rolls back her mitten, and holds out the back of her own left hand under the shelter light. Then she takes the pencil back. “No paper. Paper’s in my bag and my bag has been in a director’s office.” She writes. It is a small hand, upright and strong, and it presses hard.

PHOTO ON PAPER, NOT PHONE.

TELL EVALD NOTHING (KINDLY).

MUM’S PEBBLE?

FLOWERS, KRINGEL MAN.

She runs out of hand. She turns it over, and begins again on the palm.

chapters.title: The Music Box
chapters.html:
“Bullet points,” whispers the dark in Jaan’s hallway. “One. I am so sorry.”

Ilse has come in by the back, through a garden gate that gave under her glove and a kitchen door that was not locked, and has been standing in the passage for ten seconds with the bag against her chest, listening with her single ear to a house that is listening to her. She has waited in the lane for most of an hour. A patrol car sat at the corner of Kotzebue Street until eight, its exhaust curling, and then drove away with the unhurried air of a shift that has been told to go home. The house is wooden and two storeys high, painted the dark red of old blood and trimmed in mustard, with a porch that has icicles on its fretwork. No light shows in it. Now a head torch swings round the corner of the hall and finds her, and under it is a white face with its mouth open.

“Two,” says Taavi. “I know how this looks. Three. It looks exactly like it.”

“Put the torch down.”

“Down. Yes.” He angles it to the floor. He is in his coat, with the mustard gloves on and a woollen hat pulled to his eyebrows, and he is the most frightened thing in the house, including the mice. “I used the spare key. It was in the drawer in the office. Helle labels everything. It said KOTZEBUE, with a little heart. Which, don’t.”

“You walked out in the middle of the message.”

“I heard the message. ‘Count the pins.’ And I thought, the bread bag. Tuesday. He carried it like a baby.” He swallows. “He said ducks. In minus eleven, Ilse. The ducks are frozen into the pond. That’s not feeding, that’s a tragedy. So I came. I left my phone in the biscuit tin, in your honour.”

“I saw.”

“I’ve been here since four.” He is whispering faster, a boy emptying his pockets at the school gate. “I’ve been in every room. I’ve eaten his pickles, which are mournful. I looked in the wardrobes and the piano and the oven. The oven, Ilse. I looked in the oven twice. And I’m not an idiot, except about the oven.”

“Taavi.”

“Yes?”

“Has a car been by since eight?”

“One went past at nine and one at ten past. I counted them. They went slowly.” He pauses. “That is a bullet point.”

There is a clock somewhere, and the house breathes. It smells of old pine, pipe tobacco that has not been lit in years, and pickled things. In the beam of her little steel torch the hall shows itself: coats on pegs, a hat stand, a mirror gone cloudy at the corners, a runner of rag rug, and by the front door a long row of boots on newspaper, in sizes that go down the family: a man’s black felt boots, a pair of walking boots with the left heel worn in a slope, women’s rubbers, and something small and red.

She looks at the left heel of the walking boots. Jaan’s hip made him swing that leg. And beside them stands a felt boot, alone, a little proud of the rest, like a man with something in his pocket.

“I looked in all the boots,” says Taavi, behind her, at once. “I put my hand in. I took them out, looked, put them back. It was only boots.”

Ilse kneels. In the right boot there is newspaper. In the left, a weight. She puts in her arm to the elbow, and her fingers close on wool, and she draws it out, slowly, like a calving.

It is a vest. A billiard-green one, the twin of the one he died in, and it has been buttoned around something, carefully, in the wrong holes: the second button in the first, the third in the second, the way a child dresses a doll. Underneath the wool is the cool, squared weight of a wooden box.

Taavi makes a sound like a kettle somewhere a long way off.

“You looked in the boots,” says Ilse.

“I looked in the boots.”

“You must have walked past it forty times.”

“Forty-one.” He gestures, helpless. “He swaddled it.”

She undoes the buttons one by one. They are not easy; he tied it in the dark, a man with enormous hands. The wool falls away, and there, in her palm, is the music box she has watched for eight years on a blotter: walnut, a lid with a lip worn smooth, the steel comb behind the glass. She lifts the lid. Inside, the brass cylinder, the pins in their spiral. She counts. Seven. A stub where the eighth stood, a little bright dent of snapped metal, flush with the surface like a milk tooth that has come out.

She winds the key. It is a stiff, small turn. She sets the box on the rag rug, and the lever slides, and the cylinder begins to turn.

The notes fall in the cold hall one at a time, clear and sweet, with the tiny steel stammer of a comb: the staircase. Up, up, and over, and down. Seven steps. She has known this tune since a hospital corridor at four in the morning. And at the eighth, where the cylinder turns on, where the whole tune leans, nothing. A small blank. The turn of a page.

“That’s it?” Taavi whispers. “That’s all there is?”

“That’s what’s missing.”

“Is that —”

At the front door, a key goes into the lock.

It makes the small intimate noise of a key that fits. The bolt withdraws. The door opens inward on the porch and the snow and a cold that comes down the hall like a hand, and a man stands there with his own light behind him, so that he is first a shape and then, when Taavi’s torch comes up, a face. Neat grey hair. A jacket of soft leather. Black wool gloves with the fingertips cut off, holding a ring of keys. A brass tag among them turns and catches the torch, and Ilse sees three lions on it, passant, worn almost smooth. Jaan has carried it for as long as she has known him.

The smell comes in with him, clean and thin and mechanical: machine oil.

He coughs, politely, behind his fist.

“Good evening,” he says. “Please excuse the intrusion. I did knock, in a way.” His voice is quiet and pleasant, a little hoarse. “Mind the step.”

Ilse’s eyes go down. Brown leather boots. A tread worn smooth at the heel and sharp at the toe, a stack of chevrons, V upon V.

“I’d be grateful for the box,” says the man. “I’m sorry for the hour. I don’t want anyone else hurt.”

Ilse closes the lid. The cylinder stops. The silence is very loud, and in it she hears Taavi, to her right, mouthing something that might be a prayer or might be a meme.

“You closed his eyes,” she says.

“I did.” Something in the pleasant face moves, and is put back. “It seemed right.”

He steps in out of the cold, wiping his boots on the mat with care, and extends one cut-fingered hand.

She does not remember deciding. She remembers the box going into her coat, against her ribs, and the vest in her fist, and the coat rack, a heavy old iron thing, going over in the passage between them with a crash like a hundred spoons. Taavi had thrown it. “Sorry!” he is shouting. “Sorry! Sorry!” And the man says “Oh, dear,” quite mildly, and “Pardon me,” as he steps over the wreckage, and then they are through the kitchen, past the table with its jar of pickles and the open oven door, and out into the yard.

The cold is a slap. The snow in the yard is up to the shin. Behind them in the house a voice says, with real concern, “Please don’t run, the ice is treacherous,” and a back door bangs.

The fence is picket, painted white once, a hundred years ago. Ilse takes it in one pull, boot on the rail, over, and lands in a lane behind the woodsheds. She turns. Taavi is on the rail with his legs on both sides and his hat over one eye, and as she watches the whole stretch of fence gives way under him with a long dry sound like a very old man sitting down. He lands among the pickets on his back.

“I’m fine,” he says, to the sky. “That’s a bullet point.”

She hauls him up by the coat. They run.

Kalamaja at night is a maze of narrow lanes between wooden houses, snow packed into hard rails by a hundred winters, lamps at the corners like yellow thumbprints. Their breath goes ahead of them. Somewhere behind a boot comes down on packed snow in a steady, even stride that does not hurry and does not tire. “Excuse me,” says the voice. “I’m so sorry.” A woman walking a dog has flattened herself against a fence to let it pass. Of course she has. It is the sort of voice you step aside for.

The lane gives onto a street with tram lines, and across the junction on a pole stands a camera with a small red eye. Ilse sees it as she runs and sees, at once, the man behind her see it: there is a half-second in which the stride falters, and the head turns away from the lens and the collar goes up, a man at a funeral avoiding a photographer. Taavi sees it too. He does not slow. He scoops with his mustard glove as he goes, a fistful of snow from the top of a bin, and without breaking his run, without a thought, throws.

It is the best throw of his life. It leaves his hand like a bird and crosses twenty metres of falling snow and hits the lens dead centre with a flat, wet slap. The camera jerks. The red light flares and goes mad, a small shocked eye, and the man behind them takes three strides to the left with his head ducked and his hand raised against the flash.

“Oh my God,” says Taavi, delighted. “Did you see that?”

“Run.”

A tram is coming. She hears it with her good ear, the long ground-down groan on the rails, then the bell, two quick notes, urgent as a cough. It slides out of the snow with its windows lit like a ship. The stop is thirty metres away. They cross the tracks in front of it, a hand’s breadth ahead of the nose. The driver leans on the bell and says something short at them through the glass.

They hit the platform. The doors are opening. Ilse looks back, once.

He is on the kerb now, forty metres off, in the light of the stop, coming on at a quick, neat jog. At the kerb his foot goes out from under him on a skin of black ice. He doesn’t fall at once. He goes through a long absurd moment of trying not to, one gloved hand out, and then he sits down hard on the road, and then goes over on his back with his keys flung out in a bright arc. A small voice floats across the street. “Oh. I do apologise.”

The doors close.

The tram smells of wet wool and tea. Sitting at the front, in a plastic cabin of his own, is a ticket inspector in a reflective vest with a thermos flask between his knees; he looks at them, at the snow on their shoulders, at Taavi’s hat pulled over one eye and Ilse’s breath, and says, “Tickets,” without the faintest conviction.

Taavi taps his card on the reader like a man defusing a bomb.

“You look like people who’ve been running from something,” says the inspector, unscrewing his cup.

“The ice,” says Taavi.

“It is hard, this winter.” He pours something dark. “Sit. It’s free until Hobujaama.”

They sit. The tram takes a curve. In the rear window the street shrinks, a spill of yellow light, a small black shape standing up at last on the road, carefully, with one hand to the small of its back, and then it is a lamp, and then it is nothing. Taavi’s whole body begins to shake. He puts his gloved hands between his knees. “I broke his fence,” he says. “Jaan’s fence.”

“It was already broken.”

“He’d have liked that, that I threw a snowball,” says Taavi. His teeth are going. “He liked a bad idea. He said it at my interview. Young man, he said, a bad idea is only a good idea in a hurry.” Then he stops, and she hears his throat close, and he looks out of the window at the dark going by.

Ilse leans back. Against her ribs, inside her coat, something moves. A quick thin whirr of metal. The lever must have been knocked in the fence, because the box, still wound, has begun to play by itself. It plays into the wool and the lining and her own side, muffled and small, and she sits quite still and listens to it through her body: seven notes, climbing, a staircase in the dark. She takes it out. Taavi sees it and says nothing. On the tram’s bright floor, between her knees, the box turns its cylinder, and the seven notes ring out, and slow, and wind down, and stop, and at the place where the eighth should come, there is the blank. The page turned.

She reaches into the comb with her thumbnail. There is a tooth there, steel, bare, a hair longer than its neighbours, that no pin has ever touched. She plucks it.

It rings. It is not the flat note, the one that sags. It is not the true one she wrote in 2017, either, the one she thought she would know in her sleep. It is lower, rounder, and slower to go, a note with a different vowel in it. A note she does not remember.

Jaan retuned it.

chapters.title: Kringel at Midnight
chapters.html:
The bellboy brings it up on a saucer, as if it were a cup of something.

He is perhaps nineteen, with a neck too long for the collar of the Hotel Tuletorn and the manner of a boy who has been told not to look at what he carries. The hotel stands behind the railway station on a street of tyre shops, eleven rooms and a lift that sighs at every floor, and Marit has taken the room at the back because it looks down on the tracks. She likes a thing that moves in the dark where she can see it. Freight wagons are going by below, one after another, with no lights at all.

“A gentleman left it at the desk, Mrs Saarinen,” says the boy. “He said you’d know. He paid for the saucer.”

“For the saucer.”

“He said an envelope should never go up bare.” The boy looks at the carpet. “He tipped very well, but in old notes. Soft ones. Like they’d been in a drawer.”

She takes the envelope. It is cream, the weight of good cotton, her false name on the front in a hand she knows, upright and pale as a row of fence posts. She gives the boy two euros, which he does not expect, and when the door is shut she stands at the window and opens it with her thumb.

One sheet. Hint does not waste a sheet.

Rebane, Pille. Harju Children’s, neonatal, nights. Flat on Paldiski mnt, fourth floor. The nurse. Close her. The Committee prefers quiet, and prefers it before the weekend.

No signature. He has never signed anything he could be asked to read aloud.

She reads it as she reads a forecast, for the word that carries the weather. Not find. Not watch. The woman on Pikk Street was to be kept alive because she was a door. The nurse is not a door. The nurse is somebody who held one open in September and then, in all likelihood, spent three months lying awake about it, and she is to be shut.

Marit folds the sheet in four and burns it in the basin with the hotel’s matches. Down on the tracks a wagon goes by marked in white chalk with a number and a word she cannot read. She finds that she is not thinking about the nurse at all. She is thinking about the door on Pikk Street, which showed no mark. About the old man on his landing, whom nobody on her card had named. About a key ring that went down the stairs in a locksmith’s pocket and came back out of it, she would bet her pension, to open some other door that night.

Somebody had given that man a key. The firm had four rings, and one was in a dead man’s pocket, and three were not. She knows how you read thin ice: not where it has broken, but where something heavy has already stood.

She puts on the waxed coat. In the bag with the knitting, between the grey sock and the sock needles, she lays a second sock, the one for show.

The block in Mustamäe is the colour of porridge that has been left out. Nine floors, a hundred windows, a stairwell where the light is on a timer that gives you eleven seconds and then takes the dark back. Marit has done a great many stairwells. She finds the name on the box, KUUSK, H., fifth floor, and climbs with her hand on the rail, and every landing smells of somebody’s dinner going cold.

The fifth floor smells of almonds.

It comes out under a door at the end of the corridor, warm and sweet and slightly burned at the edges, laid over something sharper, nail varnish remover perhaps, and under that a third smell that Marit has met in kitchens in three countries and has never been able to name until now. It is fear that has been going on a long time. It smells like a house in which the radio is kept on to stop the quiet getting in.

She rings. Inside, a timer goes off, someone swears in a small voice, and the door opens on its chain.

An eye. An orange frame. “It’s midnight,” says Helle Kuusk.

“I know. I do the stairs.”

“You what?”

“The stairs. For the housing association. They cut the hours, so we do them at night when nobody’s in the way.” Marit lifts the bucket she has borrowed from the landing and shows it. In the bucket, wrapped in a cloth, are a mop-head and a tin of floor wax. She has not had to say a false thing with her face in many years, and it comes easily, because it is nearly true: she has always been a woman who gets into houses by being useful. “There’s been a complaint. Someone’s been leaving things on the fifth. I only want to see if the fire door shuts.”

“The fire door.” Helle looks along the corridor at it. It is, in fact, propped with a doormat. “Oh, that’s me. I prop it for the smell. I’m baking. I’m so sorry, I always forget.”

“It’s a good smell.”

“It’s kringel.” The chain comes off. “You’d better come and tell me it isn’t burnt. Nobody else will. Come, come.”

It is that easy. Marit has noticed this about frightened people. They will let in the first person who looks as though she is carrying a mop.

The kitchen is small and yellow and has been recently, thoroughly cleaned. A table for two. A calendar from a dentist. On the fridge, held by a magnet shaped like a strawberry, a photograph: a young man in a black gown and a flat hat on a lawn, grinning with all his teeth into a sun that is not an Estonian one. His mother’s chin. His mother’s ears, which stick out a little and have been cut into a fashionable hairstyle to hide it.

And the oven door stands wide. Helle works at it with a cloth over her hand and a tray of pastries that she turns, and turns back, and tilts to the light. The pastries are long twists, plaited like hair, glossed with egg and heaped with almonds and raisins. There are four trays already on the table. There is a fifth on the windowsill. There is flour on the floor, and on Helle’s cardigan, and in the cleft of one orange earpiece.

“Do you know I haven’t baked at night since Gert left?” She talks as she works, over her shoulder, a fast bright run of sentences with no commas in it. “Not once. Eight months. At night I used to do the whole week, Sunday to Sunday, because he’d come in at eleven with his friends from the dormitory and eat everything standing up. Now there is no one to eat it. I take it to the office. The office eats it. Well, it did.” Her voice goes up and comes down. “I’m sorry. You don’t want to hear. Have you eaten? Sit, sit. Put your bucket anywhere.”

Marit sits. She puts the bucket by the radiator. She does not take off her coat. In the heat of the oven her cheeks are already beginning to sting from the cold of the stairs.

“Your son is away.”

“In Melbourne. Studying logistics. Which is a thing I can say in front of my sister.” She laughs, and the tray rattles. “He has a visa. It’s a student visa, you know, it has to be renewed, and they like to see enough money in the account, and a stamp, and a letter, and I’m sorry, I’m talking and talking, aren’t I? It’s the almonds. They make me garrulous.”

“Is it a difficult visa?”

“It is when the stamp is late.” Helle puts down the tray. For a moment, with her back to the room, she is perfectly still, and in the stillness the oven ticks as it cools. “It is always late, this year.”

Marit takes the sock out of the bag.

She does it without ceremony. A grey sock, half made, the heel turned, four needles standing out of it like the quills of a small animal. She sets it on the table between the trays. Helle turns round with the cloth in her hand and looks at it. Her eyes go to the sock, to the needles, to the hand that laid it down, with its little finger gone at the first joint, and then, slowly, to Marit’s face.

She has expected a gun. It is in her eyes: she has been expecting one for four days. She has been expecting somebody at that door with a gun, and what has come instead is a woman of fifty-two with a mop and a sock, and the relief and the terror arrive in her together and cancel, and she sits down on the kitchen stool with her whole body.

“Oh,” says Helle. “Oh, it’s you.”

“Who do you think I am?”

“You’re not from Friday.”

“No.”

“Then you’re from the other ones.” The orange glasses come off. She rubs her eyes with the heels of her hands, and the flour goes into her lashes. “They said there would be others. In the beginning. A man in Vienna said it to us across a table, very pleasantly. Ladies and gentlemen, you will be dealing with two kinds of friend.”

Marit says nothing. It is the oldest thing she knows. You say nothing, and you let the sea come in over the gunwale at its own speed, and you do not offer a hand until the person has decided to take it.

“I’m not going to run,” says Helle. “I’ve got nowhere to run. My sister’s in Haapsalu, and she would only tell me I should have married a dentist.” She wipes her glasses on the cardigan and puts them on again, crooked. “You’ll want tea.”

“I will have whatever there is. I have all night.”

“All night,” Helle repeats. She nods, as if it were a reasonable sum. “Yes. So have I.”

The talking comes in the end like a stuck window going up. It goes up in jerks. Helle makes tea; Helle burns her wrist on the kettle and runs it under the tap; Helle talks about the cooperative that owns the block, the leak in the bathroom, a woman on the sixth who feeds pigeons and will be the death of them all. Marit sits and lets her. A boat rocks until the wind has finished with it. Then at ten to one, with the fifth tray cooling on the sill and the almond smell thick in the room, Helle sits down opposite her with both hands round her cup and says, to the cup:

“Friday at four.”

Marit waits.

“He comes on Fridays. At four. He rings the bell twice, he wipes his feet, he takes his shoes off in the hall like a good boy, and he sits just where you’re sitting. A pleasant man. A good watch. He says he is from the Directorate, and he says the word like a brand of washing powder, you know, a thing that has always been in the cupboard.” She turns the cup. “He began in September. Before that, it was the visa. Gert’s stamp was lost, you see. Lost in the post, in the ministry, in Canberra, I never understood where. And this man was so kind. He said he knew somebody who knew somebody. In two days the stamp turned up.” The cup stops. “Since then, every Friday, he asks me how the week was. And I tell him.”

“What do you tell him?”

“Where Ilse went. Whom she saw. What she said at lunch.” Helle’s mouth goes thin. “She is clever, my firewall. She doesn’t say anything at lunch. But she has a way of putting her head to one side. I could tell him that. I have told him that.”

“And the old man?”

“Jaan?” The name does something to her face. It goes still, and then it goes loose, the way a sleeper’s does. “Never Jaan. They never asked about Jaan. I said to myself, they leave Jaan alone, that is why I do it, that is the arrangement. I was so careful. I asked and asked. And Mr Tamm? Is he quite safe? And the man said, my dear Mrs Kuusk, he is the safest man in Tallinn.” She puts the heel of her hand to her mouth. “On Wednesday I was in the office at six. I went home. I made soup. And then they rang me at ten to nine, and I was eating it.”

Marit looks at the fridge. A boy in a gown, on a lawn, in a bright foreign sun.

“You did this for the stamp.”

“For the stamp. And then for the next stamp. And then because I couldn’t stop, you know, because if I stopped he would have to ask why I’d stopped.” Helle laughs, a dreadful little sound. “That’s how you do it. They don’t make you do a thing. They only make you unable to stop.”

“And before the stamp.” Marit chooses the words slowly. They are the ones Hint slipped, on the terminal bench in Helsinki, and corrected so smoothly that she almost let them go. “Before it was a visa. What did the firm make?”

The cup goes down. Helle looks at it for a very long time.

“We made a key,” she says. “Jaan made it. Ilse helped him. I did the paper. It was 2017. We were so proud, you wouldn’t believe, we had champagne in the weighing room. A key that fitted one particular lock. And a man in Vienna paid us for it, and said he had two buyers, so that it would be fairer. Two names on a contract. I signed under Jaan’s. I never read their names, only mine. I read mine three times, to be sure I had spelled it right.”

“Two buyers.”

“Two kinds of friend.”

The oven ticks. In the corridor the stair light clicks off, and nobody comes to put it on.

Marit has been a woman of few words for most of her life, and finds that this is a night on which she needs none. She sees it whole, the way you see a shore when the fog rises: a thing made in a spice warehouse and sold in Vienna and bought twice. By a Directorate whose man takes his shoes off in a hall. And by someone who calls itself a Committee and pays in softened notes and says our instrument by mistake. Whoever made the weapon sold it to the hand that is now hunting its maker. They made the lock, and the people who bought the key have sent her to close the door.

She does not ask why. She finds, with something near surprise, that she is not able to anymore.

“Mrs Kuusk,” she says.

“Helle.”

“Helle. Do not be here on Friday at four.”

Helle’s head comes up. The eyes behind the orange glasses are very large. “I can’t be anywhere else.”

“Then be somewhere else inside your head, and keep the door shut. I cannot do more tonight.” She stands. She puts the grey sock back in the bag, needles last, the points through the wool. “The kringel is not burnt.”

“It’s very good, I think.” The ghost of the old Helle comes into her face and stays for a second. “Take one. Take them all. It’s only me and the freezer.”

Marit takes one. It is still warm, long and glossy and plaited, heavy with almonds, and she wraps it in a paper napkin from the table and puts it in her coat pocket. The others she leaves where they lie, four trays and a fifth on the sill, for the woman at the oven to push into the freezer, or eat standing up, or carry into a dawn that is coming whether or not anyone bakes for it.

On the landing the light goes on for her without being asked.

The street is white and empty. A tram bell sounds somewhere past the blocks, thin and a long way off, and the snow is coming down again, straight and fine. She turns up her collar and walks. The pastry sits in her pocket against her hip, warm, and smelling of almonds, and she does not eat it.

chapters.title: Wrong Passwords
chapters.html:
Taavi’s den is colder than the street, and the street is minus eleven.

It is the first floor of an old tram-parts works in Telliskivi, over a bicycle shop called Kett, and it has one radiator that is hot on the side nobody sits at. There is a mattress on the boards. There are three monitors on a door laid across two filing cabinets, a rack of ramen cups, a jar of mustard gloves in every state of wear, and on the window, on the inside, a fern of frost. Ilse woke on the mattress at seven with her coat on and the music box under her cheek, and she lay there for a minute looking at the ceiling, which has been painted with a perfect, patient copy of the Mona Lisa’s smile by some earlier tenant, and thought: count the pins again.

She counts them now at the table, by the one lamp. Seven, in their spiral, bright as new pennies. Then the bare spot. Then, because Jaan did not say look, he said count, she turns the box over and looks at the one part of it she has never once thought about.

The base is a brass plate the size of a paperback, held by four screws as small as eyelashes. “Hang on,” says Taavi from the beanbag, and comes across the room in two pairs of gloves, one over the other, with a jeweller’s screwdriver in his teeth. “If it’s booby-trapped,” he says round the screwdriver, “I want it noted I volunteered.”

“By whom?”

“By the bullet point of my own dignity.”

The screws come out one by one into a saucer. The plate lifts. Under it is a hollow in the walnut, lined with a scrap of green wool that she knows, because she has seen it buttoned wrong, and in the hollow a paper napkin folded into a square. A pink bakery stamp, a grease spot the shape of Finland. Ilse unfolds it with the tips of her fingers.

A microSD card, the size of a thumbnail. And a plain grey USB stick with no label on it at all.

Taavi stops breathing. “That’s the token.”

“It’s a token.”

“It’s the one from his ring. I saw it in the dish on Monday, I swear it’s the same grey.” He breathes again. “Then what has the locksmith got?”

“Something that looks like it.” She turns the stick over. It weighs what it should. It is warm from the lamp, and it feels, absurdly, like a thing that has been waiting to be picked up. “Find me a reader.”

The reader comes from downstairs, in the hands of Madis, who owns Kett and the lease on the whole building and a moustache the colour of tobacco. He is sixty and wears a cap in the house. He has brought a space heater as well, and sets it down in front of the mattress with a grunt of contentment, as if he had delivered a calf.

“Ten years old,” he says of the reader. “Honest. Not like the new ones, which are clever.” He looks at the card in Ilse’s palm and then at the three of them, and with great delicacy at the ceiling, and does not ask. “I’ll stay and be useful. I have found, in life, that people in trouble need someone to hold the other end of things.”

Ilse boots the Nightjar laptop with its wireless card still in the bag at her flat, so that it can speak to nothing, and slides the card in. The screen asks for a passphrase in a white box on a black ground. Under the box it says, in Jaan’s flat, unhurried lower-case, you have ten tries, and then I am sorry.

“Ten,” says Taavi.

“I read it.”

“It wipes.” He is already at the whiteboard, a cracked square of melamine propped on the sill, and he draws a grid with a marker that is dying on him. “Okay. Okay. Bullet points. We are not going to be clever. We are going to be organised.” Across the top he writes names, and then, after thought, a column headed ILSE and another headed DOG.

“Why is there a dog?”

“There’s always a dog. It’s in the genre.”

She types Tiiu. Jaan’s wife, dead nine winters. The box shivers and says, no, and Taavi puts a stroke in her column. She types Kotzebue, then Kotzebue 14. No, and no. She types the date the firm was founded, with the dots and without. No. She types Tamm, which is cruel, and receives a dry little no that sounds like the voice of the man himself. Madis, who is perched on an upturned crate with his hands on his knees, says, “Try ‘password’.”

“He was a security man.”

“Those are the worst. They think they’re being clever.” He nods at the screen. “My brother-in-law’s was ‘Hunter2’.”

Taavi takes the keyboard. His gloved fingers hover. “Okay, I’m going to go with the swearword. Everyone has a swearword.” He types pagan, which is as bad as Jaan’s language ever got. No. He writes 5 on the board, ringed, in red. The ten are going down like a tide. “I want it noted that I don’t like this part.”

“Pontu,” says Ilse.

It comes out of her before she has decided. Jaan’s dachshund, fat as a draught excluder, dead since April, who used to sleep under the desk on Jaan’s feet with his chin on the toe of the boot. She had forgotten him for four days. She types it with two fingers and her whole face hurts.

The box does not say no.

The black ground goes grey and a folder opens. In it is one file, a photograph. A fat brown dog asleep on a green wool vest, buttoned wrong. Under it a text file, three short sentences.

Good guess, Ilse. Everybody guesses the dog. It was a good dog. Try again.

Taavi makes a small broken noise, half a laugh. He looks at the board a long moment, writes 1 under DOG, and then, with a face like a man giving a eulogy, writes 0 under ILSE.

“That’s not fair. I got him.”

“You got a decoy,” says Taavi. “Jaan got you.”

Madis blows his nose, thoroughly, on a handkerchief of great size. “I liked that dog,” he says.

The box in the corner has not closed. It is still waiting, white on black, a fresh bar for the second door. It has six tries left. Ilse sits with her hands on her knees and cannot think of a single word. Taavi, who thinks in bullet points, takes the marker, caps it, and says, slowly, as if it were coming up from somewhere:

“He gave you a hint.”

“Did he?”

“He put a dog behind the lock. Jaan. He was never a man who’d use a name.” The marker is turning in his glove. “What did he say all the time? The thing he’d say, the thing he’d get wrong?”

She has the answer before the sentence ends. She has had it since the first week she met him. She is going to be sick with the force of how much she can hear it. She types the correct one first, out of a kind of loyalty, a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush, and the box says no in the voice of a man gently correcting a pupil, and she puts down five in her head. Then she types, with her eyes shut:

a lamp in the hand is worth two in the bush

The grey goes away. A folder with four files. Madis, standing, takes off his cap and puts it back on, and says, “I’ll go and be a bicycle,” and leaves on his creaking stairs, and shuts the door behind him with great tact.

Taavi writes 1 under PROVERB. His hand is not quite steady. He stands looking at the three words on the board, ILSE 0, DOG 1, PROVERB 1, as though it were the final score of a match in which someone he loved had played.

There are four files. A folder of scans, six pages. A text called READ ME AFTER. A short log, which she does not open. And an audio file, ten minutes forty, named only Ilse.
