She plugs the reader’s output to the laptop’s wired headphones, and then, after a moment, pulls out the jack, and lets it play aloud into the cold room. Taavi sits on the floor. The heater ticks.

A chair takes weight. A cough, a long breath out through a big nose. A radiator knocks in a room she knows. Then his voice, nearer than the answering machine’s, close to the microphone, so near that she can hear his lips part.

“Ilse. I sold it.”

Her whole spine goes still.

She has heard that sentence before. She has heard it without its meaning and without its words, the way you hear a neighbour’s radio, for six years. In the old goods lift at Pikk Street, the iron cage that takes forty seconds from the street to the third floor and which Jaan took because of the hip, she has stood beside him a thousand times, with the gate rattling and the cables groaning, and in the gap between the second floor and the third he would turn his big face to the wall and move his lips. A mutter. A shape, the rhythm of a short sentence, said and said again. She took it for a man running through a joke. She took it for prayer. Once she asked him, and he said, I am practising being a person who can say a thing, and she laughed.

He has been practising it since 2019.

“I sold it,” says the voice. “Nightjar. In Vienna, in the spring of 2017, in a coffee house with a ceiling like a wedding cake. A man named Fabian Zeller, who sells things to people who need not be named, and who is the only man I ever met who wore a waistcoat with no irony whatever. I took the money. It paid for our first three years, and Helle’s accounts thank you for it, and so did your salary.”

Taavi puts his glove against his mouth.

“He said they were friends of the Gulf. Cable people. Men who watched the sea floor for boats that should not be there, and needed a key that would let them see.” A pause. A cup is lifted and put down. “I wanted to believe it, and a man who wants to believe a thing has already paid for it. Don’t say it was only a demo, Ilse. I said that. I said it’s only a demo, and you were twenty-eight, and I was the boss, and you believed me because I was kind. That is not your sin. It is the one I’ll keep.”

She does not move. Her right ear is full of him, her left of the room, with its frost and its heater and its dead silence.

“Three weeks ago I found my work humming under the floor of a children’s ward. I won’t tell you how, it is on kaka-paper somewhere and I have lost the paper. I could not go to the police; I know which police. I could not say it in the office. Somebody in my house has been telling somebody where I stand. I know it as you know a draught in a room. I do not know who. I have a guess, and I am a coward about guesses.”

On the floor Taavi has gone very small.

“The stick on my ring is from a petrol station in Rakvere. It holds a picture of a cat. Let them have it; I hope the cat is a comfort. The real one is in the napkin with the card, and it is the best thing I ever did and the worst: Pesa never revoked the retained token, because nobody at Pesa remembers that we are retained. It signs one firmware, once. Spend it on a kill by itself and every speaker forgets, and with the speakers forgets the proof, and you are a woman who wrecked a children’s ward for something nobody can show. So I did not spend it. I am an old man with a bad hip and a worse conscience, and I did not spend it, because the evidence is the only thing the dead can leave.”

A long exhale.

“On Thursday I did something smaller, under my own name. An update. It looks like a sound pack. It carries your halt, Ilse. Halt if true eighth heard: demo safety. Fourteenth of March, 2017, in your hand, I found it in the Kõla patch where you left it and I did not delete it. For once in my life it was wisdom. I have retuned the eighth. The note you wrote is on a list in a dozen offices by now. Mine is not. It is in the bare tooth of the box, where the last pin should be. When you do send a kill, the speakers will play the tune up to the place where the eighth belongs, and then they will wait. A breath, no more. Sing it into that breath, or pluck it, and every one of them will hear it and stop. Without that, a kill is only noise. With it, it is a lullaby with an ending.”

The chair creaks. When the voice comes back it is lower, and it is Jaan at his dullest and most precise, which is how she knows he is frightened.

“There is more in Thursday’s update than the halt. It is in the log. You will be angry. I would be. Read it when you have heard the rest. The rest is the paper, six pages, scanned on the copier at the library that eats coins. I have not said the other name that is on page six. The page can say it better than me. I’m tired of being the one who says things.” A breath. “There. That is the whole of it, and I did not say it well. The box will play you out. Count the pins.”

The recording ends with a click and a long, soft hiss, as of a man deciding not to switch off.

Neither of them says anything for a time. The heater ticks. Out in the yard of the works somebody drags a bicycle across cobbles with a long iron complaint.

“Okay,” says Taavi finally, in the smallest voice she has ever heard from him. “Bullet points. He didn’t push the kill. Because it signs once. And the proof goes with it.” His gloves are knotted together. “And he put a stop in. You wrote the stop, and he moved it. And he didn’t tell anyone, because somebody was listening.” He doesn’t say who. He looks at the floor. “Ilse, I need to say. It wasn’t me.”

“I know.”

“You don’t. You didn’t, on Tuesday. You looked at me.”

“I looked at everyone,” she says. “That’s different. Open the scans.”

They open on a six-page document, slightly crooked, with the grey shadow of the copier’s lid across one corner. A German heading. Kaufvertrag. A contract, English clauses under it, in a lawyer’s clean small type. Seller: Tamm Security OÜ, Tallinn. Intermediary: F. Zeller, Vienna. She reads down the clauses with her lips moving, source, documentation, exclusivity, non-disclosure, to the schedule at the end. Two lines, side by side.

Purchaser One: the Standing Committee on Lawful Access, Secretariat.

Purchaser Two: the Directorate, Liaison Office.

“Never heard of either,” says Taavi.

“No.”

“The first one sounds like a book club.”

“Yes.” She turns the page.

Page six is the signature page, ruled in boxes. Fabian Zeller has signed with a long flourishing Z like a scorpion’s tail. Under him, in blue, in a heavy hand that she could pick out of ten thousand because it signed her cheques for six years, runs the name J. Tamm. And below it, in a smaller box marked Co-signatory, Director, in a loop of green ink that wheels and doubles back on itself like a girl’s, is the other.

She knows the green. She knows the pen. She has seen that capital H sign eight birthday cards, one for each year, with a small drawing of a kringel under it.

H. Kuusk.

chapters.title: A Little Firewall
chapters.html:
“If I’m not down in thirty minutes,” Ilse says, “you go.”

“Go where?”

“Anywhere that isn’t here.”

Taavi nods. He is standing at the tram stop on Mustamäe tee with a paper cup of something steaming in each glove, a rucksack on his back that holds the Nightjar laptop, the music box in a bread bag and a grey stick in a kringel napkin, and he has the look of a man who has been given a baby to hold in a railway station. The stop is a glass shelter with one dead advertisement in it and a bench no one has sat on since the Soviet Union. A grandmother is feeding crumbs to a pigeon. A tram drifts by with its bell asleep.

“Bullet points,” he says. “One, you are going to talk to her. Two, you are going to be nice.”

“I am not going to be nice.”

“Two, you are going to be you.” He gives her one of the cups. It is hot and tastes of cardamom, and she looks at him. “It was the only one they had,” he says. “I swear it’s a coincidence.”

She drinks half and gives it back. In her coat pocket, folded in four, are the six pages of the sale and a seventh sheet, the little log, which she printed at the copy shop on Telliskivi with a clerk who did not look at either. Paper keeps its mouth shut. She does not take her hand off it all the way across the road.

“Sit, sit,” says Helle.

She has opened the door before Ilse knocks. She is in a cardigan the colour of tea, with the orange glasses on their chain and a face from which all the colour has been carefully washed, and she says it again, “Sit, sit,” and is already at the stove, filling the pot, setting out cups, taking down a plate and putting on it, in a spiral, kringel. There are a great many. They are glossy and plaited and heaped with almonds, and the whole kitchen smells like a bakery at the end of the world.

The table is long for the room, a pine one with a scarred top that must have come from a house. On the wall behind it hangs a clock in the shape of a cockerel, plastic, with a painted comb and a second hand that goes round with a cheerful tock. It is a quarter to two. The fridge hums. The photograph of Gert, in his gown, leans on it under its strawberry.

Ilse sits where the light is at her right, so that she can hear. Helle pours. Her hand is steady, a thing Ilse notices because it is the only steady thing in her.

“You’ll have eaten nothing,” says Helle. “You never do, when it’s bad. You go thin and angry and write it in a notebook.” She sets a cup in front of her, a plate beside it, a plaited pastry on the plate. “My little firewall.”

Ilse takes out the pages. She puts them on the table between the cups, face up, and turns them so Helle can read them without having to lean, and lays the sixth on top. She does not say anything. She has learned over a lifetime that there is no sentence as loud as a piece of paper put down in front of someone.

Helle looks at the green loop for a good while.

“Yes,” she says.

The clock tocks.

“Yes. That’s mine. I’ve been wondering how long.” She takes off the orange glasses and sets them on the paper, over her own name, so that the lenses make two small round windows on the ink. “Do you want to hear it in order? I would like to say it in order. It is the only thing I’m good at.”

“And then?”

“Then I’ll say it.”

It begins, as everything in the firm begins, with money.

Spring 2017, the second year of a company in a rented loft that leaked, a lease nobody could afford, three engineers owed two months’ pay, a mortgage of Helle’s own that she had not told them she had put against the firm. Jaan came in from a trip to Vienna with a face like a boy who has stolen jam. He had a contract. He said the buyer was friends, careful men, cable men, and that the thing he had sold was a demonstration, a clever noise that could not hurt a fly. He said it in the doorway of her office, with his coat still on. “Sign here, Helle, you’re a director, it wants two names.” She signed. She did not read the schedule at the end.

“I read my own name three times,” she says. “To see that I’d spelled it right.”

“You didn’t ask.”

“I didn’t ask. I thought, if Jaan says it’s a demonstration, it’s a demonstration. That is the whole of my defence. I’m sorry it’s so short.” She pours more tea than the cup will hold, and mops the saucer with a cloth. “And then the money came, and Gert’s school, and the loft was a floor in a spice warehouse. And for two years I woke every morning and thought, thank God, and it did not occur to me to ask what to.”

“And September.”

“September.” She sets down the pot. “A man came to the office on the eleventh. Jaan was at the dentist. A pleasant young man, he gave a name, Roos, and a card with a ministry on it that had no number. He knew about the visa already. That was the first thing he said, before he sat. He said he knew Gert’s stamp was late, and he said they might help. And he said that I was, as he understood it, a woman who cared very much about her people. And how would I like to help them take care of their people, in a small way? A word now and then. Where Ilse was going. Whom she saw.”

“And you said yes.”

“I said, why Ilse? I did say that.” Helle looks up. Her eyes are small and red behind no glasses. “He said she is the best, and the best are the first to be looked for by the wrong sort of people. He said it would be for her protection. And I thought, well, she is a little reckless. She doesn’t say. She goes off in the night with a recorder in a sock. Somebody ought to know where she is.”

Ilse says nothing. Her good ear is full of the clock.

“So I told him. Every evening a little text to a number, home safe, has a cold, working late. Friday afternoons the longer things, in this chair, over tea. He takes his shoes off. He’s very respectful.” She laughs, and it comes apart. “I told him you went to the hospital on Monday. I told him you were in the weighing room with the Singapore woman and the Lagos boy with the goat. I told him you’d got hold of an old laptop. I told him on Wednesday morning that you were going to see Jaan in the evening.” The cloth stops. “That one I’d do anything not to have done.”

“Did you know?”

“No.”

“Helle.”

“No. Oh, God, Ilse, no.” She has put both hands flat on the table, one on each side of the cup, and they are shaking, a shiver that comes up the tendons from the wrist, so that the cup chatters on its saucer and the tea trembles in a ring. She looks at them as though they were someone else’s. “They never asked about Jaan. I told you. They said he was safe, and I believed it, because I wanted to, because a person can believe anything for the sake of a stamp. If I had thought for one minute. If I had so much as. I made soup.”

“And then?”

“And then I was eating it when the telephone rang.”

She doesn’t weep. She has done that, Ilse can tell, in a bathroom, with the tap running. She sits with her hands shaking on the pine, and there is nothing to do with her but look, and the hateful thing is that Ilse can. She has come up four flights with a cold clean stone in her chest, and she finds that the stone has gone soft at the edges and is something worse. She cannot hate her enough. She has wanted to, since page six. She can feel the shape of the hate she ought to have, like a coat that someone else was measured for, and it does not close across her.

She pushes the plate with the pastry an inch away, and picks up the seventh sheet.

“This is the log of the update he pushed on Thursday.”

“I know it.” Helle puts the glasses on, crooked. “I typed the release note.”

Ilse’s head turns slowly, with the good ear forward. “You typed it.”

“The compliance note. Pesa wants one for every release by the retained contractor, a paragraph for their file, in a box on a form. I do them. I did that one on Thursday at nine at night, because Jaan stayed. He walked up and down. He dictated. Sound pack, three point two point one, comfort tone channel. I said, what is the comfort tone? He said, it is what the babies hear. I wrote it, and I thought: how sweet.”

Ilse unfolds the sheet. Jaan’s log is in his lower case, plain as a bus timetable, no capital letters anywhere, nothing like a confession. 3.2.1. halt hook restored (ik 2017). eighth retuned (jt). comfort tone: carrier level raised to audible in the ward. reason: so that somebody hears.

Nobody says anything for the length of three tocks.

“He wanted it loud,” says Ilse.

“I think so.”

“It had been a whisper for a hundred and seventeen nights. A thing no one could hear. He turned it up so that a night nurse in Pelgulinna would put down her chart and look at a shelf.” She reads it again. “And then he went to the hospital the same day. On Thursday. With a box of kringel. He sat an hour in the parents’ lounge, and he gave Pille a card.”

“Your card.”

“With my number, so she would ring me.” Her mouth does not seem to be quite her own. “He turned the volume up, and he made sure that someone would call me.”

“He said so.” Helle’s face has changed again. “That night. He was at the door in his coat, and I said, go home, Jaan, you look like a shirt that’s been boiled. And he said, it’s all right, Helle, tonight it sings. They’ll call Ilse. I thought he meant the contract. Pesa. That someone would ring about the new tone, and Ilse would be the one to take it.” She pushes her glasses up with a knuckle. “And on Wednesday, he rang me at five from the office and told me to go home early. Go home, make soup. I thought it was tenderness. It’s the first time in eight years he ever told me to leave before the lights.”

Ilse sits still. In a rented loft in the spring of 2017, a man with a bad hip stood in a doorway with his coat on and said it’s only a demo. In a kitchen in Mustamäe, eight years on, a woman in a tea-coloured cardigan puts the end of the sentence into her hands. He emptied the building. He lit the lamp in the window. He left the door.

“Who is Purchaser One?” says Ilse.

Helle’s mouth moves. “A woman came last night.”

“Who?”

“At midnight. A woman in a wax coat, with a mop. She said she did the stairs.” Helle almost smiles. “She sat where you’re sitting. She put a sock on my table. A grey one, half done. She had a finger missing, here.” She touches her own little finger at the joint. “She said nothing. She had all night, she said. I talked for two hours, and she took one kringel and left the others. I think she was the kindest person who has ever been in this house in order to frighten me.”

“She was from Purchaser Two.”

“From One. I think. From the other friend.” Helle is quite certain. “I’d never have known, but I looked them up in September when Roos mentioned the word, in the way you look up a thing you’ve signed. The Standing Committee. It’s on the web, if you know where to put your finger. Six security chiefs, six countries, one secretary. Latvia. Lithuania. Poland. Sweden. Denmark. Finland. They meet on the first Tuesday, and nothing is ever minuted.”

“Six countries.”

“Yes.”

Ilse puts her hand flat on the sixth page, over the two lines. She does not need the notebook. The pencil is in her coat, snapped, the cedar splinter in the page, SIX COUNTRIES underlined until it broke. The children on the screen. Finland, Latvia, Sweden, Poland, Denmark, Lithuania. The ministers’ sons and daughters in their incubators, whose weights and birth dates went out through the speakers into the dark.

They bought the key. They own a copy. Somebody has been using a key that opens their own front doors on their own children, and the people they have sent to find it, a woman in a wax coat and a man with a ring of keys and a polite cough, are not hunting a thief. They are hunting the thing they own. The hunters are customers.

“They don’t want it found,” she says. “They want it quiet.”

“That’s the word she used,” says Helle. “Quiet.”

The cockerel says it is five to three.

It is Helle who sees it, because she has got up to put the kettle back on. She stands at the window with her back to the room and her hand on the tap, looking down five floors at the yard between the blocks, at a cold square of trampled snow and a line of rubbish bins and a child’s red sledge, and says, in the voice of a woman reading a bus number:

“That’s early.”

Ilse goes to the window. A black car has come into the yard, low and polished, with a plate she cannot read from here, and stopped across the exit with its engine running. The doors open together. Two men get out. Long coats, grey, one with a bag and one without. They stand in the snow and look up the face of the block, counting, in the way men count who already know the answer. One of them takes off a glove and puts it in his pocket.

“He’s never early,” says Helle. “Roos. Four, on the minute. He told me once he is never early because early is a form of rudeness.” She turns from the window. The glasses have slipped again. Her face, which has been washed out for an hour, has all its colour back in a rush, and with it something new, calm and flat and almost cheerful, as a person looks at the end of a long and bad week. “That’s not Roos. That’s not even his sort.”

“Is there a back stair?”

“The fire door. At the end of the corridor, behind the mat.” The ghost of the old Helle goes across her face. “I told that woman I prop it for the smell.”

Ilse gathers the pages. She folds them into four and into her coat, and the seventh sheet last, and she is at the kitchen door with the latch in her hand before she turns. Helle has not moved from the window. She stands with the kettle in one hand and the other on the counter, a woman in a yellow room under a plastic cockerel, with her son smiling at her from the fridge.

“Come with me.”

“I can’t.” It is almost gentle. “If I go, he’ll know who was here. If I stay, I’m a woman who baked. Gert has a stamp.” She sets the kettle down. “Go on. I’ll say you left at half past two. I’ll say it so well you’ll believe it.”

In the yard a car door shuts. Down in the stairwell, five floors below, a heavy street door opens with a groan, and a stair light clicks on. The sound comes up the shaft to the right side of Ilse’s head, thin and complete: shoes on concrete, coming up in step.

“Run, my little firewall,” says Helle.

She crosses the kitchen to the table in three quick steps and takes the pastry that Ilse left on its plate, the glossy plaited one, heaped with almonds. She looks at it as if it were a thing she had been meaning to try. Then she sits down in the chair that Ilse sat in, at the head of the long table, under the chicken clock, and she takes a bite.

chapters.title: Dead Drop
chapters.html:
By noon on Saturday there is nothing left of Helle’s flat but the smell.

Taavi reports it from a bench in the Kalamaja library annex, in a whisper, with his hat in his lap and a hi-vis vest folded under his arm. He has been to Mustamäe and back. He went in the vest and a cap, carrying a clipboard with nothing on it and a spanner, and said “boiler” to every person he passed, and nobody on any of the five floors asked him a single question. “Never underestimate a spanner,” he says. “Bullet points. One. The door of 5C is open. No tape, no police. Two cleaners in white coats, very quiet, with a trolley. Three, the oven is still warm. I put my glove on it. The tray’s in the rack, washed. The fridge has a strawberry on it and nothing under the strawberry.”

“The photograph.”

“Gone. Gert and all.” He turns the hat over. “The woman on the sixth, the one with the pigeons, was on the landing. I said I was checking the pipes. She said two nice men went down at ten past three, with Helle between them, and Helle was carrying a tin.” He swallows. “She said Helle was quite cheerful. She waved to the pigeon lady. She said, Pipes, Maimu, it’s only pipes.”

Ilse sits very still beside him. On the long table before them lies a newspaper that neither is reading, and across the room, in a pool of green lamplight, the librarian is stamping something with the dull regularity of a woman at the end of a war. Helle ate the pastry. Ilse has gone over it on the tram, and in the night, and over the porridge she did not eat: the bite, the chair, the quick calm face. She went down five flights of stairs with a tin, in the company of two men with a bag, waving, and she took a lie with her to hold up while Ilse got away.

“Right,” says Ilse. “The call.”

The Kalamaja annex has a silent reading room, long and high and cold, with green-shaded lamps and tables worn pale by two centuries of elbows, and at the far end of it a glass booth the size of a lift, marked STUDY ROOM B and booked in the name of Madis’s niece. It holds a table, four chairs, a radiator that ticks, and a wheeled whiteboard on which some earlier occupant has drawn, in green, the full skeleton of a cat.

The laptop on the table cost sixty euros that morning at the flea market behind the railway station, from a man in a fur hat who said, honestly, that it had a past. It has no past now. Taavi wiped it in the tram, cursing sweetly, and loaded nothing on it but a browser and a small, ugly program of his own. On the headset that Ilse wears over her good ear and the one Taavi shares with her, the line crackles, clicks, and fills with the sound of a sea of rain.

Singapore comes first. Dr Mei Lin Ong sits in front of a window full of towers, with a glass mug of hot water at her elbow, and behind her the evening has gone the colour of a bruise. It is six o’clock there. She looks as she always looks, a woman who has never once been surprised in a lift.

“Good afternoon, Ilse. Taavi.” She considers the screen. “That is a cat.”

“It’s on the whiteboard. It was here.”

“Noted.”

Lagos arrives with a roar. Chidi Abara is on a pavement. Behind him are a petrol queue, a bus painted with the face of a saint, and a vast sky the colour of a tin plate, and he is wearing the loudest shirt Ilse has ever seen, and holding, she counts, three phones: one in his hand, one under his chin, one stuck in his breast pocket like a flower. “You. Ilse. Look at you, you in a library, in a library. Is it quiet? Tell me it’s quiet. I can’t remember what that is.”

From behind the glass, a long, sustained, unfriendly shush.

“That’s her,” whispers Taavi. “The stamp lady. She’s coming.”

“Sorry! Sorry, madam!” Chidi drops his voice to a stage whisper that carries a good deal further than his speaking voice, and from somewhere behind him in Lagos there comes a high, ragged, outraged meh-eh-eh-eh. Referee has found the microphone. The goat is in the frame. It looks into the lens with its yellow rectangular eye and says its piece again. In the reading room, the stamp stops. The shush that follows comes in two parts, a rise and a long fall, like a tyre going down.

Ilse turns the volume to nothing. She takes a marker from the tray and says, very quietly, “Listen. I have four things. I have twenty minutes of the glass. And one of them is that we are going to catch somebody.”

It takes her ten of the twenty minutes to say the first thing, which is what she knows.

She says it on the board, in the marker, in her small upright hand, because it is a thing she cannot hear herself say. A tool. Old. Sold in 2017 by a man who thought he was selling a demonstration. Sold twice. The implant in the ward is a descendant of it, an offspring, a bad one. She does not say Vienna. She does not say Helle, or token, or comb tooth. She holds the marker still over the board a moment and then writes, at the bottom, the plainest thing she can:

SOME OF IT WAS OURS.

Nobody speaks. In the window in Singapore the hot water steams. Chidi, who has not been silent since the age of four, looks into his phone with an expression she has not seen on him, as if somebody he liked had turned out to have a limp.

“Noted,” says Ong.

It is not the voice of the barometer. It is a different note, lower, and she holds it a little longer than usual, so that the word has a floor in it. Then she picks up the mug. “Go on.”

The second thing is the plan, and for it the whiteboard serves. In the cat’s belly Ilse draws a ward, and a box in it that is the charting-room computer, and from the box a long wavering line that goes up out of the building like a smoke. “Three o’clock every night, the machine in the charting room reads out its records into the hum. The thief takes only what it wants: ministers’ children. The speakers hear it, decode it, and send it on at 03:12 to your rack.” She taps the Singapore end. “And from there, a hop to Lagos, and on to someone. We have never seen who. We have never been able to, because everything in that line is a record of someone else’s baby.”

“Show me a baby that is nobody’s,” says Taavi softly.

“Exactly that.” She draws a small box and writes in it. “A canary. We invent a child. A child with a name that no one else has ever had, a weight that no one else has ever weighed, a birth hour that is nobody’s birth hour. We put the record into the ward’s system from the infected machine, on a night when the implant is listening. It sings it out at three. And then we watch who comes for it.”

“A fake baby,” says Chidi with real tenderness.

“With a signature. Wherever she turns up, we’ll know the road she took.”

She writes it small, under the box, as if it were a secret: LUMI TAMM-KASK. 1,611 G. BORN 02:14. Taavi reads it over her shoulder and says nothing at all. It is the name of a child with Jaan in it. Snow, in Finnish, and a birch. She does not look at him. She caps the pen.

“Unofficially,” says Ong, after a moment.

“Unofficially.”

“I will say it twice. Unofficially. I shall watch the rack at 03:12, your time, 09:12 mine, from a laptop that is not issued to me, and I shall write nothing down.” She sips. “I would add that if this record reaches the rack, I shall be able to see who reads it. Not who they are. Which door.”

“That’s all we need.”

“Then you shall have it. And since you have been honest with me, I shall be honest with you.” She lifts the mug a little, a person touching a rail. “I have been watching Rack 14-B since you called me on Wednesday. It has two kinds of reader. One I can place: it arrives by Lagos, by Mr Abara’s gateway, a courier of sorts. It is the bridge. The second I can place less well, but it is in the north: Finland, I think. They read in the morning. The files go out as the sun goes up.” She puts the mug down. “And there is a third.”

The reading room has gone quiet around the glass. Somewhere beyond the green lamps the stamp comes down.

“It has touched the rack four times since September,” says Ong. “I found the traces only yesterday, because it takes pains. It authenticates to the management plane with logins named for old streets in Singapore. Sago Lane. Hill Street. Tank Road. Streets that were pulled down fifty years ago to put up office blocks. It does not go through Lagos. It does not go through anything I can see. It reads, and it leaves no scratch.”

“A third reader,” says Ilse.

“A third kind of friend,” says Ong. “I do not know whose it is. I should like to.”

Chidi’s news arrives with a crack of the knuckles.

“So.” He holds up the third phone, the one that is not a bank or a football. “You’ll want to know. Ten minutes ago, my regulator, the Central Bank, those gentlemen in their nice grey suits, sent an announcement to every payment company in Nigeria. A surprise audit. Of Kobo Lane. Next week. They say it is routine. Hear me, you know what is routine? A man leaves the pitch on a stretcher, and the ref says, play on, it’s routine.” He laughs, his big one, and it goes on a little too long. “They have gone for the ankles. Late tackle, no ball. And do you know what date is on the letter?”

“Wednesday,” says Ilse.

“Wednesday. Five hours after our call. I counted. They kept it in a drawer three days to watch me sweat.” He stops laughing. “You think that’s the Pesa on the wall of my office. The speakers. You think they heard us.”

“I think someone knows you were curious.”

“Ah, it’s okay, you know.” Chidi lifts the phone and shakes it, as if there were rain in it. “I have friends who owe me. I have a goat.” The goat, on cue, steps into the frame and eats the edge of his sleeve. “Go on, Ilse. Do the last thing. You’ve got four minutes.”

The last thing is the thing she has been dreading since the start of the call, and now that she comes to it she finds it has been there all along, like the edge of a stair in the dark. She looks at the board. At the ward, the box, the smoke. At the canary. And for the first time she asks herself the plain question she should have asked when she drew it.

Who types it?

Not Taavi, who cannot be in the ward. Not herself, who is a name on a police form. It has to go in at the infected machine, the charting-room records computer, the one with the Events tab, the one that has been singing at three o’clock for a hundred and twenty-two nights. A record typed on any other terminal on the ward would sit in KindWard and go nowhere, because the implant reads one machine and no other. And that machine is under glass, beside the nurses’ desk, behind a login with a green lanyard on it, in a charting room watched by a smoked-glass dome.

“I need Pille,” she says.

“The nurse,” says Taavi.

“Only her. Only on a night when she’s on shift.”

“Tonight,” says Ong, who has been looking at a calendar. “It is Saturday. Tomorrow is Sunday, and the rack reads every night. I should like to see a result before the Directorate does something worse.”

“I know,” says Ilse.

“Then ask her.”

“I haven’t a phone.”

“Noted,” says Ong, gently. “Borrow one.”

The boy on the library steps is about fourteen. He is sitting on his school bag in a puffy jacket, doing algebra on his knee, and he holds a phone in a cracked case with a small, pale sticker on its back: a white pebble with a ring around it, and the word Kuula. It is a Pesa sticker. It would be.

“Twenty cents a minute,” he says.

“What?”

“The call. It’s my data.” He considers her, the white streak, the scar, the angle at which she holds her head. “It’s fair,” he says. “It’s a market.”

She gives him two euros. He unlocks the phone with a thumb and passes it over, and turns his face with great politeness into his algebra. On the stairs behind her, the stamp lady has come out for her cigarette, and is watching with the eyes of a person who has shushed more children than she has had hot dinners.

The number is in the notebook, on the inside of the cover, under the red thread. It is not in her handwriting. It was written under a shelter light on Kopli Street, in a small, upright, pressing hand, with a pencil out of a bun: PILLE, and ten digits, and a drawing of a kettle.

It rings four times. Five. She thinks of a phone in a bra, and of a ward at three in the afternoon where a woman who works nights is asleep with her feet on a pillow. Then the line opens on a clatter and a gasp and the sound of a kettle, and a voice thick with sleep says, “If you are selling me a boiler, dear, I will cry.”

“It’s the tall one,” says Ilse. “I need your machine.”

There is a pause. It is perhaps three seconds. She can hear a radiator, and a clock, and, very faintly, the breathing of a woman who has been waiting two days for this and is working out how to say it. Ilse has time to think of the boy, and the algebra, and the cold on the steps, and then Pille Rebane says, quite calmly, in a voice that has done nineteen years of nights:

“Tonight. Three.”

chapters.title: Mind the Step
chapters.html:
From the third row of the car park the hospital is a ship at anchor, all its lit windows stacked in the dark, and Marit knows which ones she is watching.

The hired Skoda is a white estate with a child’s seat bolted in the back and a pine-tree air freshener that has been dead for years. She has parked it between two vans, nose out, with the engine off and the heater on its last warm breath. Snow lies on the roof, a hand deep, and she has not brushed it off, because a car with snow on it has been sitting since the morning, and nobody looks twice at a car that belongs there. It is twenty to ten on Saturday night. She has been in it since eight. In her lap are four needles and the foot of a grey sock, and the thing she has not been doing is knitting.

A tram comes in at the stop on the corner with its bell going, lit like a lantern, and lets people out. A porter first, so tall that he has to fold himself through the door, in a donkey jacket and a woollen hat with a bobble. After him, round as a muffin, in a fur-trimmed parka with a bun on top and a pencil through the bun, comes the woman whose name was on Hint’s paper.

Marit has not seen her before. She had a picture in her head built out of other people’s words, and in the picture the nurse was frightened. The nurse is laughing. It comes across the car park in the dry cold like a bell, a big, helpless, delighted laugh, with her head thrown back and her hand on the porter’s sleeve. She has to stop, and bend, and hold her knees. The porter waits with enormous patience, a man who has done this for eleven years and would do it for eleven more. They go on toward the night door together, her head coming up to his elbow, her laugh still unwinding.

The man in the doorway is not laughing.

He steps out of the dark under the bus shelter as the pair go by. He is tidy. A leather jacket the colour of toast. Grey hair, brushed. He falls in behind them a house and a half back, on the far side of the same pavement, matching his stride to the porter’s long one, and from the Skoda she can see the way he walks, upright and unhurried. It is the walk of a man who has never been followed, because no one has thought to.

Then he looks at the car park, at the snow-roofed estate between the two vans, a lump among lumps. He pulls a small notebook from his breast pocket. He writes in it, with a pencil, three or four words. He is putting down her plate. He takes off a black glove to do it, because you cannot write well in fingerless wool at minus eleven, and when he has done he puts the notebook away, and the glove with it, and the glove misses the pocket.

It falls without a sound. It lies in the snow beside the shelter, black on white, a small crumpled hand.

He does not look back. The night door swings and takes the nurse, and the porter, and a moment later, the man.

Marit sits for the space of ten breaths. Then she opens the door of the Skoda and gets out, and puts on the knitted cap, and walks across the car park in the tracks that other people have made. She picks up the glove. It is warm, which she did not expect. It smells of clean machine oil, and at the thumb it has been darned, in grey, by a patient hand, with stitches so small and even that she turns it to the light to admire them.

She puts it in her pocket. In the snow beside the shelter, pointing toward the door, is a track she has seen before, in Pikk Street, and again in a lane in Kalamaja: a stack of chevrons, V upon V.

At that hour the lodge is a dog and the dog is asleep.

The man in it has his chin on his chest and a saucer of sunflower husks at his elbow, and Marit goes by the window with a mop bucket on one hip and a grey housekeeping tabard from a peg in the passage, the best disguise in the north after a knitting bag, and nobody sees her. The stairs behind the loading bay are concrete. They smell of cold, of old floor wax, of a dozen years of shoes, and on the third landing, where the stair turns to the neonatal wing, of oranges.

She stops. The smell is so strong and so out of place that for a moment she thinks it is in her head, a thing she has carried up from the quay at Tallinn. Then she sees it. On the radiator under the window, between the pipe and the wall, where the heat has been at it for hours, lies a long curl of dried mandarin peel. It is a single piece. A spiral, unbroken, brittle as paper, hard as a shaving of horn. Someone has sat here this afternoon and eaten a mandarin and laid the skin on the warm iron to dry, as another man might leave a coat.

She looks at it for some while. It is, she thinks, the quietest signature she has ever seen.

“Good evening,” says the man behind her. “Mind the step.”

She does not turn. She has heard the boot on the stair a half-second before the voice, a heel and then a sole, easy and unhurried. It is the sound a man makes who wishes you to hear him come, and she understands that he has known since the car park exactly whose knitted cap that was.

“You dropped something,” says Marit.

“Ah.” A pause, courteous. “Did I?”

She takes her time. She sets down the bucket, and turns, and brings the glove out of her pocket and holds it up on her open hand, and he looks at it with real pleasure. He is at the foot of the last flight, one hand on the rail. The other is bare. His eyes are mild, the colour of tea, with a deep tired crease at each corner.

“That is kind,” he says, “that is very kind. My wife darned it.” He starts up the flight. “I’d be grateful. They are so difficult to find, the good ones.”

He holds out the bare hand for the glove. It is a locksmith’s hand, broad, scarred across the knuckles, the nails kept short and clean. Marit reaches for the wrist.

She has done it a hundred times, on a deck, in a swell, to a man who was drowning and did not wish to be helped. She takes the wrist in her left hand and turns it, palm up, and the needle is already in her right, a steel double-pointed needle, thin as a pin, three inches long, and the point rests on the soft blue place below the base of the thumb where the pulse is. She does not press. She does not need to. He feels it, as you feel the first cold flake of snow on the back of the neck. He goes entirely still.

“Mind the step,” says Marit.

For a time neither of them moves. Below them, the stair light clicks off and, in the dark, comes on again at a slow thump of his heel.

“I see,” he says, softly. “Yes. I see that I’ve been rude.” He doesn’t pull. His breath goes in and out, steady, with the faint sweetness of cough sweets. “You are the lady in the lane. Wednesday night, in Kalamaja. You were looking for a glove. I remember thinking, that one has never lost a glove in her life.”

“You saw me.”

“I see most people. It’s the trade.” There is no sarcasm in it. “You let me go. I have wondered why. May I ask who you are?”

“No.”

“No. Quite right.” The tea-coloured eyes go to the needle, and back. “You will want to know why I’m here. I’ll say, to save the stair. I am asked to watch the nurse. I am asked to be seen watching her. That is all. I’m told it’s a kind of fence, a man who can be seen. Nobody is meant to be hurt.”

“A man was hurt. On Wednesday.”

His face does not close. It does something stranger. It becomes more open, as a house does when the last lamp is put out. “Yes,” he says. “I closed his eyes. It seemed the least I could do.”

She holds the wrist. She thinks of a landing in Pikk Street where an old man sat with his palms up. She thinks of a list in the lining of a bag.

“This nurse belongs to the Committee,” she says. “She is mine until Monday. If I see you on her stairs again, or her pavement, or her tram, or in a door she goes through, I shall not ask you to mind anything.”

“I don’t take instructions from the Committee, Mrs...”

“Soini.”

“Mrs Soini.” He says it as if tasting it. “But I take your point, and I’m obliged. It is not a long way to Monday.” He looks down at the needle on his pulse and gives, for the first time, a thin, rueful smile.

She lifts the needle. He rubs the wrist, once, and then takes the glove from her palm and draws it on, finger by finger, as carefully as a surgeon, and goes down the stairs, and she hears him all the way down, not hurrying, one flight, two, until the street door at the bottom opens on the cold and shuts again.

She stands on the landing with the peel at her back. Her hand, which has not been unsteady in thirty years, has a very small tremor in it, and she looks at it with interest, as if it had been left to her by a stranger.

There is one pay telephone left in the Harju Children’s Hospital, in the entrance hall between a dead fountain and a machine that sells hot chocolate in the shape of an apology. It takes coins. It has been used this winter, so the lodge man will tell you if you ask him, by three fathers, a lawyer, and once a bishop.

She dials the number she learned by heart. The Helsinki porter answers in the voice of a man at the bottom of a lift. She says a name, and waits, and listens to the high room breathe.

“Mrs Soini,” says Hint. “I did say no telephones.”

“It is a hospital.”

“That is not a recommendation.”

“I have the nurse.” She says it flatly, as she once said the position of a boat. “Rebane. On the ward tonight, and tomorrow night, and then nothing until she goes to ground. A man of the other party is watching her. I have seen him. I have spoken to him.”

“Spoken.”

“Briefly. He will not be a difficulty.”

The line is silent. She can hear the clock again, and a second sound behind it, a kind of dry whisper, like one hand turning a page against another. “And the closing?” says Hint.

“Monday.”

“The Committee asked for the weekend.”

“The Committee asked for quiet. A hospital on a Saturday night is full of lamps, and a woman who has been dead in a corridor is a headline by eight. Monday. I shall bring her in alive, and you may ask what you like. A dead nurse will not tell you where the decoder is. She has been in the room with it for a hundred nights.”

It is a good lie. It is the best she has ever told. It has a shape that Hint will recognise, a reason and a delay and a cost, and as she says it she hears herself pronounce the word alive as if it were a thing she could return.

“Monday, then,” says Hint, after a time that is longer than she likes. “You are always so reasonable, Mrs Soini. It is why we engage you. Good night.”

The line clicks and goes. She sets the receiver on its hook with the care of a woman putting a sleeper back to bed.

The linen room opens off the service corridor on the third floor, a long narrow cupboard with a door that does not close and shelves from floor to ceiling heaped with folded white things. It smells of bleach and steam and warm cotton. At the far end there is a hatch in the wall, the sort that was once used to pass trays, with a wooden shutter pushed up, and through it she can see a slice of Bay Two: a pool of green light, an incubator, a chair, and the back of a round woman with a pencil in her bun.

She did not mean to stay. She meant to look, and learn the corridors, and go. But the nurse is talking, and there is nothing in Marit’s life that has ever kept her from listening to a person who is talking to a child.

“No, dear, listen. Listen to me. It isn’t a difficult game. There are two teams and one ball and the thing is that nobody likes anybody.” Pille has a baby in the crook of her arm, a scrap in a striped hat, one hand curled round her thumb. The baby’s face is the size of a plum. He is, Marit judges, about a month early and a month old. “The Estonians are the ones in blue. They have played since the Flood and they have lost since the Flood. Their goalkeeper is a man called Aleksandr, he is very handsome, and he saves everything except penalties and his mother’s feelings. Now, tonight. Tonight it is the Finns.”

A small sound from the striped hat.

“I know. The Finns. Don’t look at me like that, it’s not their fault, they can’t help it, they’re tall.” She rocks, once, twice. “Your auntie Pille has a gentleman, did you know? He follows her tram. Ever so polite, very clean boots, he never says a word. I have decided he is a suitor. Goodness, you’ve gone to sleep. Bad referee. Well, I’m not to be held to it. I’ll tell you the score in the morning.”

She sets him in the cot, tucks the blanket over, and with two fingers draws the hat a quarter of an inch lower on the small head. Then she stands there for longer than the task needs, her hand on the rail, looking down.

Marit has her own hand on the linen shelf, and finds she has pressed a swaddle flat.

The nurse knows. She has seen the man on the pavement, and made a suitor of him for the sake of a child who cannot understand, and come in to work all the same. Marit has met that kind of courage on a deck, in people who were afraid of the water and went out on it for a living. It does not look like anything. It looks like a woman telling a baby about football.

She thinks of a night off Porkkala with a boat hook in her hands, and of the strip of eleven names in the lining of her bag, and of a man in a tidy jacket saying I closed his eyes. For nineteen years the last pair of hands was the one thing she was good at. Nobody ever told her that hands can also be kept in the lap.

From her coat she takes the phone. It is a plain grey handset that Hint’s man gave her in Helsinki, to be used in case of fire, and to be kept charged in every other case. Its small green eye has told Hint’s people where she sleeps since Tuesday. She turns it over. She pries off the back with her thumbnail, and the battery slides out into her palm, a little flat thing with a dull silver face, as warm as a pebble.

On the shelf beside her, among the stacks of white, is a row of knitted boots, no bigger than egg-cups, in pale wool, waiting for some cold foot. She knows the pattern. The Thursday knitters did these. She lays the battery in one of them, and sets the phone in another, and pushes both to the back of the shelf, where they are no one’s business but the laundry’s. Then she takes the glove out of her pocket, looks at the neat grey darn at the thumb, and puts it away again.

Through the hatch the nurse is writing something at the desk, and humming, softly, without noticing, a tune that goes up in eight steps.

Marit does not hum it. She goes to the end of the linen room, and stands where the light from the hatch lies in a square on the floor, and watches the ward lights go down, one bay at a time, as the night shift dims the rooms for the small hours. First Bay One. Then Bay Three. Then the long corridor, its white going to grey. She watches the dark come on the way she once watched a grey sea close over a harbour, steadily, without malice. It is nearly one o’clock. By Hint’s rules the courier rings at one with the hours and the doors, and by two the Committee has a map of this ward’s night. The pay telephone is forty steps from where she stands.

She does not report.

chapters.title: The Canary
chapters.html:
“Anni Põld,” Pille writes in the agency book, in her upright capitals, “locum, neonatal, on call from Mustamäe.” She reads it back, moving her lips, and puts a dot over the i with a little flourish. “There. You’re a real person now. You’ve a mother in Rakvere and a bad knee.”

“Which knee?”

“The one you’re not standing on.”

The night door of Harju is a steel one with a push-bar and a camera in a cage, and the porter holding it open is so tall that Ilse has to put her head back to meet his eye. Rein looks her up and down, from the paper cap that hides her white streak to the blue gown that Pille found for her in the sluice room, the mask hanging under her chin, the clogs two sizes too wide. “She said you were taller,” he says.

“I’m tall.”

“She said taller.” He seems to find it a puzzle, and to put it away for later. “I never saw you. I’m a porter. I see trolleys. I tell anybody anything, but nobody ever asks me the right thing.”

“What’s the right thing?”

“I’ll let you know,” says Rein, and leans on the bar, and the door shuts behind them with a sound like a held breath let go.

It is ten to three on Sunday morning. They go up by the service stair with its smell of cold concrete, and at the third-floor landing Ilse stops for a second beside a radiator, where something dry and pale is curled against the pipe. It smells of orange. She does not know why it should make the back of her neck prickle, and moves on.

The ward at night is not quiet. It is a place that has learned to talk to itself in a very small voice, and Ilse, who has always listened to the world with one ear and the floor, is rapidly learning its grammar.

The beeps come from her right: she knows that by the soft edge of them, a pulse oximeter in Bay One, a drip pump in Two with its slow, dutiful chirp. She steers by them, as a ship steers by a lighthouse, turning her good ear to the sound and walking toward the place where the sound is least. Under the beeps, in the soles of her borrowed clogs, runs a deeper hum from the building itself, a pump in the plant room, a lift coming up from the ground, the long pulse of the ventilation. Where the floor changes under her, from vinyl to the rubber mat outside Bay Three, her step softens and her whole body knows where it is. The left side of her head is a grey wall. Everything real comes in on the right.

“Walk like you’ve been here for years,” Pille murmurs. “Look bored. Look a bit cross. Locums always look cross.”

They pass the glass-walled milk kitchen. They pass a trolley with a tray of syringes capped in blue. They pass the tartan owl on its shelf, with its single button eye, and the ranks of the others beside it, seventy-one of them in all, knitted, on the shelves above every cot, watching the babies with their stitched and slightly lopsided faces. On each shelf beside them sits a white stone the size of a fist, and in each stone a ring of light is breathing, white to pale and white again. Thirteen. One shelf in Bay Four holds only a pale circle where dust has not settled.

At the end of the corridor a door stands ajar, and from behind it comes the soft, dry, quick click of two needles. Ilse turns her head.

“The linen room,” says Pille, without looking. “The pipes tick. It’s very old, the plumbing. We think it’s haunted. We think it’s a woman who died in 1962 of knitting.” She opens the glass door of the charting room and shoves Ilse into the light. “In you go, dear. Sit. Don’t touch anything and look like you’re allowed.”

The records computer stands on a desk by the window, a grey tower with a flat screen, an old keyboard with a worn space bar, and on top of it, held down by a stack of patient folders, a knitted owl in a pink hat. It looks like nothing. It looks like the machine in any hospital that has been there since before the nurse. Ilse stands behind Pille’s shoulder and looks at it for some while, a thing that has been singing at three o’clock for a hundred and twenty-three nights.

Pille logs in with a green lanyard and a six-digit number. The screen fills with grey boxes. She finds a tab marked Events, and there, as she once photographed it, is the line: Audio endpoint, active. Beside it is something Ilse had not noticed, a small grey counter, queued 17, sent 0.

“It keeps a queue,” says Pille. “Look. Seventeen records. It counts them out like a woman with a purse.”

“Seventeen.”

“Tonight’s lot. All the children of people who sign.” Pille cracks her knuckles. “And now yours. Go on, dear. Tell me who she is.”

“A girl,” says Ilse.

“Name?”

She had thought she would say it flatly, as one reads a figure out of a table. “Lumi.”

“Lumi.” Pille types. “Surname?”

“Tamm-Kask.”

The fingers stop. They stay above the keys, at a little distance, as a pianist’s do after the last note. The nurse does not turn her head. In the dark edge of the screen, in the reflection of her face, Ilse watches her mouth work.

“Kringel man,” says Pille, very quietly. “With a hyphen. He’d have said it was an extravagance.”

“He’d have said double the surname, half the baby.”

“He’d have said it wrong.” Pille laughs, and it comes out wet, and she wipes her face with the back of the wrist that holds the pencil. “Right. Right, we’re being professionals. Weight?”

“1,611 grams.”

“Nice and small. A little madam. Born?”

“02:14.”

“Poor lamb, forty minutes old. Gestation, thirty-three weeks, we’ll say.” She works down the form, field by field, with a nurse’s speed. At the bottom there is a small grey box with a label Ilse has to bend to read, Enhanced confidentiality (protected family), and a second field for the guardian’s post. “Nobody ticks this unless there’s a minister in the family, dear. In nineteen years I have ticked it four times. It’s meant to keep the records quiet.” She ticks it. In the guardian box she types, with a flourish, Minister for Maritime Affairs, Republic of Latvia. “Such a modest title. Nobody will remember a minister of fishing.”

She presses save. The screen thinks. The counter says, queued 18, sent 0.

“There,” says Pille softly. “She’s born.”

At three o’clock the speakers begin to breathe.

Ilse feels it before she hears it. She is sitting on a footstool in the charting-room doorway, with a spare cot parked beside her for the screen, her recorder in her lap under a fold of the gown, and her right hand on the cot’s cold steel rail. And the rail trembles. It is the faintest thing, a shiver, the shiver of a glass on a table when a lorry goes by in the street. She would not feel it if she were not waiting for it. Then, from the shelf above Bay One, from the shelf in the corridor, from all thirteen, the first note comes.

It is quieter than on that first night. The IT head turned it down on Monday and nobody has dared turn it up. But it is there, round and soft and slightly sorrowful, a hum with a face, and then the second note, and the third, a staircase going up in the dark. By the fifth the whole ward has joined in. The sound comes out of the shelves and the walls and the owls’ stitched faces, and the little green lights of the incubators go on shining under it, unbothered, a row of calm lamps. Ilse’s palm sits flat on the rail and reads it like Braille.

She does not crack the cardamom. She turns the recorder face up in her lap. On its screen, ten euros from a man with a past, a ribbon of colour crawls left to right, a bright line, a dark gap, the line again. Eight notes. Eight notes. She does not need the numbers. She has the shape. In her wrist, quietly, her own pulse is running at what she recognises, with a small cold shock, as ninety-four.

“Is it all right?” whispers Pille from the desk. She has taken a chart and is pretending to read it. “Is it, you know? Behaving?”

“It’s reading.”

“To whom?”

“I don’t know yet.”

On the screen, at the foot of the Events tab, the counter ticks. Queued 18, sent 1. Then, a frame later, sent 2. The tune goes round and round the ward like a child on a ring road, and with every hundred seconds or so, with a patience that makes Ilse want to take hold of something, a note sags. Flat, and tired, and then the proper tune again. A full stop. A carriage return. Another line leaves the building, another small stranger in a blanket with a name.

Thirty-three minutes pass, and she feels each of them in the rail. Pille tops up a bottle. A pump alarms in Bay Two, a long rising complaint, and the nurse goes quickly and silences it and comes back with her hand over her chest, saying nothing. Twice a trolley goes by in the corridor, pushed by a porter who looks only at the floor. Somewhere in the walls a pipe ticks like needles.

At twenty-six minutes to four, the counter reads queued 18, sent 17.

Pille puts down her chart. She comes and stands in the doorway with her hand on the frame, round and silent in the green light. The tune has gone on again, and the speakers breathe, and Ilse counts, because it is what her heart is doing anyway. The notes climb. The seventh. And then the eighth drops, as it always drops, a half-step of tired air, a note with its shoulders down.

On the recorder’s ribbon a line begins that she has never seen. It is thin and bright, a little different in its rhythm, as a voice is different when it says a name you know. She watches it cross the screen in eight-note steps, and the counter, without any fuss, turns its small grey face over.

Sent 18.

“That’s her,” says Pille.

“That’s her.”

Lumi Tamm-Kask, born at 02:14, one thousand six hundred and eleven grams, a minister of fishing’s only child, leaves the building as a tune. She goes out through the white stone on the shelf above the cot, up through the ceiling of the ward and over the roof, through the cold, along a cable, to a rack in the south, and on. Ilse has imagined it for six days, and it is smaller than she thought. It is not a flash. It is eleven seconds of a lullaby, slightly flat, going out into the dark in the ordinary way, while somewhere an unseen reader writes her down.

She says, aloud, to nobody, “Go on, then.”

The lights go out.

It is not a flicker. The whole third floor drops into black at once, ceiling, corridor, desk lamp, screen, and the white rings on the thirteen stones go out like thirteen eyes shut. The hum stops dead in the middle of a note. The rail under her hand stops shaking.

Ilse does not move. In the dark her good ear opens like a hand. She hears Bay Two’s pump, still going, on its own battery. She hears a baby turn over in a cot with a small wet sound. She hears her own pulse, and she counts it, one, two, three, and under the count a long way off a lift cable shudders and lets go.

A hand finds her sleeve. It is round, strong, smells of chlorhexidine. “Battery, dear,” whispers Pille, so close that Ilse feels the words. “Every incubator in the building’s on battery. They don’t even blink. Look.” And there they are, in the black, the green lights, a long double row of them going away down the ward, calm as a runway. “Nothing happens to my babies. Nothing. I’ve been doing this nineteen years.”

“I know.”

“That’s not us.” The hand tightens. “That’s not the ward, Ilse. That’s the building. Somebody’s turned off the building.”

Three. The lights come back with a heavy thud, ceiling by ceiling, and everything in the world has been put one inch to the left. The hum has not begun again. The thirteen rings are dark, and then, one by one, they come on, white, breathing, like animals who have slept. The screen on the desk wakes, with a small stupid chime.

And at the far end of the corridor, under the smoked-glass dome, stands a man.

He is a long way off. At that distance he is a neat shape, a leather jacket the colour of toast, grey hair, a pair of hands held a little in front of him like a man who has come to the wrong door at a party. He has taken off his hat. On both hands are black wool gloves with the fingertips cut away. He stands very still on the vinyl. From where Ilse sits, in the doorway with the cold rail under her fist, he seems to be looking, with great politeness, at her.

He lifts one hand and gives a small apologetic wave.

“Oh,” says Pille, in a voice with the bottom gone out of it. “That’s my suitor.”

Ilse is on her feet. The recorder goes into the front of her gown. And Pille, without another word, has dashed into the equipment store at the end of the charting room and come out again with her arms full: a coil of black power cable, two grey adaptors, a spare charger in a plastic bag, all of it bundled together in a white cellular blanket, folded round and round and tucked at the end into a small neat head. She pushes it into Ilse’s arms. It is heavy and awkward and rustles. In the gloom it looks, exactly, like a baby wrapped for the night.

“Nobody stops a woman running with a baby,” says Pille. “They get out of her way. Hold it by the head. Don’t drop it, it’s very expensive.” Her face is white, the pencil sticking out of her bun like a flag. Down the corridor, a heel and then a sole come toward them on the vinyl, unhurried, light, and at the foot of the ward the dome watches. “Run with the baby.”

chapters.title: Laundry Chute
chapters.html:
The sluice room smells of bleach and boiled rubber. Ilse arrives in it at a run, in clogs two sizes too big, with a white bundle clutched to her chest and her deaf side turned to the door she has just come through. Anything could be behind her. Pille is the one who looks back. She does it twice, quickly, the way she looks at a monitor, and then she closes the door with her hip and does not let it bang.

They have come the back way, through the charting room and the equipment store and out by a door Ilse took for a cupboard. Pille does this ward with her eyes shut. She has done it, on certain nights, with someone’s baby in each arm.

“He’ll do the bays first,” she whispers. “He’s polite. He’ll want to see that everyone is asleep.”

A row of steel sinks. A bedpan washer the size of a wardrobe, ticking as it cools. On two chairs pushed together under the window lies the second porter, Mihkel, twenty-three years old, with his boot heels up on a linen cart and Saturday’s paper tented over his face. He snores in two parts, a long rasp and a short whistle, like a kettle that has been taught manners.

“Your ward,” Ilse says, very low.

“Kadri has the ward. Kadri has Bay Two and the cot in high dependency, and she’s better at this than I am, so don’t tell her.” Pille steps round a mop bucket without looking at it. Her pencil has slid sideways in her bun and she shoves it straight. “What I can’t have is that man on my floor with me on it. He knows my tram, dear. He’s practically family. Mihkel, sweetheart, you have been a joy. Sleep.”

Mihkel would sleep through the Last Judgement and then ask who had moved his chair. They go past him on their toes.

At the back wall is a steel hatch the size of an oven door. A printed sign says NO PEOPLE, and under it, in biro, in a hand Ilse knows from a drawing of a kettle, someone has added (this means you, Rein). Pille hooks the hatch open with one finger. Warm air breathes out of the dark. It smells of bleach and milk and something else that Ilse decides to leave down there with the rest.

“Where does it go?”

“The linen bay under the east wing. Three floors.” Pille shakes out an imaginary tablecloth. “Rein did it in 2016 for a bet and won two hundred euros and a week of light duties. Feet first, knees together, arms in. Like a bridesmaid.”

“Is that how bridesmaids go?”

“It’s how I went at my cousin’s, and look how well I turned out.”

Ilse looks at the hole. Her pulse has begun its old trick, and she feels it in her wrists, in her throat, in the bundle against her ribs. Ninety-four. “And then?”

“And then there are sheets. Go on, I’m right behind you. Mind the step.” Pille hears herself, and her face folds. “Oh, I’ve caught it off him. Go!”

Ilse sits on the lip of the hatch. The steel is cold through the gown. She tucks the bundle under her chin, crosses her ankles, and lets go.

It is dark, and it is much faster than a bridesmaid. The tube turns once at the second floor and slams her shoulder into its wall with a boom she feels in her teeth. A clog leaves her foot. Then the dark opens under her and she drops through it into cotton, an enormous soft gasp of it, which closes over her to the chin and is warm.

Pille arrives a moment later, with a squeal that runs the length of the tunnel and comes back again, and lands across Ilse’s shins.

“Oof. Sorry, dear. Sorry.” Her head comes up out of the sheets, cap gone, bun askew. “Everyone in one piece? Nobody think about the bottom layers. It’s mostly milk.”

The heap is warm because the bay sits over the boiler pipes, and because the night’s linen has been tipped here from three floors of sacks and nobody has yet carted it away. Ilse climbs down the slope of it on her hands and her one remaining clog. She still has the bundle. She has not let go of it at any point, which strikes her as a small and ridiculous triumph. Under the gown, the recorder lies warm against her ribs.

The bay is long and low, a cellar of white-lagged pipes and wheeled cages stacked with canvas sacks. As they pass the cages Pille takes an empty sack from the nearest and tucks it under her arm, the way another woman might pick up an umbrella. At the near end stands the service lift, a steel door with a little red number above it and, beside it, a green fire door with a push bar. At the far end, past a gallery where clean sheets hang from ceiling rails to air, are roller doors and the faint orange of a lamp.

Above the lift, the red number says 3. As Ilse watches, it says 2.

“That’s him,” says Pille.

“How do you know?”

“Nobody else is awake enough to use it. Hold on.” She has already crossed to the fire door. From the pocket of her tunic she takes a black rubber wedge, as another woman might take out a handkerchief, and kicks it under the door so that it stands open on the cold stairwell. “Facilities put a safety on this lift in 2019. If that door is held open while the car is on its way down, the lift decides the building’s on fire. It stops wherever it is, shuts its eyes, and waits for a man with a key. Rein found out with a thermos. Two hours.”

“And the man with the key?”

“Comes at seven. Toomas. He has a bad back.”

The red number says 1. Then the cable sings one long rising note, and stops. Something settles with a sigh between one floor and the next, and the bay goes quiet except for the pipes.

From inside the steel, high up, come three small knocks. Patient, like a man at a neighbour’s door.

“Excuse me?” says a voice in the shaft. It is muffled and perfectly courteous. “Hello? I believe there is something the matter with your lift.”

Pille’s eyes go round with delight. “Oh, he’s lovely,” she breathes. “Run.”

They go down the bay between the cages and in under the first rail of the gallery. Clean sheets hang here in rows from hooks in the ceiling, hundreds of them, delivered at midnight and left to cool before the morning round, and the draught from the dock door at the far end makes them all lean one way together, slowly, like wheat. Ilse runs with one foot in a clog and the other in a wet sock. She is halfway down the second row when she hears the hatch.

A clang, high behind her, the lid of something flung back. Then a boot on a rung, and another, the thin ring of a maintenance ladder inside the shaft. Of course there is a ladder. A lift in a hospital has more ways out than the hospital has. Two feet land on concrete.

Then nothing.

Pille’s hand closes on her sleeve and they stand where they are, in the white, with their mouths shut.

He is in the bay. Ilse knows it the way she would know a stranger in a dark flat, by the shape of the quiet. But where? The cellar is all echo, concrete and pipe, and her good ear is turned toward the dock while the other one is an empty room. Every sound she gets arrives from the right or from nowhere. A man could be at her left shoulder, with his hands held a little in front of him, and she would not know until he coughed.

So she does not listen. She reads. It is what she does with a spectrogram when the loud bright lines are no use: she looks for the shape that does not belong. The sheets all lean toward the dock, all together, lazily. She lets her eyes go soft and travels along the rows.

Third row, to the left and ahead. A run of five sheets leans the other way, one after another, a slow push through the white, as if a hand were parting a curtain.

She does not point. Pointing is noise. She lifts the bundle in both arms and throws it as hard as she can into the deaf side, over the rail and down the next aisle. She does not hear it land. She sees a sheet jump forty feet away, and swing, and hang.

The slow push stops. It stays stopped. Then it turns, rustling, away from them and toward the thump.

“Now,” whispers Pille.

They run. Behind them, a long way back and a little sad, the voice says, “Oh, dear.”

“He’s unwrapped the baby,” says Pille.

“It was cables.”

“It was a lovely baby. I’d got fond.”

The dock door is chest-high and half open, and past it are snow, a ramp, the orange light, and a white van with its lights off and KETT in small letters on the side. The engine is not running. Through the windscreen Ilse sees the hands first: two mustard-coloured gloves on the black wheel, at ten and at two, precisely as the instructor taught them. They do not wave. The side door slides open before they reach it.

“Taavi, lamb,” says Pille, falling in. “You are a prince among men and I will marry you.”

Taavi says nothing. He nods once toward the back seat. He waits until the door has been dragged shut, which takes two tries because of the snow, and then, without lights and without a word, he lets off the handbrake.

The van is Madis’s and it is electric, because Madis likes to be smug at traffic lights. It does not start. It simply begins, along the service road past the clinical-waste cages and the oxygen store, in a silence so complete that Ilse can hear the snow ticking on the roof. Taavi drives at a walking pace with his shoulders up round his ears, his eyes moving from mirror to windscreen to mirror. He is twenty-seven and panics well. He does not panic. He has not made one joke, not a meme, not a bullet point, and the absence of them sits in the van like a fourth passenger.

“Taavi,” says Ilse. “How long have you been—”

One glove lifts from the wheel, a finger raised, and goes back. Wait.

At the end of the service road is the staff barrier, a red-and-white arm with a laundry lorry’s sensor loop cut into the tarmac in front of it. And beside the arm, on the public side, with its engine ticking and its lights out, idles a black Audi. Its plate carries the blue strip and the two letters of a ministry. Exhaust unwinds from its tail into the orange light. Inside, the driver is lit from below by a phone. He is not looking at the barrier. He is looking at a screen.

Taavi does not slow and does not speed up. The arm rises for the van’s weight on the loop. They glide under it, so close to the Audi’s tinted rear window that Ilse could knock on it. In the back seat Pille has stopped breathing. In front, Taavi’s gloves have not moved. The driver does not look up. The Audi stays exactly where it is, ticking, patient, a dark thing that has not yet been told what it is waiting for.

They reach the main road. Taavi switches on the lights. Ilse turns in her seat and looks back at the long block of the hospital, the third floor lit in a row like the decks of a ship, nothing moving in it. Three seconds of dark for the whole floor, and nobody has yet said whose hand is long enough to do that. Seven hundred metres on, Taavi lets out a breath through his nose, one long thin sound, and still says nothing.

It is Pille who breaks. A snort first, then her hand over her mouth, then the laugh itself, the huge laugh Ilse first heard in the corridor six nights ago, a laugh with no floor to it. She laughs until the van rocks, until her bun comes down and the pencil falls into her lap. She says “the lift,” and “Toomas, with his back,” and “the baby,” and cannot go on. Her shoulders shake. She laughs until she is gasping.

Then she stops, quite quickly, as if a tap had been turned. Without looking, she reaches down beside her feet for the empty canvas sack she carried out from the bay under her arm the whole way, which is the most nurse-like thing Ilse has ever seen, and is sick into it, neatly, with her eyes shut.

chapters.title: A Mother in Kopli
chapters.html:
“Aksel!” Her mother stands in the doorway of the flat in her quilted dressing gown, the cord knotted twice, at ten past seven on a Sunday morning, delighted. “Is the car fixed?”

Pille, on the landing, holds the banister and decides to be Aksel. It is easier. Nineteen years of nights have taught her never to argue with a patient about who the patient thinks you are. She is still in the ward fleece and the paper trousers, her hair smells of bleach and warm cotton and something less nice, and the first tram of the morning has shaken the last of the laughter out of her and left a sort of ringing.

“New wing mirror, Mum. Good as new.”

“I told Pille. I said, he sells cars, he’ll know a man.” Salme turns and goes ahead down the hall, small and straight, eighty-three years old, with her chin up the way she has carried it into every room of her life. “She never listens. She’s my husband’s second cousin and she sits in my kitchen eating my biscuits as if she’d bought them. Wipe your feet.”

“I’m Pille, Mum.”

“That’s what I said.”

The hall smells of cabbage and floor polish and a thousand cups of tea. Pille wipes her feet. Her plan, formed in the van and refined on the tram, is modest: to check the dates on her mother’s blood-pressure pills, fill the little plastic week, and sit for ten minutes in the one flat in Kopli where nobody has ever wanted anything from her but company. Then, at the kitchen door, she hears a cup set down on a saucer, very gently, by a man.

“Tarmo’s come,” her mother announces, in the voice of a woman revealing a surprise party. “Look, Tarmo. It’s Aksel. He’s mended the car.”

In her late father’s chair at the kitchen table sits the polite man from the ministry.

His jacket, the colour of toast, hangs over the chair-back. His grey hair is as neat as it was in the ward corridor. Both hands, in their black fingerless gloves, are wrapped round Salme’s good cup, the one with the gold rim, and on the oilcloth in front of him stand the teapot in its knitted cosy, shaped like a hen, and a saucer of pickled herring that has not been touched. He rises as he rose on the ward, to exactly the height at which rising is polite.

“Mrs Rebane. Forgive me. Your mother was kind enough to let me in, and I have been given a part.”

“He’s Tarmo,” says Salme firmly.

“Tarmo was my husband,” Pille tells the kettle. “For six years. He left in 2009 for a woman in Pärnu and a better sofa.”

“Then I gather I am a disappointment,” says the man. “I have done what I could. Leonid Sarapuu. ‘Facilities’ was a little untidy of me.”

Pille stands with her bag on her shoulder and takes her own pulse without touching anything, by watching the second hand of the kitchen clock. A hundred and ten. Quick, regular, nothing to write home about. She left this man in a lift three hours ago, with a rubber wedge and a grin, and he has beaten her to her mother’s kitchen. The thought is so enormous that it comes out of her as something small and domestic.

“Have you eaten?”

“Your mother has been generous with the tea.”

On the stove stands Friday’s pea soup, so thick that a spoon will stand in it unaided. Pille has the lid off and the ladle in her hand before she knows she has decided. It is the oldest answer there is. When the bailiff comes, when the vet comes, when the war comes: soup. She can think of nothing better, and in her experience people who are eating soup are seldom doing anything else. “Sit,” she says. “You’ll have some.”

“That is very kind.”

He sits. She ladles. He eats the way he does everything, upright and unhurried, the spoon moving away from him. Salme puts the saucer of herring in front of him again with a click.

“Tarmo. Herring.”

“Thank you, Mrs Rebane.” He does not touch it. Salme, satisfied, trots off down the hall to look for a hot-water bottle she is certain he left behind in 2009, and the kitchen shrinks to two people and a clock.

“Your pigeons,” says Sarapuu quietly. “On the Wednesday, on your ward. Mr Olesk was a saint with a small car, and you had been feeding some pigeons. I thought about the pigeons for a day and a half. It seemed to me that I owed you something true.” He lays the spoon in the empty bowl, handle at four o’clock. “I have a son in Narva. Roman. He is twenty-six and works for the border service, and every Sunday at noon he rings to tell me that I eat badly. That is all. I would like you to know it.”

“Why?”

“Because you have been told a great many things lately that were not.” His eyes are a pale, clean grey, and his hands, round the gold-rimmed cup, are perfectly steady. “I am not here to frighten you. I would ask only that you not be foolish. There is a small grey recorder, ten euros, of the kind sold by a man with a past. A tall lady has it. I should like it, and I should like to go home afterwards and have no opinion.”

“I don’t know where she is.”

“No.” He seems relieved. “I did not think you would. I thought I would ask in a kitchen. I have been in a great many kitchens this winter, Mrs Rebane. They are the only rooms in a house where people tell the truth. I should like this to be the last one.”

It is, she thinks, the most frightening thing anyone has ever said to her over soup, and he has not raised his voice or moved his hands or said one word she could repeat to a policeman. He has asked for a recorder. He has told her about his son. That is what she keeps coming back to, ladling nothing, with the pot lid in her hand: that the whole of the threat is in how nicely he has asked.

“Tarmo!” Salme is back in the doorway, hot-water bottle held like a trophy. “The herring!”
