Sarapuu looks at the saucer for the length of one breath. Then he picks up a fork, spears a piece, and eats it, the way a man takes medicine from a child, with a faint dignified wince. His eyes water. “Delicious,” he says thickly.

“He never ate it,” Salme tells Pille, with deep satisfaction. “Twelve years. Not once.”

He washes his bowl at the sink. He dries it, and puts it away in the correct cupboard, which he finds without asking. Then he puts on the toast-coloured jacket, and at the kitchen door, with his hat in his hands, he says, “Your mother’s front lock was stiff, Mrs Rebane. I took the liberty. You will find it turns very sweetly now.”

Pille opens her mouth.

“And there is a loose tread on the second landing. The third from the top. You will want to speak to the housing association.” He inclines his head to Salme, as to a duchess. “Mind the step.”

She listens to him go. Slow, even, rubber-soled. At the second landing there is a pause, and she waits for the creak of the loose tread, and it does not come. He has stepped over it. Then the street door sighs, and he is gone.

Pille shuts the flat door and turns the key. It turns like butter. She hates it so much that she has to put her forehead against the wood.

“He’s thinner,” says Salme from the sitting-room doorway. “But he ate the herring, I’ll give him that. Tarmo never ate the herring.”

“Mum, that wasn’t Tarmo.”

Salme considers this with her head on one side, the way she once considered a column of figures at the cooperative. “No,” she agrees. “He had better manners.”

Pille laughs. It comes out wet and high, and she puts her hand over her mouth, and her mother, pleased, pats her arm.

In the sitting room, on the shelf between the wedding photograph and a china cat with a chipped ear, the Pesa stands as it has stood since Christmas, white and fist-sized and polite, its ring of light breathing slowly. The hospital gave one to every staff family, in a box with a bow. Pille carried this one home on the tram and set it up with her own hands, because Salme likes to ask it the time.

“It hums at night, you know,” says Salme, following her eyes. “Quietly. When I can’t sleep. I thought it was your father.”

Pille does not laugh at that. She has been a nurse too long to know whether to believe it, and a daughter too long not to. She crosses the room and takes the plug out of the wall. The ring does not fade. It simply isn’t, like an eye that has been closed.

“Who turned off the pebble?”

“I did, Mum. It was tired.”

Her phone shivers in the fleece pocket. She takes it out.

Nurse Rebane. Following events on Ward 3 at 03:40 and your departure from your post, you are suspended from duty with immediate effect, pending review. You will not attend Harju or access any hospital system. Please return your lanyard by post. E. Vilu, Director.

Pending. The hospital has a great many things pending and is in a hurry about only one of them. She turns the phone face down on the mantelpiece.

“Who writes to you at this hour?”

“A very rude wedding invitation, Mum.”

“Don’t go. They’ll want a present.”

The stone is warm in Pille’s hand, and lighter than she expected. Ilse’s pebble from Bay Four sits behind police tape on Pikk Street. This one came out of a private flat in a box with a bow, and no ward has ever touched it, and nobody can say afterwards that a nurse made it up.

She could give it to someone. That is the thought that comes first, and it comes in the kindest voice. The boy in the gloves would be here with the van in twenty minutes. The tall woman would take it from her on any pavement in Tallinn. She has only to hold out her hands. And she sees, clear as a chart, what it looks like when other people carry it: an old man in a wrongly buttoned vest, who sat an hour in her parents’ lounge with a box of kringel and said call Ilse, and is dead; and a tall woman with one good ear, sliding three floors down a chute in one clog. She let the thing into her ward herself, for fifty euros and a kettle. Everyone since has been carrying the cost of it.

She goes to the hall wardrobe instead. At the back, behind her father’s coat, is the blue quilted baby bag with a duck on it, bought in 2008 for a cousin’s baby and never given, because the cousin moved to Perth and the postage was a scandal. From the kitchen cupboard come the rusks: three packets, because Salme buys one every time she goes to the shop and has forgotten the others for twelve years. From the sofa she takes the grey knitted owl with the wonky ears that the Thursday knitters send home with every staff mother. The stone goes into the bag in a nest of rusks, the cord coiled beside it, the owl sitting on top like a hat. Anybody who looks will see a woman on her way to a baby shower with an unwise amount of biscuit.

The bag goes into a brown paper carrier from the Kopli bakery, one of the hundred in the drawer under the sink. Pille takes the pencil from her bun and writes on the side, in capitals, pressing hard: EVIDENCE. A woman who writes EVIDENCE on a bag has stopped hiding it. Good. She is tired of hiding.

“Aksel,” says her mother at the door, straightening his collar, which is not a collar. “Mind the car.”

“I will, Mum.”

On the second landing she steps over the third tread from the top. Then she steps back and tests it with her toe. It wobbles. He was right. He was right about everything.

The bus stop is outside the bakery, in the thin blue snow of eight o’clock. The bus, when it comes, is the long kind with an accordion in its middle, nearly empty on a Sunday, and it kneels at the kerb with a sigh. The doors fold open. Pille lifts the paper bag onto the top step, and then she does not get on after it. She stands on the pavement with her arms hanging and finds that she has let go. It is the best feeling she has had since September. Her hands are empty. The cold gets into her fingers. Someone else is carrying it now, someone with a ticket and a place to be.

The doors fold shut. The bus kneels, rises, and pulls away, with a paper bag marked EVIDENCE sitting on its top step like a dog left outside a shop.

She watches it go. She sees what she has done. She sees the old man in the vest, and the tall woman with one good ear, as plainly as if they were standing beside her on the kerb, and then Pille Rebane, forty-four years old, with a bad knee and nineteen years of nights, picks up her feet and runs.

“Wait!” She has one arm over her head, the way women have flagged down buses in this city since there were buses, and she is shouting in the voice that has stopped fights in four wards. “Wait! That’s mine!”

chapters.title: Who Else Hears
chapters.html:
“Nine thirty-six,” says Dr Ong. “Out from the rack’s public address. Forty-one seconds, one point nine kilobytes, to a number in Lagos. That is your first reader.”

She is a square on the left-hand screen, in front of a window of rain-bright towers, a glass mug of hot water at her elbow with a thread of steam going up. It is nearly midnight in Singapore. She has not hurried one syllable since the call began. She holds each line of the log up to her camera as if it were a specimen in a jar, and reads it aloud, and does not send it. “Unofficially,” she says again. “I am a woman reading a clock.”

In the den in Telliskivi it is twenty to six on Sunday evening and has been dark for two hours. Frost has grown inward from the corners of the windows. The Mona Lisa on the ceiling looks down on three screens, three time zones, and one cup of tea gone cold since noon in a mug shaped like a cat. Ilse sits on an upturned crate with the notebook on her knee and a pencil behind her good ear. Taavi, in his mustard gloves, types with the speed of a man who has lately learned how much rides on his fingers. On the whiteboard, under ILSE 0, DOG 1, PROVERB 1, he has drawn three boxes and lettered them A, B and C.

“The Lagos address is mine,” says the right-hand screen.

Chidi Abara is in the server room at Kobo Lane because it is Sunday and the building is empty, and he says it is the only place where nobody can tell him to take a day off. He wears an orange shirt. His three phones lie in a row on the desk like a hand of cards. Behind him the racks hum in a cold blue light and, from somewhere beyond the door, comes the indignant voice of a goat.

“Not mine, mine,” he corrects himself. “On my relay. My gateway, you hear me? The pipe a whole country pays its electric bill through. Somebody has been using it as a drainpipe since September. Two thirty-six this morning our time it comes through, and from my gateway it goes on to a wallet. You know who tops up that wallet? Hartmann Edge. First of every month. Same hand that pays for Mei Lin’s rack.”

“Pelican Marine Brokerage,” reads Taavi. “Lagos. Two directors, both lawyers, both born on the same day.”

“Noted,” says Dr Ong.

Ilse writes in the notebook, in her smallest hand: A. Lagos. Pelican. Hartmann pays. “Two buyers,” she says. “Two readers on that rack all autumn. One of them sits in Helsinki in the mornings. Whoever the Lagos one is, he is the other buyer.”

“You say the Directorate like it’s a dirty word,” says Chidi. “I have a guy who says it in his sleep.”

“Nine forty-one,” says Ong. “Helsinki.”

Ilse unfolds page one of the contract from the inside of her coat. She printed it herself, on Friday, on paper, because paper keeps its mouth shut, and it has been folded so long that the creases have gone soft as cloth. Taavi reads out sixteen addresses in a block. Her finger goes down the page and stops. Purchaser One. The Standing Committee on Lawful Access, Secretariat. The same post-box office, the same street. Not a hint of disguise. They did not think anyone would ever check.

“B,” she says.

“Nine fifty-two,” says Ong, and for the first time since the call began she puts down the mug. “This one I do not like. A consumer fibre line. A flat. Block 112, Toa Payoh, fourteenth floor, installed twenty-three days ago in the name of a retired schoolteacher who died in March. The login is Pickering Street.”

“One of the old streets,” says Ilse.

“Sago Lane, Hill Street, Tank Road, and now Pickering. It read Lumi and it left no scratch. I should like to ask the flat a question.” She types. In the small square her face is lit from beneath, and perfectly calm. “Reply. Reply. Reply.” A pause the length of a held note. “Request timed out. Request timed out.” She sits very still. “I have asked the registry. The registry says there is no such line. It was there four seconds ago. I have watched many addresses stop answering, Mr Mägi. I have not before watched one stop having been there.”

“Listener C,” says Taavi, hushed, and writes it on the whiteboard in a box that is already empty.

Ilse writes C in the notebook. She leaves the line beneath it blank. After a moment she adds a question mark so small it could be a speck. Two of the three are customers, men who bought a weapon and have come to see what it carried. The third bought nothing. The third came in by an old street’s name, in the small hours, and watched a baby leave a building, and took its router out of the wall.

“You see?” says Chidi, suddenly loud. “You see this, now?”

He has turned his laptop on the desk, and in the right-hand square the room swings: racks, cold light, a window in a door. “Hold on. Hold on, my guy.” Beyond the glass stand four men in grey shirts with lanyards, a woman with a clipboard, and a seventh figure in a suit and no lanyard at all, who waits at the back with his hands folded. They do not break in. They have a key, and have had it for some time. The first of them says something polite about the Central Bank examination directive and a letter dated Wednesday.

“This is the surprise audit,” Chidi tells the camera, standing up, spreading his arms. “You see how surprised I am. Look, they have parked the bus. Four at the back, nobody’s scoring today.” His voice is a performance, bright and loud, a man whistling past a graveyard, but his eyes have started to go from face to face, counting. The men in grey begin on the racks. One at a time they unplug a unit, ease it out, and coil the cable over the elbow, while the woman writes a label on a strip of tape and reads it back. “You notice they coil? In my country that is a man who has been to a good school.”

His three phones ring. All three, together: the bank, the regulator, the football. The sound fills the little square like a flock of birds, three different tones landing at once. Chidi throws back his head and laughs, a great shout of a laugh. “Everybody loves me today! Ha! Everybody—”

He picks up one phone, and then the second, and then the third. The laugh goes out of him piece by piece. In the cold blue light, his face does something that looks like arithmetic. “It is the same number,” he says, in a voice she has not heard from him. “On all three. That is not a Lagos number. That is not any number I gave to anybody.”

The man in the suit turns his head and looks into the camera. He does not smile. A hand comes down from above and closes the laptop lid, gently, the way you close a door on a sleeping child, and the right-hand screen is black.

For a while nobody in Telliskivi says anything. The frost ticks on the glass. The cat mug goes on being cold.

“Seventeen fifty-four,” says Taavi, who has been timing. He swallows. “We said Pelican at seventeen fifty. Four minutes.”

Four minutes. Nobody gets from the Central Bank’s office to a server room in four minutes on a Sunday. They were already in the car park, with the engine running, waiting for a reason. And someone gave them one. Ilse thinks of the four of them on the call, Ong, Chidi, Taavi, herself, and her eyes go to Taavi’s gloved hands and rest there. She does not believe it. The part of her that believes things puts it down at once. The other part gets up and looks round the room, as she would look round a client’s server cupboard: not for who, but for what has ears.

A bike lamp with a dead battery. A jar of screws. A tin of noodles. And on the shelf above the whiteboard, between the jar and the lamp, a Pesa Mini wearing a hat.

The hat is knitted, in the red and white of a football club she does not know, and it has a bobble. She has looked at it a dozen times since Friday. Her eye filed it with the pot plant and the Mona Lisa, as part of the ordinary mess of a young man’s room. The ring around its base is white, and it breathes.

“Taavi.”

“What?”

“How long has she been on that shelf?”

He follows her eyes, and for a second he does not understand. Then he does. “No. Ilse, no, that’s Susan. She’s a bit. I bought her for the group chat. Two weeks ago, for a joke, the hat’s from a pub in Riga. I never even set her up. She’s not connected to anything.” His voice climbs. “She is on the wi-fi. Madis gives the password to everyone, it’s on a beer mat downstairs.”

“Since?”

“The twenty-second.”

Ilse sits quite still on her crate. Ten minutes and forty seconds of Jaan’s voice, played aloud in this room by a man with a card reader and a space heater: Ilse. I sold it. The names. The token. Helle’s signature. And two grey coats on a stair in Mustamäe, an hour early. She puts that thought down very carefully, like a full cup, and does not pick it up again.

Taavi has gone the colour of porridge. He crosses the room in three steps, takes the plug out of the wall, and holds the stone in both gloves, with the cord hanging and the hat sliding off over the bobble. “Sorry,” he says. “Sorry, Susan. Sorry, Ilse. Sorry. Sorry.” The ring does not fade out. It simply is not there, as a word is not there once it has been rubbed from a board.

“Is there anything else in this room that listens?”

“The laptops are wiped. There’s the card reader.” He hesitates. “Your pockets.”

“What about them?”

“There’s a paper from Bochum.” He wipes his nose on a mustard wrist. “A phone in the next room can hear a cardamom pod crack and tell it from a knuckle. It’s the crunch, it has a fingerprint. I’m not saying anyone has your pods. I’m saying you do a lot of cracking.”

Ilse takes the three pods from her coat. They are the last she has, small, green, papery, each one a small decision she has not yet had to make. She tears a square of foil from the lid of last night’s noodles and wraps them in it, twisting both ends, like a sweet for a funeral. When she puts the twist back in her pocket, it is silent. It has never been so silent.

On the left-hand screen Dr Ong has not moved. Her mug has stopped steaming. The towers behind her go on shining in the rain, a long way off and perfectly bright.

“Mei Lin,” says Ilse. “The stone on this shelf was a Pesa. It has been plugged in since the twenty-second. Everything we have said to you since Friday, and everything you have read tonight, I have to assume has been heard.”

Dr Ong looks into her camera for a long time. Then she folds her hands.

“Noted,” she says, and the call drops.

chapters.title: A Spiral of Peel
chapters.html:
At a quarter past three the Christmas market is taking itself apart. A man in a bobble hat unscrews the plywood roof of a gingerbread house and lays it flat on a pallet. A woman carries a cauldron of mulled wine, still steaming, across the cobbles to a van, one hand under each handle, her face set like a mother’s with a sleeping child. The last strings of lights have come down from the stall roofs and lie in coils on the stones, unlit, and the dusk, which in Tallinn in this week of the year starts in the middle of the afternoon, is being drawn over the Town Hall in grey layers, as a tarpaulin is drawn over a boat.

Marit Soini crosses the square by the long side, along the front of the old pharmacy. She does not look for him. In nineteen years of sea rescue she learned to find a person in water by looking at the water: the swell breaks differently where something is. Here it is the pigeons. They stand about the third bench from the well in a close grey crowd, shoulders touching, all facing one way, as pigeons face only one kind of man.

He has put a newspaper down on the slats for her. That is the first thing she sees. Then his hands.

They are broad in the palm and clean and not large, the hands of someone who has spent years holding out seed to things that were afraid of him, and has had the patience to be right. Between the first finger and thumb of the right one he holds a mandarin. The overcoat is charcoal wool, good, not new. Under it, a pale grey cardigan with a darn at the cuff.

“Mrs Soini. Aleksei Novik. Please.” His voice is soft and very slightly hoarse, the voice of a man who has never needed to be heard from the back of a room. “The slats are cold, so I have put down a newspaper. It is yesterday’s, I am afraid, but the weather has not changed.”

She sits. She sits as she has sat on every bench for nineteen years, feet apart, weight forward, as if the bench might move.

“You sit like a person who has worked on boats,” he says. “They never trust the furniture.”

“Yes.”

“Do you like pigeons?”

“They are honest.”

“That is what I like about them.” He tears the corner off a bread roll in the paper bag on his knee and scatters it, and the whole grey crowd moves as one animal with forty necks. “They have never once asked me what I do. Would you like to throw some?”

“No.”

“Quite right. It is the kind of thing one should do with one’s own hands.” He finds the first edge of the peel with his thumbnail and begins to turn the fruit, slowly, the skin coming away in a single ribbon. “May I tell you what I know about you, to save us both an hour? You may stop me. Nineteen years with the sea rescue at Porkkala. You lost the end of a finger to a mooring line. You like Savo. Eleven years ago, in a dentist’s waiting room in Lappeenranta, you read about a farm near Kallavesi. Thirty-one hectares, eleven of them forest. A barn with a roof that does not leak.”

Marit watches the peel. It is coming off the fruit in an unbroken spiral, a thin bright rope that turns in his fingers and does not part.

“Who told you?”

“Nobody told me. It is the sort of thing one finds, if one looks at a life for long enough. It is not clever. Mostly people want what they looked at in a waiting room.” The ribbon lengthens. “I have a pension fund with a good name and no staff, Mrs Soini. I have a farm, very like yours, presently owned by a company that would be glad to be owned by you. These are small things to me. They are a fraction of what you are owed, by all accounts, for six years. I should like to put both in your name.”

“And?”

“And you would bring me the decoder. A laptop, I think, or a cassette, or a woman. I am not particular.” Segment by segment, now, he takes the fruit apart. “And the nurse would be left alone.”

A pigeon walks across Marit’s boot and looks up at her with an orange eye. She does not move her foot. What she is noticing, with the slow attention that a long rescue gives, is the shape of his sentences. They all go up at the end. Do you like pigeons. May I tell you what I know. And? A threat is a statement. He has made no statement but the weather. He has put down a newspaper and asked her questions, one after another, politely, and every one of them has a place in it where she could put her hand and be bitten.

“And who would you like to be safe?” says Novik.

It is the same voice in which he asked about pigeons. She counts to eleven, the way you count between waves, and says, “The nurse.”

“Of course. Mrs Rebane, who gives soup to people who come into her mother’s kitchen. Leonid says it was pea.” He puts a segment in his mouth and eats it. “She is safe so long as nobody asks the Committee.”

“The Committee has asked.”

“On Thursday,” he agrees. “Rebane, Pille. Harju Children’s, neonatal, nights. Flat on Paldiski mnt, fourth floor. The nurse. Close her. Mr Hint underlines his verbs. He thinks nobody has noticed. You did not answer. You burned the card in the washbasin at the Hotel Tuletorn, and in the small hours of Sunday you told Mr Hint that you would bring her in alive on Monday.” He glances up at the Town Hall clock. “It is Monday. At six Mr Hint will be at the Katajanokka terminal, in the café where he sat with you, in front of a coffee he will not drink. When you do not come, he will ask the Committee again. And do you know what they will say?”

She understands it then, all at once and from below, the way a swimmer understands a roof of ice. Every envelope Hint ever gave her came with its seal whole. A whole seal is what a well-read letter looks like. She has carried the Committee’s orders for six years, and each one was read by this man before it reached her hands.

“No,” says Marit.

“Nor do I,” says Novik gently. “That is the difference between a man who reads paper and a man who writes it.”

He offers her a segment on his open palm. She looks at it. She does not take it.

“Not yet,” she says.

“Not yet is a very good answer to a farm.” He eats the segment himself. “I shall be here until the pigeons tire. And I should tell you, Mrs Soini, since I am telling you things, that I have no quarrel with paper. The list in the lining of your bag, for instance. Eleven names. Everyone should keep a list. I would only keep it somewhere dry.”

Marit stands. The bench gives a small sigh as it loses her weight.

“Thank you for the newspaper.”

“It is yesterday’s,” says Novik, and turns his face up to the last of the light, and takes a second mandarin from his pocket.

She does not hurry. A person who hurries is a person who has been told what to fear. She walks the long side again, past the pharmacy and the shuttered mulled-wine stall, and she does not look back, because she knows what she will see. At the far end of the square, where the last gingerbread stall still has its lamp on, a woman in a man’s camel overcoat leans against a pillar with an unlit cigarette between her fingers and a paper cone of gingerbread hearts she has not touched.

Marit rang her yesterday from the lobby of the Tuletorn. Raud, said the voice, on the second ring, a voice like a gravel path in the rain, and Marit said, I have paper, and the voice said, Slowly, and then, when Marit had said it slowly, Again. Eleven years of December postcards, each with a pencil boathook on the front, and in all that time they have exchanged perhaps four hundred words.

Anneli Raud looks older than the woman Marit pulled out of the Gulf. Her hair, cut like a boy’s, has gone entirely white. She does not say hello. “You look,” she says, “like a woman who has eaten something she shouldn’t.”

Marit takes the tin out of her bag. It is an old tea tin with a stag on the lid, dented at one corner, and it weighs what paper weighs. She slides it into the pocket of the camel coat herself, as she once put a rope into a pair of hands that could not close.

“The Committee’s orders. Six years. Hint’s hand on every page. This month’s are on top. The card with three names: Kantor, Tamm, a nurse.”

“And the strip?”

“At the bottom. Eleven names. Under them a twelfth, which is mine. I was not told to write them. I kept them.”

“What became of them?”

“It is on the strip. Each one has a date.”

Raud’s eyes, small and pale and used to bad news, stay on her face. “Eleven years,” she says, “I have owed you a drink. I don’t think this is the drink.”

“No.”

“They will find you.”

“Yes.”

“The sub-editors will weep, and the lawyers will weep.” Raud tucks the cone of gingerbread under her arm and closes a hand over the tin through the pocket. “Slowly, Marit. Again. Who is the man on the bench?”

“A man who feeds pigeons.”

“I have been to a great many parks,” says Raud, and puts the cigarette in her mouth, and goes.

At the next stall a woman in felt mittens is wrapping slippers in tissue, row on row of grey and cream, each pair stitched with a small red heart. Marit buys a pair she does not want, for twenty euros, and asks whether she may use the telephone, because her own is dead, because it is for a daughter. The woman hands it over without a question. Phones leak. Marit knows it as she knows her own pulse, and any wire that listens to a nurse’s telephone has been listening all week. She will say nine words, then, and hope that the sea is bigger than the wire.

She does not need to look up the number. She read it once, on the duty rota pinned over the linen shelf at Harju, between a roster of Christmas swaps and a notice about herring, and she has never in her life forgotten a number written beside a name.

It rings four times. “Yes?” says a voice, breathless and wary, the voice of a woman who has learned lately to answer a stranger the way she would lift a lid. “Who is this?”

“The old pipes.”

A silence. Then a short delighted intake of breath that travels down a telephone line as plainly as a smile. “I thought so,” says Pille Rebane. “I found your boots.”

“The Nightboat. Cabin 7118. Bring what you took.”

“I’ve got it in a bag with rusks.”

“Good.”

She ends the call. She gives the phone back to the woman in the felt mittens, who has wrapped the slippers in a little extra tissue, and Marit takes them, and thanks her in Estonian, the one language in the square she speaks badly.

At the end of the long side she turns, as she has turned at the end of every rescue of her life, to count what she is leaving. The stalls are down. The lights lie in their coils on the stones. The bench by the well is empty, and a pigeon has taken the place where he sat. On the newspaper where Marit sat herself an hour ago, laid out as neatly as a rope on a deck, lies a mandarin peel in a single unbroken spiral.

chapters.title: The Commits
chapters.html:
The phone in the freezer is still humming.

A man in a paper suit has opened the door and is holding the tin at arm’s length, the way he might hold a bird that has flown into a window. It is Helle’s baking tin with the robin on the lid, and the hum comes out of it in a thin, patient line, an octave under the tune, a refrigerator trying to remember a song. He looks at his colleague. His colleague, who wears blue plastic covers over her shoes so that she will leave nothing of herself in Ilse’s kitchen, which strikes Ilse as a little rich, writes something on a form. The tin goes into a bag the size of a pillowcase. The robin looks out through the plastic.

Ilse sits at her own kitchen table, in her own coat, and watches it go. She came for the wireless card. She told Taavi so at the kerb, in a whisper, and Taavi said it was the worst reason in the world, which it was. The card lives in a bag in the toe of a winter boot at the back of her wardrobe, and the Nightjar laptop is a paperweight without it, and whatever she is going to do with Jaan’s token she cannot do on a machine that has never heard of a network. “Five minutes,” she said. Then the lift opened on the second floor, and on her doormat a man in a paper suit was stooping to put on his overshoes.

Now a technician draws a small bag from the boot. In it is a card the size of a stamp. Ilse watches her reason for being here go into evidence.

“Ms Kantor.” The woman across the table has not stood. She is fifty or so, in a long navy coat she has not taken off, with grey hair cut by someone who respects it and an umbrella, furled, laid across her knees like a rifle. “Kaie Lõhmus, Prosecutor’s Office. I have a warrant with your name in it, spelled correctly. We have been here since half past four. Your freezer has a very loud telephone.”

“It’s a long story.”

“I have all evening,” says Lõhmus, in the voice of someone who does not. “Unlawful access to a computer system. Preparation of an attack upon one. I am obliged to read you the article, so I shall read you the article.”

She reads it. It takes a minute. Around them the paper suits go about the flat with the grave speed of people laying a table for a dinner no one will eat: two laptops out of the wardrobe, a third from under the bed, a stack of drives, the router, a man on a chair unscrewing the smoke alarm. Somebody has opened the baking drawer and is looking into it with great suspicion.

“Pockets, please,” says Lõhmus. “The coat.”

Ilse puts the notebook on the oilcloth. Black cloth, a red thread marking the place. Beside it, from the other pocket, goes the twist of foil. The technician lifts it to the light with a gloved finger and thumb.

“Item fourteen. Three seeds, or pods. In foil.”

“Cardamom,” says Ilse.

“Why in foil?” asks Lõhmus.

“I was told phones can hear me crack them.”

The technician writes it down. Ilse watches the pen go. Reason given for foil: to prevent audio detection. It sounds guilty. It is true, which is the same thing. Lõhmus’s mouth does something that on a less tired face would have been a smile, and then is not.

She slides a tablet across the oilcloth. On it is the plain grey page of a leak site called Daylight, which went up at twenty to six and has been copied to forty mirrors since. A folder tree. A file called kola_patch. A list of commits in small clean type, and on every line her own name, and the year she was twenty-eight.

kola_patch, 14 March 2017. IK: halt if true eighth heard: demo safety. JT: Do not tell anyone how well.

Ilse reads it twice, though she could recite it. She has seen those two lines in exactly one other place in the world, on a grey laptop with a nightjar sticker, in a rucksack that is at this moment on a young man’s back across the road. So the leak has not come from her. It has come from the copy that somebody bought.

“You wrote that,” says Lõhmus. “Demo safety. A demo of what, Ms Kantor? Something that listens to babies?”

“A demo of a bug I wanted fixed.”

“There is more.” Lõhmus turns the tablet. “At eighteen hundred, the Secretariat of the Standing Committee on Lawful Access issued a statement from Helsinki to six news agencies.”

The Committee has identified Ilse Kantor of Tallinn as the principal author of the software known as the Lullaby, and Jaan Tamm, deceased, as her associate. The Committee is cooperating fully with the Estonian authorities and will make no further comment.

Associate. Jaan would have hated the word. He would have tried it aloud, like a man pressing a bruise, and then said something about a stitch in time that meant the opposite.

“I tell you the rest so that you understand the shape of it, not to be unkind,” says Lõhmus. “Mr Abara’s company accounts were frozen in Lagos at four this afternoon, at the request of a body in Helsinki. Mrs Rebane’s director has filed a complaint, and Mrs Rebane is to present herself at Kesklinn at nine tomorrow. It has been a busy day for your acquaintance.”

“And then?”

“And then, Ms Kantor, you come with me.” Lõhmus stands, and with a certain reluctance puts the umbrella under her arm. “You are detained on suspicion. You may have a lawyer. I would suggest the lawyer.”

They take her down by the stairs, a paper suit on either side, because the lift is full of evidence bags. A warm wind has brought rain, the sort that falls as snow and lands as water, and in the courtyard the lamps stand in wet halos. Across the road, at the bus stop, with its side door open and its lights off, is the white van. Beside it stands Taavi.

He has done the one thing she asked him not to. He has taken out a phone, a cheap new one in its jacket of foil, and he is holding it up in both mustard gloves with the blue light on his chin, filming her walk to the car like a boy at a concert. His mouth is open. On his back is the rucksack with the grey laptop in it, and a music box in a bread bag, and a napkin with a stick of plastic inside, and that is the only thing on the entire street that matters.

At the far end of the block, under the last lamp, with its engine ticking and its lights out, waits a black Audi. She knows the plate by now: the blue strip, the two letters of a ministry.

Ilse shakes her head. It is a tiny movement. Taavi does not see.

A man steps out of the Audi’s shadow. Toast-coloured leather, grey hair, a hat in his hand. He crosses the road in a dozen unhurried steps, and none of the paper suits looks up, because a raid makes the street invisible. He comes at Taavi from the left and takes the phone out of his gloves the way one takes a toy from a child in a restaurant: gently, and with no possibility of argument. He lays it on the wet pavement. He considers it. Then, with all the ceremony of a man laying a table, he puts one boot on it.

She sees the tread in the lamplight. A chevron. Size forty-four. She does not hear the glass go. She sees the blue light on Taavi’s chin go out.

“Sorry,” says Sarapuu. She reads it off his mouth. He says it to the phone, or to Taavi, or to her.

Taavi runs. He does not look at the man, or at her. He runs the way an animal runs when the part of it that thinks has been switched off, straight for the van, the rucksack bumping, and Ilse, without any decision at all, says “Go” aloud, quietly, as one tells a dog to sit. “Go, Taavi.”

“Who are you talking to?” asks Lõhmus.

“A friend who has just lost his phone.”

The van door slams. The van, which has no engine to start, begins to move, and slides away from the kerb into the rain with its lights out. The man in the leather jacket does not follow it. He bends, picks the SIM card from among the pieces, puts it in his pocket, and walks back to the Audi, which lights its lamps as he gets in, and goes.

Lõhmus has turned to watch it. “Who was that?”

“A locksmith.”

“Should I be concerned?”

“Yes,” says Ilse.

Lõhmus looks at the tail-lights going away down Peterburi tee, and Ilse sees her read the plate, and sees something in the tired exact face rearrange itself and then settle, carefully, back into place. In this country there are only so many ministries. The prosecutor says nothing at all. She opens the door of a grey Škoda and says, “Priit will drive you. He does not talk,” and shuts it.

Priit does not talk. He is a broad young man in a rain jacket with the hood down, and he drives with both hands on the wheel at exactly the limit, and the radio is off. The rain comes harder on the way to Kesklinn, and the wipers go across the windscreen in their slow arcs, left, right, left. Ilse watches them. Peterburi tee goes by in orange smears, then Ülemiste, then the ring road, then the dark glass of the offices. She has no phone, no notebook, no pods. Her hands have nothing to do. They are, she finds, in her lap, counting.

A double stroke of the wipers takes a second and a half. Sixty-three of them make ninety-four seconds. She counts sixty-three and starts again. Behind her breastbone another count keeps time with it, the one she has carried since the rail trembled against her palm. In the front seat Priit drives. The rain comes. Nobody else in the car is counting. Perhaps nobody else in the country knows what the number is for.

The custody sergeant, a woman with reading glasses on a cord, takes her belt, her bootlaces and the drawstring from her hood, and writes them in a book.

“What’s that?” Ilse says, looking up at the corner of the ceiling above the desk, where a white stone sits in a wire cage.

“Building management. It does the lights and the heating. It doesn’t do anything else.” The sergeant caps her pen. “Don’t mind it.”

The cell is two metres by three: a bench with a mattress as thick as a book, a steel basin, white tile, a blanket the colour of a sticking plaster. The door closes with a sound like a drawer. Ilse sits on the bench, and looks up.

In the ceiling, in a wire cage like a lamp, is another stone. White, fist-sized, polite. A ring of light runs round its base.

As she watches, the ring turns from white to blue.

chapters.title: Holding
chapters.html:
The blue lasts nine seconds. Then it sinks to a small slow amber blink at the base of the stone, the blink of a creature asleep with one eye open, and the ring goes dark.

Ilse puts her back into the corner of the bunk and turns her good ear to the wall. The cell is now on her dead side, a room of white tile and a basin and a ceiling, and the sounds of the building, a radiator ticking, a drunk two cells down explaining something about a boat, reach her only through the wall, through the bone of her skull, thick and warm as bathwater. If the stone hums, she will not hear it. If she does not hear it, she will not flinch. A woman who flinches has told a listener where her ears are.

She sits like that for an hour. She applies Jaan’s rule to everything, the one he taught the firm before the firm had a name: whatever you would not say on a kitchen table, you do not say in a room. She applies it to thoughts as well, which is not required, but a thought kept for long in a room with a stone comes out of the mouth sooner or later, like a hair in the soup. Taavi, the van, the rucksack: not thought. The token: not thought. She thinks about tile. Twice her hand goes to the pocket for the foil twist, and finds the pocket clean, with only the lint in its seams. They have taken the pods. It is odd how much of a hole three small seeds leave. She had meant to crack one when she was sure of the pain, and now she cannot be sure of it.

The ninety-four goes round in her wrists. Thirty-eight times it goes round, and part of a thirty-ninth, and then she loses count to something that is nearly sleep and is not. At the end of the hour the stone is still blinking its one amber eye. Nothing has sung.

When she is as certain as she can be, which is not very, that the stone is only a stone, she puts her forehead against the cold tile and hums the eighth note into the wall.

It is not the tired flat note that sags out of the tune every ninety-four seconds. It is the other, the one on the comb tooth in the music box that Jaan retuned: lower, rounder, a note with its feet on the floor. She plucked it once, on a tram, with the box winding down in her coat, and it lives in her right thumb now, in the small resistance of the tooth, more than it lives in her ear. She hums. It comes out a hair sharp. She tries again, and it is a hair flat. She has one ear to judge by, and for a week she has listened to a bent note, and the true one has been pushed out of her head by the false. The tile takes the sound in and gives nothing back. Overhead the amber blink goes on, steady and untroubled, as if the stone had only heard a woman clear her throat.

A third time. No better. Nothing answers. She had not expected it to. She only wanted to know how far wrong she was, and she knows.

The key turns at ten past one.

“Up,” says a voice she knows. “Come.” Lepik fills the doorway like a wardrobe, in the ear-flap cap, with two paper cups of coffee in one hand and a packet of biscuits in the other. He looks as though he has been awake since Wednesday. He has. “Not the interview room. The stairs.”

The stairs are the fire stairs, between the first floor and the second. There is a window with rain running down it, a landing the size of a table, and a vending machine humming to itself in the corner with a light on its face. Lepik lowers himself to a step and puts his knees up round his ears.

“The only place in the building with no Pesa,” he says. “Nobody could find a socket.” He pushes a cup at her. “Coffee. From the machine, so it is a disgrace. And a biscuit.” He holds up the packet. “From the drawer.”

“The one marked Evidence.”

“Expired evidence.” He eats one. “Your Mrs Kuusk ate three, last time. I counted.”

Ilse sits on the step above him and takes the coffee. It is a disgrace. She drinks it anyway.

“I owe you an apology,” says Lepik, to the biscuit. “I have not worked out for what. It is a large one, so I am starting small.”

“Start with the door.”

“The door.” He shuts his eyes. “No force. I wrote it in the report on the Thursday. A man opened that door with a key. And then a woman arrives with a laptop, and all I can think is, who had the key? Four key rings. You, Kuusk, the boy, Tamm himself. And I looked at the one who was standing on the landing with a laptop. It is what you do. It is a stupid thing to do and it is what you do.”

“It’s what I’d have done.”

“I had Tamm’s bank records this afternoon. From a girl at the bank who did not want her name said, so I shall say only that she wears green. April 2017. One point two million euros, coming in from an account in Vienna. ‘Consulting.’” He says the word like a man putting down something hot. “A firm that owed everybody. By June the loft roof was mended, the wages were paid, the tax was clear. By July the money was gone. Where does a man like Tamm get a million from Vienna for consulting?”

Ilse says nothing. The vending machine hums.

“You know,” says Lepik.

“Yes.”

“You are not going to tell me.”

“Not on a stair. Ask me when you have found out who your superintendent is afraid of.”

“Afraid of.” Lepik takes off the cap and rubs his bald head with the flat of his hand, and puts the cap back. “At six this evening he took me into his office and told me there is a committee on this file and I am not to ask what the committee is. I asked. I have been asking since four. A man who tells you not to ask what a thing is has been told by something that is.” He looks at his biscuit. “I am not sure of anyone any more, Ilse. Not my superintendent. Not the prosecutor. A little, not myself. Is that a thing one can say in a police station?”

“Only on a stair.”

His phone buzzes against his ribs. It buzzes again, and a third time, like a wasp in a coat. He takes it out and reads the screen and says a word in Estonian she has not heard him use, and then, without a word, he turns the phone round and hands it up to her.

THE COMMITTEE’S PAPER. By Anneli Raud. Handwritten orders obtained by this newspaper instruct a courier to “close” the witnesses to the so-called Lullaby breach, among them a night nurse at Harju Children’s Hospital. The orders are in the hand of Ülo Hint, secretary to the Standing Committee on Lawful Access. A list of eleven earlier names, with dates, was kept by the courier herself, who describes herself as “the last pair of hands.”

Below it are photographs of cards. Small upright writing, a thin pencil, the verbs underlined. Kantor, Ilse. Tamm, Jaan. The night nurse. Under the second name, a date: the Tuesday. He was found on the Wednesday. Ilse reads it all the way down, and scrolls, and reads it again. At the bottom is the list. Eleven names, a date after each, and after the dates, in a different hand, short words that she does not look at for long.

“Tuesday,” says Lepik, who is reading upside down. “Tuesday.”

“Who held the pencil on the Wednesday?”

“Nobody in that story says. It would be a very tidy world.” His phone begins to ring, and the name on it is SUPERINTENDENT, and he turns it face down on the step and lets it ring itself out. “I think now I go and find out what that does to a prosecutor.”

“And then?”

“And then,” says Lepik, getting up, a long job, one knee at a time, “there is somebody in Interview Two who says she will speak to nobody unless you are in the room.”

Interview Two has a table, four chairs, and a stone in the ceiling with a yellow label stuck across its ring. OUT OF ORDER, in capitals, in Lepik’s hand. “Ten past one,” he says. “I did it myself.”

Helle is sitting with a plastic folder under her palms.

She looks twenty years older. She wears the orange glasses on their beaded chain and the same cardigan as on Friday, slept in, and her hair is grey at the root for the first time that Ilse has ever seen. There is no lipstick. The skin under her eyes is the colour of weak tea. Beside her sits Saar, the lawyer, a thin man in a raincoat still dark with rain, who rises half an inch for Ilse and sits again. Helle does not say my little firewall. She does not say sit, sit. She looks at Ilse across the table, and goes on looking, and that is all she gives her.

“My client wishes to make a statement under caution,” says Saar. “She understands that she may be charged.”

“Eight payments,” says Helle. Her voice is dry as paper, with nothing sweet left in it. She opens the folder. “Four thousand three hundred Australian dollars each. To the University of Melbourne, for G. Kuusk. Paid from Hartmann Edge Pte, Singapore. Hartmann Edge was funded by Larkspur Holdings, Limassol. Larkspur was funded by Pelican Marine Brokerage, Lagos. When I telephoned Pelican in October and asked for Mr Roos, the Liaison Office answered.” She turns the pages with one finger. “I kept every transfer. I am an office manager.”

Lepik has taken something out of his coat. It is a black cloth notebook with a red thread marking the place, and he should not have it; it should be in a bag in a drawer. He opens it on the table beside the ledger and puts his thick finger on a line in Ilse’s smallest hand. A. Lagos. Pelican. Hartmann pays. Then he moves his finger, one inch, to the ledger. Pelican Marine Brokerage. He doesn’t say anything. For a good while no one in the room says anything, and the stone with the yellow label goes on not listening.

Helle signs the statement. It takes her three pages. At the end of her name, out of long habit, her pen makes a small loop and a curl, a pastry, a kringel, and Saar stares at it, and Lepik looks carefully at the wall.

At twenty to four he comes back with a form. “Prosecutor Lõhmus rang at ten past three,” he says, “which is not a time that people ring with good news. She cannot drop the access charge. It is the law and it is written down. But she will not apply for remand, and she has seen a certain number plate, and she is, I think, making some inquiries of her own.” He puts the form on the table. “Conditions. You stay in Estonia. You report here at nine every morning.”

“Estonia is big.”

“Not that big.” He gives her back her belt, and the laces, and the hood-string. He does not give her the notebook, which goes back into his coat, or the pods. “There is a white van across the street with its engine running. For an hour. A skinny boy in yellow gloves. I sent a constable to ask what he was doing. He said he was warming up.”

“Warming up.”

“I have never seen a van warm up for an hour.”

In the lobby the rain is loud on the glass doors. Helle is standing near the vending machine with Saar, her handbag held in front of her in both hands. She has a small package wrapped in greaseproof paper. As Ilse passes she holds it out. She says nothing at all, and Ilse takes it, and their fingers touch, and Helle’s are cold. The eyes behind the orange glasses stay on hers, steady and dry and unrepentant. Ilse waits for the word. The word does not come. Then the glass doors open on the rain, and across the street a white van sits in the dark with its engine running, and a pair of mustard gloves rises from the wheel in what may be a wave.

“Bullet points,” says Taavi, when she is in. His voice has come back, and it shakes. “One. I am sorry about the phone. Two. I did not use my brain. Three. There are noodles in the back.”

He pulls out into the rain. Ilse unwraps the greaseproof paper on her knee under the dashboard light. On top is a kringel. Under it, folded in four, are pages in a small hand, in green ink: the original ledger, every transfer, every date, which the police do not have and the Committee does not know exists. She turns each sheet to the light. There is no word on any of them. There is no sorry anywhere. Helle does not say it, and it is never going to be said.

She eats the kringel, all of it, while Taavi drives. It is cold, and perfect, and tastes of almonds and long fear.

chapters.title: The Nightboat
chapters.html:
The lie takes Pille three tram stops to build, and she makes it the way she makes a bed on the ward: tight at the corners, with nothing underneath that a patient could feel through the sheet. A baby shower. A niece in Helsinki, first child, due on the twentieth. A tin of kringel from the Kopli bakery, one knitted owl, three packets of rusks. Nobody has ever asked a woman with a baby bag a question she could not answer with her eyes wet.

“What’s the stone?” says the man at the X-ray belt.

He is sixty or so, in a harbour authority jacket cut for a bigger man, and he has plainly been watching bags go through this machine since before it had colours. On his screen the duck bag lies open in orange and green. Rusks, owl, tin. And in the middle, packed round with biscuit, a dense dark oval the size of a fist.

“Teething stone,” says Pille. She has never said the words in her life and they come out like scripture. “You chill them in the fridge. Babies like something cold on the gums.”

“My Kadri had one.” He sends the bag down the rollers with two fingers, as a man hands back a hat. “Congratulations to your niece.”

“I’ll tell her, dear. She’ll be over the moon.”

She goes up the gangway in her father’s fur hat, which smells of pipe tobacco and Kopli rain, with the bag on her arm and her pulse going like a call bell. The Nightboat is thirty years old and looks it. Rust runs down the white flanks from every rail, like mascara after a christening, and someone has taped a cardboard star to the funnel. The crossing is cheap because it happens in the dark, when nobody can use the view. Pille last took it on her honeymoon, to buy a camera and a coat. She spent the night in the cabin with a flannel over her eyes while Tarmo explained the horizon to a bar. She still has the coat.

In her pocket, folded in four, is a summons. Nurse P. Rebane will present herself at Kesklinn at 09:00 on Tuesday. It is set in a typeface that sounds like a door. She has pictured the constable at five past nine, looking at an empty chair, and for the first time since the hum began she feels a step ahead of something instead of being driven in front of it.

The reception desk is on the sixth deck, a low counter under a garland of plastic holly, and the queue for cabin cards winds round a pillar in the shape of a long grumble. The clerk has fox-red hair and the face of a woman who has told two hundred people that the lift is not working. Pille has no card to collect. She is only passing, head down, fur hat low, on her way to the stairs, when she sees the hands.

They are folded on the counter, third from the front. Black. Fingerless. Wool.

Above them, toast-coloured leather and grey hair as neat as a pillowcase. He waits his turn with that courteous attention of his, a man preparing to be sorry. Pille has now had Leonid Sarapuu in a ward corridor, in a service lift and in her mother’s kitchen eating herring. At this rate he will be at her funeral and know where the sandwiches are. He has bought himself a cabin, of course. A man who thinks about a nurse’s mother’s herring thinks about beds.

She does not run, because running is what a woman does who has something to run from. She turns, with the casual swing of someone who has forgotten her purse, and walks into the first thing that offers, which is twenty-six pensioners in crimson scarves.

They stand at the foot of the stairs being counted. A tiny old man with a pitch pipe on a ribbon goes down the ranks touching shoulders, one, two, three, like a priest with a censer, and loses his place at nineteen and begins again. The Nõmme Pensioners’ Chamber Choir, bound for a carol evening at the Estonian House. Pille learns it in four seconds, because the woman next to her has pushed a music folder into her arms.

“You’re the new alto.”

“Contralto,” says Pille. “With a bad knee.”

“We all have bad knees. Stand behind Leida, she’s tall.”

Leida is tall. Pille stands behind her. The choir goes up the stairs in a body, a crimson caterpillar with a conductor for a head, and in the middle of it a woman in a fur hat learns the alto line of a carol she has never heard by following Leida’s elbow. At the foot of the stairs the queue shuffles on. She does not look down. There is a place at the back of her neck that knows exactly where he is, and she gives it nothing.

The lounge on the eighth deck smells of cinnamon buns, diesel and wet wool, which is the smell of any ship, and of beer, which is what this ship is for. On a plywood stage a karaoke machine is murdering a Finnish ballad. The words crawl by on a screen, and the singer, a bearded man in a Father Christmas tie, follows them a bar and a half behind, like someone running for a tram. The choir takes two tables by the window. Pille slides in with her back to the door and the folder held up in front of her face, the way a child holds a menu.

In the black glass, between the reflections of the tinsel, she watches the door behind her. At ten to eleven the toast-coloured jacket comes in with a cabin card between two fingers. He stands at the head of the stairs and does what he did on the ward: counts the exits.

The nearest is across the dance floor. She is working out how a woman of forty-four with a bad knee might cross twelve metres of lino unseen when a hand takes hers.

“Rouva.” It belongs to a very large Finn in a felt hat with reindeer ears, red in the face and as happy as a man who has been to Tallinn for the beer and found it. “Valssi,” he says, and bows so deeply that she fears for the floor.

“Dear, I don’t—”

But he has her. The ballad is in four-four and he waltzes anyway. The horror of it is that he is good. He steers her out between the tables in one slow turn after another, his hand warm in the small of her back like a hot-water bottle, and nobody looks at her twice. They are all looking at him.

“Pentti,” he shouts, tapping his chest. “Kouvola. My wife says, Pentti, go to Tallinn, drink, be ashamed. So.”

“Pille. Nurse.”

“Ah! Nurse!” He is delighted. “I have a hip.”

“Everyone has a hip, dear.”

On the turn, over his elbow, she sees the door again. Sarapuu is working down the wall by the window, not hurrying, and his eyes have stopped on the choir’s table. On the grey fur hat above the empty chair. Of course. She has worn it since the harbour, and a man who counts exits also counts hats. The next turn will bring her face to face with him across eleven metres of floor.

Take what’s in reach, Salme used to say, of everything from handbags to husbands. With one hand Pille whips her father’s hat off and into her coat. With the other she lifts the reindeer ears from Pentti’s head and claps them on in its place. Then the turn arrives, and she meets the pale grey eyes across the lounge with her chin down and her whole forehead under felt, and nothing happens. Nobody in the world looks at a woman in reindeer ears. It is the finest disguise she has ever worn. His glance goes over her and the glad ridiculous room and moves on.

“Rouva!” cries Pentti, hatless, bereft. “My hat!”

“I’ll send a postcard,” says Pille, and lets go, and goes.

She leaves by the swing doors beside the toilets and takes the aft stairs two at a time on her bad knee, which is how she learns how bad.

On the landing of the seventh deck, between a machine that sells toothbrushes and a machine that sells nothing at all, stands a vending machine with a picture of a cheese on it. Her hands are shaking in the fine fast way she has told a hundred relatives is perfectly normal. Shock wants salt and fat; she has said that too. She feeds in coins, presses B4, and the spiral turns, and something falls with the clang of real metal.

It is a tin. On the label a smiling spoon and the word HERNEKEITTO. Pea soup, with a ring-pull, and no stove, and no spoon, and no reason.

“I wanted cheese,” she tells the stairwell. “I got Finland.”

She laughs. It comes out too high and goes on too long, and she stops it with the back of her wrist, because laughter in an empty stairwell is how the other thing begins. Soup. Friday’s soup on her mother’s stove, the man who ate it, the oldest answer in the world. The sea has simply sent her another. She puts the tin in the bag beside the stone. If the polite man finds her, she will offer him dinner. It is the only trick she has.

The corridor on the seventh deck is long and carpeted the colour of a bruise, and the doors go by with their numbers and their small brass eyes. 7101. 7103. Behind one a man snores in the key of the engines. She counts as she walks, because counting is something to do with a mouth, and the mouth, left alone, finds the tune.

She does not notice. It is the only song her mouth knows now: eight notes, the eighth sagging flat, hummed to Ott on Saturday, hummed in the van, hummed into the pillow. She is at 7109 when the bag answers.

One note. Thin and wrong, from under the rusks, at her hip, like a kitten in a sock. Pille stops dead on the bruise-coloured carpet.

She lifts the owl. The stone sits in its nest of biscuit crumbs, and the ring round its base is alive: a thread of white as faint as breath on glass. Ilse told her once, in the van, that the things have a cell inside no bigger than a thumb, so that a smoke alarm can still shout in a power cut. An hour of life, perhaps two, if something wakes them. Something has. A mouth, in a corridor, humming at them.

She does what she would do for any baby that has found its own cry. She swaddles. The rusk packets go round the stone, one, two, three, tight as a bandage; the scarf goes over; the owl settles on top like a hen on a nest, and she presses it down with both hands until the flat note dies into wool and the ring thins to a hair and goes out.

“Our Father,” says Pille, to the bag. It has been thirty years. “Who art...” and nothing else comes. She tries in her own words. “Dear Lord, it’s Rebane, Pille, Harju, nights. I don’t call often. I’d take it as a kindness.”

Nothing answers. In nineteen years of nights she has found the Lord a good listener and a poor correspondent. She walks on with her mouth shut tight.

Cabin 7118 is by the main stairs, as promised, between a fire extinguisher and a door marked CREW. She knocks twice and then once, which means nothing; it is the only knock she knows. The door swings inward under her knuckles, unlatched, on a room the size of a hospital lift. Two bunks. A steel basin. A kettle on a shelf. And on the lower bunk, feet apart and weight forward as if the bed might move, a woman with a grey braid, knitting.

She finishes her row before she looks up. “You are the nurse.”

“And you’re the old pipes.” Pille’s voice has gone high and silly. “I found your boots.”

“Yes.”

“I put them back. Both. I thought, somebody’s mother taught her that heel.”

“Yes,” says the woman, and something happens at the corners of her mouth that is not quite a smile but lies down in the same bed. She sets the sock aside, stands, and pours from the kettle into a tin mug. The tea comes out as black as a bell. There is sugar in it that Pille can feel with her teeth.

“How many?”

“Four.”

“Shock?”

“Yes. Drink.”

Pille drinks. Her hands stop. “You’ve done this before.”

“Nineteen years.”

“Same,” says Pille. “Different end of the pier.”

The woman crosses to the door. She opens it a hand’s width, her left hand flat on the steel edge, and puts her head to the gap and listens up the corridor and down it with her whole body, the way Pille listens to a ward at four in the morning. Pille, who notices hands for a living, notices these. The left is whole, all five, square-nailed, scarred along the thumb. It is the right that stops early: the little finger ends at the first joint, healed clean, an old job well done. The woman checks the corridor with the hand she has more of.

“He’s on the boat,” says Pille. “The polite one. He was in the queue at reception. I danced with a Finn.”

“I know.” The door closes. A bolt goes across. “He bought a cabin.”

“That’s what I thought.”

It is a relief to say it, and the relief comes out of her as a small sound, and the small sound is the tune. She is humming. It is the third time tonight. In the bag at her feet, under the owl and the scarf and three packets of rusks, the stone answers, flat and muffled, a bird in a coat.

The woman does not raise her voice. She sits down on the bunk opposite, takes up the grey sock, and finds her place with a needle.

“Sit down,” she says. “Don’t hum.”

chapters.title: Ice
chapters.html:
The ship slows at ten past midnight, and Marit knows it in her feet before the engines change their note. A long even shudder comes up through the deck, the sound of something heavy being asked to lean on something harder, and out beyond the steel the sea stops being water.

She has sat in 7118 for five nights with a kettle, a sock and a number of things she has not let herself think about. Now she lays the needles down and stands as she has stood on every deck she ever worked, knees soft, weight low. Grey ice. Young, two hands thick, the colour of a dead television. She could draw the plate edges from the sound.

“It is the ice,” she says. “It will be loud. It is only loud.”

The nurse sits on the opposite bunk with the baby bag between her feet and the reindeer hat at last off, her hair standing up in a grey-brown halo, a pencil through the bun like a flag of truce. She has stopped humming. She has stopped doing everything else too, which is worse. In two hours she has not made one joke, and Marit has seen enough of the sea to know what it means when the talkers go quiet.

“He will come here,” Marit says. “Not yet. When the corridors are asleep and the ice is loud. A locksmith likes noise. It does his listening.”

“Then we go.”

“You go. I stay. He must find somebody.”

Pille looks at the left hand lying flat on the blanket. “That is the worst idea I have ever heard.”

“Yes.”

Marit has always known where the lifejackets are, on every vessel she has boarded, as other women know the exits of a cinema. On this deck they are aft of the stairs, behind a steel door with LIFEJACKETS in four languages and a spring catch worn smooth by thirty years of thumbs. The room inside is a wardrobe that someone has walked into. Orange jackets on shelves to the ceiling. A coil of line, a boathook, a green battery lamp in a wire cage, a smell of rubber and old rope and cold. At the back, on a rail, hang the children’s jackets, small and orange and in a row, and behind them is a space the width of a woman.

Pille looks at them. “Like a nursery,” she whispers.

“Sit. Whatever you hear, do not speak.”

“I’ve kept my mouth shut for worse.”

“No,” says Marit, kindly. “You have not.” She takes the swaddled stone from the bag, still faintly warm, and puts it in the nurse’s lap. “Hold it quiet. If it sings, it sings to him.”

The door will not latch. She pulls it to, and it settles a finger’s width open, and swings back as the ship leans, and settles again. She leaves it so. A door that has been shut is a door that has something behind it.

In 7118 the ice reaches the hull. The first scrape comes up from below the waterline, long and rising, a sound like a man shouting one word through a wall, and then another, and the whole ship takes on a slow roll, a lean and a fall, a lean and a fall. Marit sits on the lower bunk with the half-made sock and works the toe. Inside the toe, where nobody will look who has not unpicked a sock, lies a card the size of a stamp. It came on a saucer on Monday morning, under a bellboy’s thumb, and she has not yet decided what it is for.

At ten to one there are three knocks, evenly spaced, the knock of a man who has knocked on a great many doors and been let in by most of them.

He stands in the corridor in the toast-coloured jacket, a canvas roll under one arm, his hat in the other hand. His grey hair is damp. Under the strip lights he looks tired in the way of people who are very good at something they have begun to dislike. “Mrs Soini. I am sorry for the hour.”

“No.”

“No,” he agrees. “I am sorry for what comes after it, which is a different thing.” He looks down. Cabin doors on this class of ship stand eight centimetres proud of the deck, a steel sill against the sea. “Mind the step,” says Sarapuu, softly, to himself as much as to her, and steps over.

She takes the glove from her coat pocket and sets it on the shelf by the kettle. “You dropped this.”

He looks at it for some time. The thumb is darned in grey wool, small even stitches, a woman’s careful work. “Aili,” he says. “She says I am hard on a thumb.” He puts it on, and it fits as a hand fits a hand. “You might have thrown it into the Gulf.”

“I thought I might need to find you.”

“And did you?”

“No. You found me.”

He unrolls the canvas on the lower bunk, beside the sock, and lays his tools in a row on the blanket: a tension wrench, two picks, a flat pry, wire cutters, a torch, a short thin knife with a hooked blade for trimming weatherstrip. He squares them to the edge of the blanket with one finger. It is how a surgeon says he is sorry, in advance, to the table.

“I have been asked three things,” he says. “Where is the nurse. Where is the stone she carries. And at what hour the Committee has called the vote. Today, I should say. It is today now.”

“I do not know the hour.”

“The Colonel says you do. He says Mr Hint is a man who writes things down and forgets he has been seen writing.”

“Not yet,” says Marit.

“Ah.” Sarapuu nods, as at a recipe he has met before. “He said that is what you would say. He said it is a very good answer to a farm.” His eyes pass over the sock and do not stop. “He asked me to tell you the farm still stands.”

So the wire was not smaller than the sea. She gave a cabin number to a stallholder’s telephone, nine words, and it has come down the Gulf after her in a toast-coloured jacket. She notes it as she would note a leak: a thing to be bailed, not wept over.

Sarapuu bends to the sill. When he straightens there is something pale between his finger and thumb. He turns it to the light, and smells it, and she knows before he says it.

“A rusk,” he says. “For babies. Mrs Rebane carries three packets. I think she carries them as other people carry a medal.” He lays the crumb on the blanket beside the knife. “They go out of your door, Mrs Soini, and along the corridor, one at a time, to a door with a lifejacket on it. I have not opened it. I wished to ask first.”

Nineteen years of looking at water, and she has never once looked at what falls from a woman’s bag.

“You were sea rescue,” he says. “A frightened person on a pier: you put them where there is something orange. I would have done the same.” He is rolling the tools back into the canvas, quickly, in reverse order, all but the thin knife, which he does not roll. She watches it go up his sleeve. “I am sorry. Truly. Please stand aside.”

“Leonid.”

It is the first time she has used his name, and it stops him with the roll in one hand. “She is a nurse,” says Marit. “She has a stone and a tin of kringel, and she gave you soup. Go and sit in your cabin.”

“I would like to,” says Sarapuu. “I would like that very much.”

The corridor is empty and lit like a dentist’s. He walks to the lifejacket door without hurrying, and she walks beside him, a little behind, on his left. At the door he puts out his hand and she takes the wrist, thumb on the pulse, as she did in the stairwell at Harju with a sock needle. This time there is no needle. There is only the wrist, and under it a locksmith’s tendons, and she feels him decide, a small flat thing, like a latch dropping.

They go in together. It is not a fight as films make fights; they are not people who would shout. It is quiet and close and ugly, two bodies in a room the size of a wardrobe, with the walls full of orange. The first lurch of the ice takes them both against the shelves and a soft absurd rain of lifejackets comes down, their little whistles on cords. The green lamp swings in its cage. The door swings with it, and bangs, and settles, and bangs. He is strong in the hands, as a man is who has spent thirty years persuading steel, and she is strong in the back, as the sea made her. She sees the thin blade come out of his sleeve and sees that he holds it low and away from her, like a man opening a parcel. He does not want her. He wants the rail at the back, and its small orange people.

She puts her left hand round the blade.

It is a neat cut, almost a letter opened; she feels it as cold across the palm. The ship leans, a long groaning lean, and they go with it, and she throws out her hand to catch the frame, and the door comes back on its hinge with the whole weight of the Gulf in it. There is a small plain sound, like a latch.

Marit does not look. She holds his wrist with her right hand, which has known worse, and kicks his legs from under him on the pitch of the deck, and he goes down among the orange. His head touches the edge of a shelf. He sits, winded, with blood at his hairline and the knife on the floor between them.

“Oh,” says Sarapuu. “Oh, I am so sorry. Your hand.”

Behind the row of small orange jackets there is not a sound. Not a breath, not the crackle of a rusk packet, not the shift of a knee. Marit has listened for the living in the dark for nineteen years, and she knows how a person sounds who is trying not to be one. The sound of it fills the room.

The ice goes on shouting along the hull. How long, she could not say. When the engines come astern and the whole ship shakes, Helsinki arrives in the porthole of the stairwell, low and orange.

Sarapuu has got to his knees. He does not try for the knife. He gathers the other tools instead, the ones that spilled, the wrench, the picks, the torch, and sets them on the lid of a crate in a line, squared to its edge. The thin knife he picks up last, by the blade, and lays at the end of the row.

“That one I used,” he says. “I should like there to be no argument about the others.” He sits down on the crate beside them with his hands on his knees, a cut on his scalp, an expression of great relief. “I think I shall be arrested, Mrs Soini. I have been in a great many kitchens this winter, and I find I would prefer a cell. It is the only quiet room left.”

She leaves him there and goes to find the night mate.

He is a boy of twenty-five with a spotty chin and a torch, and he goes the colour of milk at the sight of her hand. She tells him in Finnish, the language in which she has never been polite. A man in the lifejacket store. A knife. He is not to be hurt; he is waiting. A passenger who must get off first. The boy, to his credit, does not argue. His radio spits.

At half past one the Nightboat noses against the quay at Katajanokka under the sodium lamps, and the gangway comes down, and the Finnish police come up it: two constables in black, and a border guard in green with a face like an unmade bed. They find a man seated on a crate with a cut scalp and his hat on his knee, and in front of him, laid along the lid in order of size, a wrench, two picks, a pry, the cutters, a torch and a short thin knife with a hooked blade. He rises as they come in, to exactly the height at which rising is polite.

“Good evening,” says Sarapuu, in English. “I wish to make a statement. The knife at the end is the one. Forgive the disorder. There was a ship.”

Marit parts the row of small jackets. The nurse is sitting on the floor with the bag at her knee and the stone in her arms, and her lips are white from being held shut. She looks at Marit’s hand and at once the nurse arrives in her face. “Give me that.” The scarf is off the bag and round the palm in five turns, tight, and she lifts the hand above Marit’s heart and holds it there with both of hers. She does not say a word about what is missing from the little finger. Her own hands are quite steady. “Pressure, and up. Don’t look. That wants a surgeon inside the hour.”

“There is an ambulance.”

“Good.”

Marit takes from her pocket a slip of paper, folded once, and puts it in the nurse’s hand. A number, in her upright pencil. “A woman will answer. She will say, Slowly. You say it again. She will find the tall one.”

“Slowly,” says Pille. “Again?”

“Yes.”

“And you?”

“A hospital. I will be quite well.”

Pille lays her free hand over Marit’s right one, on the short finger, and says nothing, which for her is a speech.

Then she goes down the gangway with the other passengers, in her reindeer ears, the duck bag on her arm, through the cold orange light and past the constables, who have a man to look after and do not look at a woman in a funny hat. Marit watches from the rail. She watches the ears go under the first lamp and come out the other side, and the bag swing, and a tin of kringel catch the light like a small moon. The nurse steps from the end of the gangway on to the quay of a country she has never visited, a stone in a nest of rusks against her chest, and goes on walking, and does not turn her head.

Marit stands under the quay lamp with the bandage already red through. She holds her left hand up beside her right and looks at the pair of them. Nine and a half fingers now, she makes it. She was never any good at fractions, only at people.

chapters.title: First Ferry
chapters.html:
By the time the ferry clears the breakwater, Helle’s ledger has been in the lining of Ilse’s coat for two hours. She sewed it in on the floor of the van at half past five, by a bike lamp that Taavi held in his teeth, with a needle from his glove-repair tin and a length of mustard thread: four sheets of green ink, folded small and flat, lying along her ribs so that every breath she takes is measured against them. The scans are on the grey laptop in the rucksack, fed through Madis’s invoice scanner at seventeen seconds a sheet while the shop heater clicked. The paper itself goes where she goes. A heavy coat is a very good lie.

She has bought the ticket in her own name. That was the van’s decision, taken somewhere between the sewing and the noodles: a false name needs a false card, and the only man in Tallinn who sells them does not answer before nine. KANTOR, I., one adult, window. The girl at the counter types it without looking at her face, and the system that could tell the whole Gulf where Ilse is for the next two and a half hours is, at half past seven, still asleep. At nine Inspector Lepik will look at an empty chair. In the room across the corridor, at five past, he will look at another, Pille’s. She hopes he finds a biscuit.

Beyond the bow window the harbour ice is grey, young and two hands thick, and the ferry leans into it and it breaks in plates that tilt and slide and roll along the hull, each one crackling as it goes, like someone walking on a very large bag of crisps. Ilse stands with her right ear to the glass and her left to the room, and feels the whole building shudder in her palm.

“Bullet points,” says Taavi, arriving with two coffees and a paper bag. He has not slept, and it has made him formal. “One, it is a Finnish bun. Two, the Finns put cardamom in it, I asked the girl, she looked at me like I was a tourist. Three, I thought you should be in the vicinity of a pod.”

It is plaited and glazed and the size of a fist. She picks three pods from the crumb with a fingernail, green and papery and a little sticky, and puts them in her pocket, and the pocket is full of something for the first time since Monday. She does not crack one. There is no telephone within ten metres of her. She does not crack one anyway.

“Say it,” she says.

“I keep saying the plan in my head and it sounds like a bad idea in a good accent.”

“And then?”

“And then I stop, because the alternative is Helle’s pastry on a policeman’s table and Jaan on a stair.” He pushes his gloves further up his wrists. “I’m in. I only wanted it on the record that I’m frightened.”

“Noted,” says Ilse, and he looks at her, and almost laughs.

Helsinki at a quarter past ten is blue snow and a low gold sun and trams ringing their bells along the Esplanade. The Hotel Pohjola stands on a corner with a doorman in a long grey coat and a lobby that smells of coffee and floor polish, and its breakfast room is a long white hall in which two hundred people in lanyards are eating rye bread with the concentration of those who must defend a treaty by three. The lanyards say GULF CABLE ACCORD in letters you could read from the door. The clatter of cups comes at Ilse from the left as one grey wall, which her left ear hands straight to the dark, and she crosses the room by faces.

Dr Ong sits at a table by the window in her grey cardigan, with a steel flask the size of a baby’s leg and a glass mug, and a lanyard at her chest that reads TANJONG VAULT, DELEGATE. She does not stand. She lifts the mug an inch.

“You flew,” says Ilse.

“Finnair, ten to six. The seat was acceptable.” Ong pours hot water for Taavi without being asked, which is, Ilse understands, an honour. “Tanjong Vault holds a seat in Hall A for the data sovereignty session. It has been empty since August, because my director dislikes ministers. He believes I am at a cooling-systems fair in Frankfurt.” She slides two blue paper wristbands across the cloth. “Technical staff. A delegate may bring two, when the vendor audit clause applies. The names are written at the registration desk, in marker, by a volunteer who has looked at four hundred faces since eight o’clock and has stopped seeing any of them.”

“Which clause?”

“Fourteen. A delegate may inspect any connected device in the hall.” The mug does not move. “I intend to inspect sixty.”

At ten past eleven the laptop rings, and Chidi arrives in a small square, shouting.

“Can you hear me? I can’t hear me! This is a bad line! It is the line, not me!” He stands on a Lagos pavement in the thin early light, in a lime-green shirt, with a shop shutter behind him and a motorcycle taxi cutting the picture in half. Somewhere off-camera a goat offers its view. “You hear that? Three phones. Since yesterday afternoon, one number, same number, ringing. I have not picked up. My mother says pick up, my lawyer says don’t, the goat says nothing. I put them in a bucket, you hear me? A bucket of ringing. I am walking round Lagos like a church bell in a bucket.”
