“Don’t answer,” says Ilse.

“I am many things, but I am not a fool in a bucket.” He pushes his face at the camera and drops his voice, which in Chidi means that it is merely loud. “Listen. Kobo has until Friday. After Friday I am a man with a nice shirt and a lawyer. You do what you do, you give me the minute. I have four hundred and eleven thousand people who think I sell football shirts. On your minute, I sell something else.”

“Noted,” says Ong.

“She said it! Mei Lin said it!” He points at the sky, as if for a witness. “Play to injury time, you hear me? The ninety-fourth minute is where it is won.” The square goes grey with a flicker of goat.

At half past eleven every lanyard in the breakfast room turns its head, because a woman in a felt hat with reindeer ears has come in carrying a baby bag with a duck on it. She stops in the doorway and takes in the two hundred and the tablecloths and the flag of the Accord on its pole, and says to the nearest waiter, in clear carrying English, “Dear, I’m told there’s rye bread.”

She has the look of a person who has been dragged through a hedge by the ears and then sat on by the hedge. Ilse is on her feet before she has decided to be. She is not a woman who hugs. She gets her right hand onto Pille’s shoulder and leaves it there, and Pille, who is, hugs her round the middle with the whole bag, so that the owl is pressed against the ledger in Ilse’s lining and a rusk breaks.

“A girl with a car,” says Pille into her coat. “Raud’s. I said the number. She said, Slowly. I said it again. I’ve said everything again, I’m very good at it now.”

She unpacks the bag on the white cloth in the order of the crossing: the tin of kringel, the tin of soup (“it was meant to be cheese”), the owl with the wonky ears, three sad packets of rusks, and, in the middle of a scarf, the stone. The ring is dark. Dr Ong lifts it by the cord with two fingers, as she would lift a specimen from a jar, and turns it to the window, and looks for a long time at a small white thing that was once a gift to a nurse’s mother.

“Noted,” she says, very quietly.

Taavi has opened the kringel and is eating one with his eyes shut. Pille watches him do it, and her face does what faces do when they have been brave for ten hours and are asked for something small. “There’s a message,” she says. “Meilahti. Fourth floor, the bed by the window. She says she has a sock for you.” She waits. “I took that for blood loss.”

“What happened to her?” says Ilse.

“A locker door. The end of a finger. A great deal of blood.” Pille’s chin works. “On account of my mother’s biscuit stone, and I’m not making the joke. Somebody else make it.”

Nobody does.

The fourth floor at Meilahti smells of lemon polish and boiled milk. Marit lies in the bed by the window with her left hand in a white club of bandage, propped on two pillows, and her right outside the sheet with its short finger. Her braid is over one shoulder. On the locker a pair of needles lies useless on a paper bag. She watches the three of them come through the door as she might watch a boat come in.

“Yes,” she says. “Sit.”

She tells it in the order of distance, as a rescuer reports a wreck. The pigeons. A newspaper laid on a cold bench. A farm in Savo with a barn that does not leak. A man on a ship with a roll of tools who asked her three things for the Colonel, and asked none of them like a question.

“Where the nurse is,” she says. “What she carries. And the hour.”

“The hour of what?” says Ilse.

“The vote.” Marit’s eyes go to Ilse’s left ear and then, correctly, to the right, and she shifts her head on the pillow to speak to the good side. “The Committee moved it. Sunday night, to be over before a newspaper could wake. Hint put the hour on a card, for me alone, so that I would stand in the right gallery. He does not trust his walls any more. The Colonel has the day and not the hour. He asked it three times in one night and never once as a question. A man who wants one thing very much does not ask for it. He feeds pigeons.”

“What would he do with it?” says Taavi.

“Arrive at the minute. With a laptop, or a cassette, or a woman. And tell six ministers whose children they are.” She tips her chin at the locker. “Under the pillow. A sock.”

It is grey, half made, the needles still in. Ilse turns it inside out and finds the toe, and in the toe a card the size of a stamp, folded four times, in small upright pencil with the verbs underlined.

Tues. Hall A. Press pool in 15:00, out 15:05. Doors close 15:05. Clause nine called 15:10. Gallery, second row. U.H.

She reads it twice. Five minutes of open doors, and ten to the vote. A hall full of everyone who matters, and not one of them able to leave.

“You could have given it to him,” Ilse says.

“Yes.”

“And then?”

“Then I would have a farm.” Marit looks at her bandage. “I have a policeman outside who is twenty years old and brings me tea. It is also very good.”

Dr Ong has borrowed a box of paper clips from the concierge and a floor plan of Hall A from the summit’s delegate pack, and by ten to one they are laid out on a low glass table in the lobby, between a potted palm and a bowl of Christmas oranges. The hall is a long oval. Sixty paper clips ring the ceiling in a pale chain, one every four metres.

“The sponsor’s gift,” says Ong. “Pesa Concert units, set into the cove lights. Wired to one white box in the glass booth at the back. The box is the only door the hall speaks to the speakers through. Hand it a signed release, and it speaks to all sixty at once. Then it telephones Pesa to say a new release is installed, and Pesa’s server, seeing a signature it knows, offers the same letter to every other nest on earth in the hour that follows.”

“Forty thousand,” says Taavi.

“A little over. Noted.”

Ilse puts a finger on the paper clip nearest the booth. “The pumps? The monitors in the wards?”

“On their own board. The speakers sit on the building network. They play and they listen and they do nothing else. Nobody at Harju loses a drip.”

“I would stake an ear on that,” says Ilse.

“You only have one,” says Pille, from the sofa, and it is the first joke she has made since the Nightboat.

Taavi turns up his cuffs. “The sponsor loop. Pesa’s logo goes round on the big screen between sessions, off the same box, with the release notes underneath. Helle typed Thursday’s. We type this one. Three listeners and their addresses. Dr Ong’s logs. The ledger.”

“Hint’s card says the press pool comes in at three,” says Ilse. “We send at three.”

“The speakers take a little under two minutes to accept a letter,” says Ong. “Then they sing the whole tune aloud, up to Jaan’s seventh note, and wait for the eighth. They will wait ninety-four seconds. After that they return to what they were.”

“And I sing.”

“With one ear,” says Pille.

“With the box.” Taavi has opened the rucksack: the music box in its bread bag, seven notes and a bare tooth. And under it, in a pink-stamped bakery napkin, the other thing. He unwraps it on the glass between the oranges and the paper clips and says nothing at all, because it does not need him to.

A plain grey stick of plastic with a gold tongue at one end. It looks like something from a petrol station. It signs once.

Ilse picks it up. It has been against his chest since Friday, under three layers of wool, and it is warm. She closes her fist round it, and it sits there like a pebble taken out of a pocket on a long walk.

chapters.title: Cloakroom
chapters.html:
On the pavement outside the Merikatu Congress Centre, between a flagpole and a police van, Ilse gives away the only thing she owns that matters.

“Left glove,” she says. “Palm.”

“I sewed a pocket.” Taavi has gone the colour of the snow, and his voice stays level as a plate stays level in a waiter’s hand. “At six, in the van, after the ledger. I didn’t know what for. I thought a person should have somewhere to put things.”

“Nobody looks at gloves.”

“Everybody looks at gloves. They think, that boy has a condition.” He slides the grey stick into the lining and closes his fist over it. “Bullet point. If I drop it I will lie down in the road.”

“Then don’t drop it.”

Behind them the Gulf lies grey under a low gold sun, a plate of ice with a bright crack across it where the icebreaker has been. The Congress Centre is a long block of glass and pale granite facing the water, with the flags of the Accord in a row along its front and a banner twice the height of a man: OFFICIAL SOUND PARTNER, and under it, in white on blue, the small round shape of a Pesa, smiling as a stone smiles. Ilse looks at it for the length of one breath. Then she pulls down the navy wool hat that Dr Ong bought in the hotel shop for twenty-two euros, over the white streak, to her eyebrows, and goes in.

The volunteer at registration has a cold and a green marker and writes ANNI PÕLD on the blue wristband without looking up. Anni Põld has had a busy week. On Sunday she was a locum in a borrowed gown; today she is technical staff to a delegate from Singapore. “Welcome to Helsinki,” says the volunteer, to a point beside her head, and snaps the paper round her wrist.

The security frame is the airport kind. Two guards in black watch the belt, and the coats go through it, and Ilse’s goes through in one long dark shape that holds four sheets of Helle’s green handwriting, and nobody blinks, because paper is not a thing that frightens a machine. Taavi follows through the frame with his hands held out from his sides, like a man carrying two bowls of soup. It does not beep. Nobody looks at the gloves.

OUTER GARMENTS MUST BE CHECKED, say the signs, in four languages. The cloakroom is a long room beside the main doors with a counter, a brass bell and rails of hangers running back into the dark like the stacks of a library. The queue is a slow river of dark wool. Ministers hand over their fur hats at the counter as they have handed over everything in their lives, without looking where it goes: a Dane with a hat like a sleeping badger, a Pole in an astrakhan collar, a Swede who surrenders his scarf folded into a flag. A student with a rubber stamp gives each of them a brass disc on a loop of string. The hats go on the shelf above the rail in a long soft row, and the room smells of damp wool and aftershave and, from somewhere near the head of the queue, oranges.

She smelled oranges once on a radiator in a hospital. Ilse turns her right ear to the front.

He is at the counter in a charcoal overcoat worn open over a pale grey cardigan, folding a scarf. He does not look round. He takes his time, as the old do in a bank, and when the student reaches for the overcoat he says something that makes the girl laugh. Then he turns, as if he has remembered something, and walks the length of the queue against the current, with people parting round him as water parts round a post. By the time she thinks to move, he is behind her.

“Ms Kantor. Aleksei Novik. Allow me.”

The hands are on her shoulders before she can answer, broad in the palm and clean and not large, and they lift the coat away from behind, the way a man helps a woman at a restaurant. For a moment his arms take the weight, and a very small pause goes through them. “Heavy,” he says pleasantly. “It is a wet country.”

She turns. He is shorter than she expected, soft in the face, the cardigan darned at one cuff. Up close he smells of wool and oranges. “Do I know you?”

“No. But you have been on my desk for a month. I have read your commits. They are very tidy.” He carries the coat to the counter himself, and the student, seeing a lanyard that says OBSERVER and a voice that has never been refused, gives him a hanger instead of a disc. “Please. I should like to.”

He hangs it with care. Shoulders squared, collar turned, a palm drawn down the sleeve, the way one hangs a thing one expects to want back.

“Did Jaan sleep, at the end?” he asks the coat. “I was told he sat on the stairs. His hip was bad. I hope it was not too uncomfortable.”

“He was dead.”

“Yes. I meant before. It was a long climb.” He lays his hand on the coat’s shoulder, as a man pats a horse. “Does the cold trouble the left ear? Or only the noise?”

“Only the noise.”

“I thought so.” He turns and looks at her, kindly, over the heads of the queue. “Deaf at six, and reading mouths ever since, so that you believe nothing until you have watched it being said. It is why you have been watching my hands since the door.” He holds them up, empty. “They are ordinary hands. I feed pigeons.”

“And then?” says Ilse.

“Ah. And then. The question of an engineer.” Novik seems pleased. “Mine is a smaller one. Who would you like to be safe?”

The queue moves around them. A minister in an astrakhan collar lays a hat on the counter and is given a disc.

“Everyone in that hall,” says Ilse.

“Everyone is a great many people. I find I can manage about four.” He takes a mandarin from the pocket of the cardigan and turns it in his fingers without starting it. “May I tell you three things I know about you, to save us both an hour? You may stop me. The first you have heard. The second is that you count when you are frightened. Your lips have been moving since the pavement. Ninety-four, I think? I should like very much to know what it is for.”

She had not known her mouth was moving. She closes it.

“And the third. You have Jaan’s last gift on you. In the coat, I should say, beside poor Mrs Kuusk’s ledger. A very heavy coat for the weather.” He slides a brass disc across the counter. It says 212. “I shall keep it safe. You will want it afterwards.”

“Afterwards,” says Ilse.

“People generally do.”

She does not look at the door. She does not look at the boy beside the fire notice, who is studying it with the whole of his attention, his left fist closed. She picks up the disc, which is warm from the student’s hand, and walks out into the lobby, and behind her on her right, small and exact, comes the tearing sound of a thumbnail going in under the skin of a mandarin.

The lobby is marble and glass and full of weather. Along the far wall the press move as a single animal with forty cameras, following a minister who walks and talks and does not stop, and in the eddy beside the doors to Hall A stands a thin man in a grey overcoat the colour of the carpet, with pale scrubbed hands. Ülo Hint owns no telephone. He cannot call a guard, or a colleague, or the Committee. He can only look, and he does: at the white streak escaping the hat, at the scar through her eyebrow. His mouth makes the beginning of her name.

He takes a step. A cameraman walks backwards into him. A woman with a boom swings it across his chest, and a minister arrives in a ring of lights with six aides, and by the time the tide has passed there are thirty bodies between them, and the bodies are press, which he has spent six years keeping out of every room he sat in. He cannot cross it. To shout her name here is to say it into forty microphones.

Ilse lifts two fingers to the brim of the hat, as one greets someone across a field, and goes up the stairs.

Hall A is an oval with a ceiling like an upturned boat, and in the cove light that runs round it, one every four metres, sit sixty small white stones. Each wears its ring: white, steady, idle. She has seen a good many of these in her life, on shelves and cots and in a cell, and never so many in a room so large and so quiet. She cannot hear the room. She stands at the back by the glass of the booth and lays her palm against it, as she once laid it on a cot rail, and a thin steady tremor comes up through the pane that is only the air handling. She keeps her hand there anyway.

The booth is a glass cab, like the cab of a crane, with a desk the length of a sofa, and on a shelf above it a white box the size of a bread bin with one blue light. A man in black is eating a rye sandwich over a keyboard. He is Pekka, of Lumo AV; he has been here since five; and he reads the paper that Ong gives him twice, the way a man reads a parking ticket he is not sure is his.

“Clause fourteen,” he says.

“Any connected device in the hall,” says Ong. “I intend to inspect sixty.”

“My boss says do what the delegates ask until three.” He looks at the sandwich. “I am to stay in the booth.”

“You are most welcome,” says Dr Ong, and sets her glass mug down on his desk, on a coaster, and he is lost.

Taavi sets up the grey Nightjar laptop beside the desk and opens it offline. Ong plugs a stick of logs into its side, and the screen fills with two pale lists and a column of cold numbers. The release has a form, like a tax return: a number, 3.2.2, and a field headed REASON, in which the cursor blinks. Thursday’s reason is still there from the old version, in Jaan’s flat capitals. SO THAT SOMEBODY HEARS.

“Change one word,” says Ilse.

Taavi’s gloved fingers do not hesitate over it. SO THAT EVERYBODY HEARS. Under it, line by line, he types the three listeners and their addresses, and the dates, and then three names from the ledger in a column, Hartmann Edge, Larkspur, Pelican, each with the amount that Helle kept, because she is an office manager and kept every transfer.

At half past two the doors at the back of the hall begin to open, and the hall begins to fill. Ministers come first, in dark suits, trailing aides, and sit in the first three rows with their folders squared. Behind them come the delegates in their lanyards, and the interpreters, and a party from a Gulf delegation in white. In the gallery, second row, six men in identical grey take their seats in a line, with one empty chair left at the end. Ilse sees it as she sees everything now, through mouths and shoulders, without a sound. The press pool waits at the doors in a bright restless knot, lenses up, hungry, a flock for the feeding.

Under the gallery, at the aisle seat nearest the side door, a man in a pale cardigan sits with his hands in his lap. He has not looked toward the booth once. In his hands there is a mandarin, and the peel has been started, and a long thin spiral of it hangs down over his knee.

Over the stage door hangs a wall clock with a red second hand. Ilse has timed worse things by worse clocks. She stands behind Taavi’s shoulder with three cardamom pods in her fist, uncracked, and watches the red hand go round, and the thin minute hand creep, and Dr Ong’s mug does not move, and Pekka’s sandwich has stopped halfway to his mouth.

The clock reads 14:58.

chapters.title: The Whole Tune
chapters.html:
At three o’clock exactly the chair taps the microphone, and Ilse, who cannot hear it, sees the whole hall turn its head to the right.

That is how she has learned to hear rooms: by what the heads do. From the glass cab at the back, the oval below is a field of dark shoulders and bright paper, with the photographers crouched in the aisles like men at a river, and the ministers in the first three rows leaning toward their aides. The six grey men in the gallery sit in a line. The seventh chair at the end is still empty. The aisle seat by the side door holds a cardigan and a long unbroken ribbon of peel.

“Doors in five minutes,” says Dr Ong, who is reading the red hand on the wall.

Taavi has taken the grey stick from his left glove. His hand shakes so that the gold tongue chatters against the port, and he says “Sorry, sorry” to the laptop, and puts his other hand over the first, and it goes home.

On the screen a plain grey window opens, in a typeface from 2017. RELEASE 3.2.2. SIGN WITH EMERGENCY TOKEN. THIS KEY WILL BE SPENT. Below it, one button, and a line of small print. She reads the small print because she is Ilse. One signature. No recall.

Jaan’s thumb has been on this button. His thumb has done nothing since the Wednesday. She puts her own over it.

“And then?” says Taavi, very quietly.

She presses.

The token’s light goes from green to amber to nothing. A file appears, 3.2.2.SIGNED. Taavi copies it to a plain stick in two clicks and carries it the length of the booth, ten steps, held out on his open palm like an egg on a spoon, and pushes it into the white box. The blue light turns white. A line crosses the monitor on the desk.

Release 3.2.2 received. Verifying signature.

Pekka stops, with the sandwich halfway. “Is that supposed to be on my screen?”

“Yes,” says Ong.

“I have no release scheduled.”

“No,” says Dr Ong. “You have a delegate.”

Signature valid. Updating 60 of 60 units. 2%.

“What does it do?” says Pekka, to nobody, in the voice of a man who has stopped wanting to know.

“It tells sixty small stones to sing,” says Ong.

“Sing.”

“In tune, I am told.”

Pekka looks at his sandwich. Then he lays it down on its paper, with great care, as a man puts down a thing he would prefer not to be seen holding.

Ilse has watched progress bars for twenty years and has never wanted one to move so badly. It does not move. Below the glass the chair says something long, the pool shuffles into the aisles, and she lays her palm flat on the pane as she once laid it on a cot rail, and the hall breathes against it. 9%. Behind her breastbone the count goes round: ninety-four, ninety-four. 17%. The little white stones in the cove sit and look as stones look. 31%. A man in the third row coughs into his fist and looks at his watch. 48%.

At 63% she feels it in her hand.

Not a sound, at first. A tremor, fine as a hair, then the glass itself taking up a note. She looks up. Round the whole cove, sixty rings that were white and steady have begun to breathe, slow and pale, in and out, all together, like a field of sleepers. Then the hum arrives, and she gets it with her right ear alone, with no direction to it, as weather: a warm front passing over the roof. One note. Then the second. Then the third, climbing, and the fourth, which her mouth has shaped on its own since the first night in the ward, and it is coming from every stone at once, quiet, whole and patient, through a hall built for speeches, into the ears of the people who sign things.

The first minister turns his head. A short grey beard, a man who joked once on the news about having no sleep for a fortnight. Salmivaara does not look at the stage. He looks up at the ceiling, the way a man looks up in his own house when he hears someone singing in a room where he did not leave a radio on.

The chair stops in the middle of a word. Ilse had been reading it off the chair’s lips, distinguished delegates, if I may, and now the lips simply stay open. Two hundred phones come out at once with the clatter of a flock of birds leaving a roof. Heads tip back. Along the front row a woman puts her hand over her mouth, and an interpreter in a glass cab of her own takes off her headset and looks at it as if it had bitten her. The gavel comes down once, from habit, on nothing. Pekka slaps the master fader to zero, and slaps it again, and stares at the desk, and says something in Finnish that Ilse needs no ear to read, because the sound is not coming through his desk. It is coming from the roof. It has been coming from the roof, in other roofs, for a hundred and twenty-five nights.

Five. Six. The seventh, which sags a little, the way it always sags.

Then it stops.

A hall of five hundred people leans for the eighth note, as a foot reaches for a stair that is not there. Ilse sees it in their shoulders. It is a thing she has never seen before: so many bodies waiting at once for the same thing and not knowing what it is. The rings in the cove stay lit, at the top of the breath. Wait.

“Ninety-four seconds,” says Dr Ong.

“Now,” says Taavi, with the music box already in his hand. He holds it to her right ear, the bread bag still crumpled round its base, and plucks the bare tooth with his gloved thumbnail, once.

It rings. Low and round, a note with its feet on the floor. It is in her ear and her jaw and her palm on the pane, and it is the one she hummed a hair sharp, and a hair flat, to the tile of a cell, and it does not matter any more, because she has it now. It is where Jaan left it.

She slides back the hatch in the glass, the small sliding window that lets a technician hear his hall, and the air of the hall comes in, warm, and full of faces. She puts one hand on the frame. She has never sung in front of anyone in her life.

She sings.

It goes out over the ministers’ heads, long, unsupported, uncertain at the start and then not, over the photographers in the aisles and the lenses that swing up like a field of sunflowers, up into the cove where the rings hang at the top of their breath. A single low note. She holds it as long as the air holds, and a little longer, and on her right, from the ceiling, a sound answers it like a door settling into a frame.

The rings go out.

One, then the next, then the next, each half a second behind the last, round the whole oval, like lamps going out down a long street. The hum goes with them. When the last has gone there is a silence in the hall so entire that she can feel it in her left side, where there should be nothing, and in the booth nobody moves at all.

Then someone stands.

A tall, tired man in the second row, with a grey face and a lanyard that says LATVIA. He stands up between his aides as if he did not decide to, and the pool’s cameras swing round to him, and he does not seem to see them. “That is the song at Harju,” he says. His English is careful and carries. “In the ward. Every night at three. My daughter is in Bay Three, she is seventeen days old, and I have been sleeping in the parents’ lounge, and I thought—” He stops. He tries again. “I thought the building was singing to her.”

Nobody says anything. Salmivaara has turned in his seat and is looking at the Latvian, and then at the ceiling, and then, with a movement so slow it is like a man waking, at his own hands.

“Mine too,” says the Finn. “In the nursery, at night, since last week. My wife said it was the radio. I said we do not own a radio.”

On the great screens on either side of the stage the smiling stone dissolves, in the middle of its loop, and white type begins to climb the blue.

RELEASE 3.2.2. REASON: so that everybody hears.

LISTENER A. Relay, Lagos. Pelican Marine Brokerage. Paid by Hartmann Edge Pte, funded by Larkspur Holdings. Customer: Liaison Office, the Directorate.

LISTENER B. Helsinki. Secretariat, Standing Committee on Lawful Access.

LISTENER C. Unknown.

The pool is on its feet. Ilse reads the questions off a hundred mouths in six languages, and they are all the same question. Who? Who did this? Cameras swing from the screens to the ministers and back, and the ministers, who are used to being asked what they intend, find that they have been asked something else. Behind them a steward in a dark suit is talking into his sleeve.

In the gallery the second row does not move. Six grey men look at the screens as men look at a bill, and not one of them stands. Then one of them does, a heavy man at the end of the line, and takes three steps toward the stairs, and the steward at the gallery door shakes his head, once, politely, because it is five past three and the doors are shut. At the back of the hall the great doors close on their slow arms, and beyond the narrowing glass a thin figure in a grey overcoat arrives, too late, and puts both hands flat on the pane like a boy at an aquarium.

Down by the side door the aisle seat is empty. A man in a pale cardigan is walking out beneath the gallery, unhurried, as if he has remembered an appointment, with a mandarin in his hand and his thumbnail in under the peel. It comes away in one spiral. At the door he turns his head and looks up the whole length of the hall to the glass cab, to her, and inclines it, a very little, as one acknowledges a good move at a board. Then the door closes on its arm, and a thin bright rope of peel lies on the carpet where he went.

Two men in black are coming up the aisle toward the booth. They are not running. Pekka sits with both hands flat on the desk, like a man at a séance. Taavi has taken Ilse’s sleeve in his glove, the one with the empty pocket, and he does not say sorry, which for Taavi is the same as a speech.

“Forty-one thousand, two hundred and six,” says Ong, reading the monitor. “And counting. All acknowledging.” Her mug is a little to the left of where it was. “Noted.”

Ilse looks at the list as it scrolls: every kitchen, every nursery, every bay of every ward, one small white ring after another going dark. She has done a thing. It has a size. It will be written down.

And then, in the column beside the others, among the long run of identical lines, there is one that does not belong. Taavi sees it a half-second after she does. “That’s not a Pesa,” he says. “They don’t send text.”

No. It has come from an address the console does not know, and it has no name. It has been signed with nothing. It is a single line, in lower case, in a field headed note, which no Pesa has ever filled in.

chapters.title: The Last Pin
chapters.html:
The thaw comes on a Thursday. Water runs everywhere in Tallinn. It comes off the eaves in Pelgulinna in long bright ropes, and drums on the lids of bins, and races ankle-deep along the gutters toward the drains with a sound like a very small crowd applauding, and Ilse, who has spent three weeks learning what her right ear can do, hears all of it. She walks to the hospital. A tram would be a room, and she has the time. The prosecutor has given her little else.

Kaie Lõhmus read her the article again on the Monday after the summit, in a room with a window, with the umbrella across her knees. One count. Unauthorised access to a computer system, by means of a release signed on a Tuesday afternoon in Helsinki, in the presence of five hundred witnesses and forty cameras. “It is the law, and it is written down,” said Lõhmus. “The rest of it is also written down now. In a good many places.” Trial in March. A passport in a drawer. Nine o’clock on Fridays at Kesklinn, where Lepik gives her a biscuit from the drawer marked Evidence and tells her nothing, loudly.

Other things she knows by heart, because Taavi reads them aloud to her off the news. Ülo Hint resigned by letter, in pencil, on the Wednesday, and the Committee has paused itself, which is what committees do instead of dying. In Singapore Dr Ong has sworn to what she saw before a judge who writes with a fountain pen. Chidi is on every channel he owns. In a Finnish cell a man called Sarapuu is said to have asked for a duster. Helle is in Haapsalu with her sister and has been seen at a bakery counter, buying nothing, reading the labels. And of the man with the mandarin there is no word, because the country he serves has never been named, and says nothing, which is what it does.

The doors of the third floor open on quiet. It is not the quiet of a Monday night in December. It is the quiet of a room from which something has been taken. Ilse stands at the end of the corridor with her good ear to the ward and her deaf side to the glass, as she stood once, and waits for a number she cannot hear, and there is no number. The shelves are bare. On each one, in the dust, a pale circle the size of a fist shows where a stone sat. The knitted owls remain. All seventy-one are still in their rows, with their wonky ears and their button eyes, looking at the empty circles with an air of having expected this.

“I keep checking the shelves,” says Pille, behind her. “Three weeks. I go round at three in the morning with my head on one side, listening for it, like a woman who has stopped smoking and keeps patting her pocket. Dead is very quiet, dear. This is just empty.” She comes up on Ilse’s right, where she has learned to stand. “Look who’s escaped.”

She is in the green fleece, with the pencil through the bun and her hands smelling of chlorhexidine, and she has put on a stone in the weeks since the Nightboat, or lost one, Ilse cannot tell which. The Director who suspended her has gone to spend time with a solicitor. The Director who has replaced her reinstated Pille on a Tuesday morning by sending a bunch of tulips with a card that said sorry in capital letters and was signed twice. Evald Olesk is on leave, in a sense that will take some time to explain. Pille takes Ilse’s elbow and steers her down the corridor to the milk kitchen as if returning a patient.

“I’ve got something. Shut your eyes.”

“I can’t hear with my eyes shut.”

“Then open them and be quick.”

It is a Kopli bakery bag. Someone has crossed out EVIDENCE across the side in thick pencil and written under it, in the same hand, PRESENT. Inside is a box of pale birch the size of a loaf of rye, with a darker owl inlaid on the lid, and when Ilse lifts the lid she sees steel and brass: a comb, a cylinder, and a spiral of pins. She counts without meaning to. Eight.

“A Mr Pihlak, in Pärnu,” says Pille. “Nine days. Taavi gave him the recording from the hall, and he tuned the last tooth against it with a fork. I thought it was time Pärnu did something for me.” She sniffs. “Tarmo’s sofa is there.”

Ilse winds the key. The cylinder turns and the comb takes up the tune, one, two, three, bright and small in the milk-kitchen air, up through seven, and then the eighth, round and low, a note with its feet on the floor. It does not sag. She holds the box to her right ear and listens to it all the way down, and when it has run out she goes on holding it.

“Hold this,” says Pille, and puts a baby in her arms.

She does it the way she does everything, quickly and without warning, from the Bay Four crib that has no shelf above it. Swaddled tight, in a striped hat. A girl, nine days old, nineteen hundred and eighty grams, with a mouth like a rosebud under a hand. Ilse has not held a baby since she was a child herself. She stands with her elbows wrong and her heart going, and the baby gives a small damp sigh against the wool of her sleeve, and Ilse hears herself humming.

She hasn’t been asked to. It is only the tune, low, in the back of the throat, the way a person hums over a sink. One. Two. Three. All eight. The baby’s fist opens against her wrist and does not close.

“There,” says Pille, very softly. “That’s the end of that.”

Taavi is waiting in the lobby when she comes down, with a Thermos and a face that has been up since five. “Soup,” he says. “Pea. For Pille’s night. I thought, soup, it’s the oldest answer.” He sits on the radiator and the Thermos steams between his gloves. “Bullet points. One, I sleep with my phone in the bathroom now, under a towel, with the tap dripping. It’s not that I think it’s listening. It’s that I think it might be thinking about it. Two, Raud rang.”

“And?”

“She says your Courier has a job.” He has never once, in three weeks, said Marit’s name. “Mending nets, on Kallavesi, for a man with a smokehouse. No stairs, she said. She sent Pille socks. Grey, with a note, three words, I wasn’t told which.”

Ilse says nothing. In her coat pocket, behind the foil twist that the prosecutor’s office returned to her in a clear bag with a form, lies a postcard Raud sent over on the Monday. A pencil boathook on the front. Blank on the back. She turns it over with her thumb. One does not know, she thinks, how to write to a woman who kept a list of eleven names, and lost the end of a finger for the twelfth. She has not decided. She has until March.

At four the parents come for Ott.

He goes down the corridor in a car seat the size of a bread bin, held in front of his father with both hands like a crown, a tall man in a jacket that still has the shop fold in it. Two thousand four hundred and ten grams. Off everything. His mother walks behind with the bag, and in the seat beside him, with its ears at two different angles, sits the grey owl with the wonky ears that went to Helsinki and came back.

“Right,” says Pille, planted in the middle of the corridor, with her arms folded across her chest like a woman barring a door. “Instructions. Feed him. Burp him. Keep him away from any woman with a bag of rusks. If anyone offers to fix your lock, say thank you and use the window.” The father laughs, uncertain. The mother takes her hand. “And you’ll write. A card. A photograph. Nothing with a speaker in it.”

“We will,” says the mother.

“And he’s to have his jabs on time, he’s a good boy, he’s the best boy on the ward, he’s—” Pille’s chin goes. She says, “Oh, dear,” in quite a different voice, and puts the back of her wrist against her mouth, and the tears come at once and in a rush, like a tap that has been stiff for years. The mother puts an arm around her. Ott, in his seat, regards the ceiling. Nobody in the corridor says anything for a while. Ilse stands with the box in her pocket and her good ear to the whole of it.

Then the lift doors close on the three of them, and the corridor is empty.

She goes to the window at the end of the ward. It faces west, over the roofs of Pelgulinna, and the thaw has turned them all to a dark wet shine, and the gutters pour, and out beyond the last block, small and silver under a low sun, the sea has lost its ice at the edges. She stands with her hands on the sill. She hears the water, and a gull, and her own breath, and in all of it, for the first time in months, no machine.

It does not feel as she had thought. It feels like the quiet after a long note. She takes a pod from her pocket, the first she has dared to crack since Monday week, and cracks it in her teeth, aloud, with nobody and nothing to hear. The seed bursts bright and bitter. Somewhere there is a listener who has not been named. A third kind of reader, who came in by the name of an old street, who watched a child leave a building, who answered a hall with a line of lower-case text and then went quiet. They may be listening still. They may be listening now, through the glass, to a woman at a window eating a spice.

“Kurat,” says Ilse, mildly, to the sea.

And a note sounds on her right.

It is not loud. It comes from the corridor behind the lift lobby, a hall she cannot see, round the corner: a woman’s voice, low, a hum over a baby’s head as the lift waits. Ott’s mother. One. Two. Three. The tune is the one that every kitchen in Europe has learned this month, off every screen: seven notes, up the stair, and then the stair stops. The voice reaches the seventh, and hangs, and does not know the rest.

Ilse puts down the pod. She turns her right ear to the corridor and opens her mouth, and supplies the eighth note, aloud, low and round, and lets it ring.
